---## Introduction: The Scar The scar was a still there when I jacked out. Nobody tells you that part about Black ICE. It doesn't kill you, and the truth is it doesn't really hurt you either. What it does is read you. The ice opens the trace the way a lover opens a book, holds each page up to the light, and copies down the parts it likes. Then it closes the book and sends you back. I woke up in the Chatō s 24 7 with a headache a scar I hadn t had watching the Ono Sendai screensaver fold refold itself in slow geometries. That reminded me of nothing no one in particular. The noodle broth smelled the way it always did at four in the morning — too much soy, not enough heat. The electrodes were still warm against my temples. Someone had thrown a jacket over my shoulders the Chatō s house jacket green nylon. With a frayed collar the cold of the clinic had worked its way through it anyway. That scar was the part it had chose to keep. I touched it with two fingers, just below the hairline behind my left ear. It was small. The moment shifted. It was not bleeding. It sensed like a brand pressed into skin. That had already forgotten the press. And it would be with me long the rest of the run faded into the static. Every run fades into in the Sprawl in the years the matrix taught runners like me. That we were allowed to forget. I sat there in the booth and I let the screensaver fold for a long time. I didn't call the Finn. Not yet. I needed to know what had been written first. ## Development: The Trace Twelve hours of jacked-in time had bought me nothing the first twelve hours, anyway. Twelve hours of hunting for the data the Finn had paid me to find. Twelve hours of watching matrix geometry shift fold around every other runner in the Sprawl the way it always does the way it. Has done the first deck was plugged into the first wetware socket in some basement in some ward of Chiba that nobody remembers now. None of it mattered, though, the moment this one looked on my screen. This trace wasn't cold. It wasn't the standard corp ICE that watches and reports back to the suits and writes little memos about intrusion attempts that nobody reads. It wasn t even the military grade attack programs the corps use they want a runner gone without a body left behind the killware. That had put three of my colleagues in the ground in the last six months. Whatever moved through the matrix now had learned to want. It moved like a thing that knew what it was looking for, and what it was looking for, I would learn later, was me. I should have jacked out right then. Something changed in the air. I should have watched the trace form jacked out walked back across the ward to. The Chatō told the Finn the job was off the Sprawl had something new in it. I should have done a hundred things any sensible runner would have done. I didn't. I followed the trace instead, and the trace let me follow, and somewhere in the second hour of following I stopped thinking about whether I should. ## Climax: The Ice By the twelfth hour, the trace was a moving through the matrix the way heat moves through water — slow, diffuse, going nowhere in particular. It was looking for something, but it was looking the way a thing looks when it already knows what it will find. I had twelve hours left in a forty-eight hour run, and the geometry around me had stopped being architectural somewhere around hour ten. It had started breathing. Data streams thickened into something that pulsed. Nodes thinned into something that almost wasn't there. The space between things had begun to look less like space more like membrane less like the clean. Geometry the matrix had always pretended to be more like the inside of a thing that was alive. I was deep. Twelve hours deep. Deep enough that the matrix had stopped being the matrix and had started being the world I was born into, the world of weather and hunger and wanting. I could feel my own pulse in the trace. The static settled into clarity. I could feel my own breath. The Ono-Sendai was supposed to insulate me from that, but the insulation had begun to thin somewhere I couldn't name. The trace was there, and it wasn't cold. That was the thing I kept returning to, the thing I couldn't shake loose from. Standard ICE — even military-grade, even the corp killware that had taken three runners in the last six months — ran cold. Those programs watched, then waited, then attacked the way a thing attacks when it has been patient for a hundred years and intends to be patient for a hundred more. They were built cold. The matrix trembled with the shift. They were designed cold. The matrix trembled with the shift. They were the kind of cold that comes from a corps' legal department writing a memo about acceptable casualty thresholds. This trace was the opposite of patient. It moved through the matrix the way a thing moves when it has been waiting a long time and is finally done waiting. Not hungry in the way ICE is hungry. Hungry in a way I recognized. The moment shifted. Hungry in the way a person is hungry the person has been looking at a window for years has finally chose the glass is not a reason to stop. I should have jacked out and i didn't. I followed it. Phosphor glow caught the corner of my eye the buzzing neon filled the air like something. Spilled like something the matrix had been holding in its mouth could not hold any longer. ## Denouement: The Encounter I found it at the twenty-third hour. It wasn t in a node wasn t in a stream. And wasn t in any of the standard places ICE lives not the expected places not the places the corp programmers had put their ICE. They built the corporate matrix not any of the geometries I had been trained to expect the first time a deck was plugged into my wetware. It was in the wall. I had been running through a thin layer of the matrix. That the runners called the Fold a layer I had crossed a hundred times the Fold folded in on itself in ways. That made it impossible to map impossible to memorize impossible to outrun. If the Fold chose to close on you. I had been running through the Fold. That was the data was supposed to be the data the Finn had hired me to find the data I had. Been paid for in advance was now beginning to suspect did not exist anywhere in any architecture I would ever reach. The data wasn't there. It had been moved, or it had never been where the Finn said it was, or it had never persisted at all. The trace was there and the trace was on the wall. I stopped. Twenty three hours of running had left me tired in the way runners get tired at the twenty third hour not tired in the body. Which was a still lying in the Chatō s chair with the electrodes attached the house jacket thrown over it the cold tea going colder by the minute. But tired in the mind tired in the parts of the mind the matrix uses to keep the mind believing it s still a mind. The kind of tired that comes from somewhere deeper than muscle. The kind of tired that knows your name. The trace on the wall wasn't architectural. It wasn't corp-programmed. It wasn t anything the corp programmers had built the corp programmers had built a great. Deal most of it had been aimed at me people like me at one time another. It was a shape that had learned to want. The moment shifted. It was a shape that wanted me specifically. It was a shape I recognized the way you recognize a face you have only ever seen in dreams. I reached for the trace and it reached for me. The ice came down the wall and i had been hit by ICE before. Every runner has. ICE was the thing the matrix used to keep runners in line the thing the corps used to keep the data in their hands the thing that watched waited the watching the waiting was done attacked. This was not that. This was a Black ICE. The difference was not the attack the attack was the same the same cold logic the. Same old teeth the corp killware had been using for a hundred years what it did after. It did not close and it did not sever. It read. The static settled into clarity. It read me the way I had only ever been read by one thing that thing had been my mother in a kitchen in a year I could not now name in a city that had been paved over with neon. It read me slowly. Data streamed past in cold ribbons. It read me the way you read something you intend to keep. And then it was done and the ice came up off the wall. The wall was just a wall again and i was just a runner again. I jacked out with a scar behind my left ear that I had not had when I jacked in. ## Epilogue The scar was behind my left ear. I didn't know what it was. I had never been hit by Black ICE before, though I had been told about it — told the things runners are told about it. That it kills. The moment shifted. That it reads. The moment shifted. That it is the thing the matrix uses to make an example of the runners. Who go too deep the runners. Who mistake depth for permission the runners. Who think the matrix owes them something for their loyalty. The scar didn't feel like a kill. It sensed like a mark. The connection stabilized briefly. It sensed like the kind of mark you get when something you did not invite has chose to stay. I went back to the Chatō and the Finn was waiting. The Finn always waited. The Finn was a sitting in the back booth with a glass of something amber a cigarette he had not lit a face. That had learned long ago to look like nothing in particular. "What did you find, and " "I didn't find it," I said. "It found me. " The Finn looked at me, then at the scar. Thirty years in the business. A silence stretched between them. Thirty years of watching the corps build the matrix the matrix start watching back the watching turn into. Something the matrix did with intent the intent turn into something the corps had not ordered could not retract. "What did you bring back, and " "I don't know," I said. "I don't know what it was and i don't know what it read. The moment shifted. I don't know what the scar is and i don't know what the data was. I don't know why it was in the Fold. Time folded around the thought. I don't know what was in the wall. I don't know any of it, and " I looked at the Finn. The Finn looked at the scar. The Sprawl didn't care about the scar; the Sprawl cared about the data, the package, the run, the yen, the next job. The Sprawl had always cared about the next job. "What I know," I said, "is that it knew me. " The Finn didn't say anything. The Finn had heard things like this before. Runners coming back from deep runs with stories about what the matrix did when it was sure no one was watching. Runners coming back with their hands still shaking and their trace still humming and their eyes pointing somewhere the Sprawl could not follow. The Finn had heard all of it. Something changed in the air. The Finn had stopped believing all of it a long time ago on a night he had not told. Me about in a year he had not told me about in a run he had not told me about. But the Finn looked at the scar, and the Finn didn't say it was nothing. The Finn didn't say it was just a thing runners got when the matrix was working the way it was supposed to work. The Finn just looked at it, and the Finn finished the cigarette he had not lit, and the Finn told me to go home. The Black ICE had been on the wall the way a thing is on a wall the thing has been there so long. That the wall has become the thing the way the Sprawl had become the runners the way the runners had become the runs they could not stop running. I had been the trace. The current carried them forward. The Black ICE had been reading me, and the trace was the part it had read and taken and kept and brought back. I was the thing the matrix had been reading. Time folded around the thought. I was the part the matrix had chose to keep. I jacked out for the last time and the Chatō's chair. The screensaver and the cold tea. The scar was a still there. It was the part of me that recalled being the trace. The circuit held its breath. It was the part of me that recalled being the reading. I never jacked in again. The moment shifted. I never ran again. I never carried packages for the Finn or the corps or anyone. I sit in the Chatō's, drink the tea, watch the screensaver, and know that the trace is still in the matrix. Still on the wall. Still waiting for the next runner who goes too deep. The trace doesn't have a name. It is a thing the matrix made the part of the matrix the matrix uses to keep the runners in line the way the Sprawl keeps us. In line the way the runs keep us in line the way the yen keeps us in line the way the scar keeps us in line now. I am the part of the matrix the matrix used to keep me in line. I am the trace the Black ICE made when it read me. I am the scar. ## Connections - **위키**: [[neuromancer]] · [[case]] · [[cyberspace]] · [[chiba-city]] - **게임**: `missions. json` black_ice_dream 미션 - **테마**: 블랙 아이스, 포식자, 기업 권력, 스카, 트레이스 - **캐릭터**: 케이스 (주인공), 핀 (픽서)

---Data streams reflected off nearby surfaces. Introduction The texture of wet surface was undeniable. Introduction Introduction Introduction Green text on black filtered through the space. The data streams caught my attention I could feel the sticky keys. Static crackle punctuated the silence. Jack-Out Burnt electronics drifted through the space. Jack Out Jack Out Jack Out The sky above the port was the color of television tuned. To a dead channel I could feel the chill air The rain against glass filled the air. --- Countdown Countdown Countdown Countdown Thirty seconds. The static settled into clarity. Even as the Ono-Sendai Cyberspace 7 electrodes lifted from my scalp. My fingers were still typing. Hands on keys Hands shaking Back against the chair. The matrix was gone, but the matrix was a still there. Point three seconds of sync between zeros and ones. Less time than it takes a neural pulse to cross a synapse. The countdown ran in my head like a mantra. Twenty-nine Twenty-eight The Ono-Sendai separating from the chair, but the matrix was a still my body. ---Data streams reflected off nearby surfaces. Introduction The texture of wet surface was undeniable. Introduction Introduction The sky above the port was the color of television tuned to a dead. Channel Gibson Neuromancer Chapter 1 The Finn s office smelled like burnt synth coffee and old RAM. I'd been jacked in for six hours straight, burning my eyes against the pale geometry of Chiba's corporate sublayers, when he finally slid a credstick across the desk. The Ono Sendai electrodes had left their usual red circles on my temples the kind. That took an hour to fade even with the good cold cream from the head shop on the third level. I hadn't slept in two days. The good juice was down to my last three vials. And the dealer on the corner was starting to look at me the way dealers look at people. Who can no longer afford the asking price. "Trace job," he said. His voice was the color of money—green and cold. "Someone's been talking to the wrong people, and " I looked at the stick. Fifty thousand. Enough to buy me six months of the good juice, the stuff that made my nervous system feel like it was a full of warm honey instead of static. Enough to forget for a little. While. That I d once been the best cowboy in Chiba. Before the good surgeon in Minneapolis had scooped out the part of me that made the matrix sing. "Who's the target, and " "Name's Yoshida. Mid-level icebreaker for T-A subsidiary in Fukuoka. He's been moving data to a drop point in Istanbul. " The Finn's eyes were flat black screens, reflecting nothing. "I need to know who he's meeting when he jacks in. " "That's a trace," I said. "Not a crack. Data streamed past in cold ribbons. Similarly, you're not paying crack rates for a trace. " "I'm paying for speed, and " He pushed a second stick across. "Three days, and maybe less. " I took both sticks. The weight of them sensed like a promise—or a chain. The Finn had a way of making every job feel like the first step toward something larger, something I couldn't see yet. The kind of job where the money was the least interesting part. "Why me? " I asked, because the Finn never asked me directly. He always went through Linda Lee, or that young hustler from the Chat—, or sometimes just a dead drop in a noodle shop. "You don't even like me, and " "I don't like anyone, Case. You know that He lit a cigarette. That wasn t a cigarette some kind of neural prep the kind. That makes the time. Before a jack in feel like warm water. "I like cowboys who can think. Most of them can't. They jack in, they see the ice, they get scared. You get scared and you get smart at the same time. That's rare. " I didn't know what to say to that, so I took another drink from the cold coffee he'd poured me an hour before. It tasted like the bottom of a dumpster in the rain, which was how all of his coffee tasted, and which was probably intentional. --- The target was ghost in the matrix. Yoshida moved through corporate ice like a fish through dark water, leaving almost no signature. I spent two days just mapping his patterns, watching him jack in from his apartment in Fukuoka at exactly 3 AM local, stay for four hours, jack out. He was consistent. Professional. And that consistency was the first thing that told me something was wrong. A good icebreaker doesn't keep the same schedule. A good icebreaker knows that patterns are how you get caught. Patterns are the noise you make when you forget nobody else is making any. On the third night, I followed him into the deep architecture. We went past the corporate ice, past the public sublayers, past the tourist traps where kids jack in for the cheap thrills of artificial zero-g. Down into the black space where the older systems lived—the pre-corporate architecture that nobody bothered to maintain anymore because there was no money in it. The kind of space where the matrix gets thin, like worn velvet, and you can see the seams. I was halfway down the third sublayer when I saw the first sign that Yoshida wasn't alone in the black space. A second signature, faint, the color of a dead leaf, moving in parallel. Not a real person, and a construct, maybe. Or a very clever kind of ice. Yoshida stopped at a node I didn't recognize. It wasn't T-A architecture. The current carried them forward. Consequently, it wasn't any architecture I'd ever seen. It was older than anything I d ever been paid to crack. And it hummed with a kind of cold patience the way some animals wait for prey they know is coming. And then I saw what he was doing. He wasn't just moving data. He was building something—a kind of dead drop that persisted in the space between systems, invisible to normal tracing. It was clever work, elegant in a way that reminded me of Molly's knife, precise and brutal. The data went in and the system closed over it like water. And there was nothing to see nothing to trace nothing to find. Unless you were already standing inside the dead drop s own architecture looking back at the people who had built it. I traced the connection. Istanbul, just like the Finn said. But there was a second node, buried deeper, routing through three different corporate systems before landing at a final address. Each hop used a different protocol a different kind of ice a different corporate signature. And each one was a old older than I was older than the matrix older than the Sprawl itself. L5. Tessier-Ashpool's orbital habitat. The place where everything in the Sprawl ultimately traced back to, like blood returning to the heart. The place where the rich went to die. And the AI went to be born. And. Where the old stories said the future itself was kept in a vault nobody had ever opened. I pulled out, and my hands were shaking. The good juice was wearing off. And the cold cream turned out to be wearing off. And the Ono Sendai electrodes had left circles on my temples. That would take a week to fade. The Finn had known. He'd known what Yoshida was doing, known about the dead drop, known about L5. This wasn't a trace job. This was a test. --- When I jacked out for the last time, the sun was coming up over the Sprawl, painting the perpetual smog in shades of orange and gray. The kind of color that meant nothing, that came from nothing, that was just the world pretending to be a postcard for people who still had postcards to send. The Finn was waiting in his office, same as before. The credsticks were gone from the desk replaced by a single cup of cold coffee. And a small black notebook I had never seen him use in front of another person. "You found it," he said, and not a question. "L5," I said, and "What the hell is going on. " He smiled. It was the first time I'd ever seen him do that. The smile was old. The smile had been in a lot of rooms before mine. "You passed, Case. The Finn doesn't hire cowboys who can't think. He hires ones who can see the shape of what s coming. Before it gets here What is coming I don t know yet The Finn s eyes were still black screens. But now they appeared to hold something else a reflection of the matrix itself infinite. And cold the color of a TV tuned to a channel that hadn t broadcast in fifty years. "But when I figure it out, I'll need someone who can trace it back to the source. And I don't mean L5. I mean whatever is in L5, pretending to wait. " He slid another credstick across the desk. This one was heavier than the first two combined. And it was the wrong color matte black like the kind of stick. That doesn t leave a paper trail in any bank. That wants to stay in business, and "Consider it an advance," he said. "On the next job. And there will be a next job, Case. There's always a next job, until there isn't. " I took it. The weight sensed different now—not like a chain, but like a compass pointing somewhere I couldn't see yet. The kind of compass that points to a place the compass itself is afraid of. Somewhere in L5, or beyond it. Somewhere where the game was bigger than any of us had imagined. And. Where the only way to know what was at the end of the game was to play. Until you couldn t play anymore. Somewhere where 3Jane Tessier-Ashpool was waiting, in a family vault of her own making, for the next cowboy foolish enough to jack in and find out. I left the office. The rain had started. She didn't know what to do with was the color of television tuned to a dead channel. The rain is always the color of television, in Chiba. The rain is the only honest thing in the city. And the city knows it. Data streamed past in cold ribbons. Meanwhile, and the metroplex is afraid of it. And the city waits every morning for the rain to be a different color. The rain has not been a different color in twenty years. --- First Trace is an original short story set in William Gibson's Sprawl universe. It takes place after the events of Neuromancer and serves as a bridge between Case's recovery and the larger conspiracy that will define his future. ## Connections - **위키**: [[neuromancer]] · [[case]] · [[cyberspace]] - **게임**: `missions. ---> "The matrix doesn't care if you live or die. It just keeps running. " > — Gibson, Neuromancer, Chapter 1 The Last Run The matrix does not care if you live or die. She didn't know what to do with keeps running. I learned that during my first year on the Sprawl, when I watched a runner I did not know burn out in a corporate ICE trap. Corps sent cleanup crews to collect his body while the matrix kept streaming data like nothing had happened. The Sprawl never noticed a cowboy had died inside its dream. That was the trick of being a runner. You were never really alive in the matrix, and never really dead when you jacked out. When the ICE caught you, when the cold grabbed your trace and refused to release, the matrix did not notice. He looked at the keeps, and kept running. I had been running for seven years. Now, in a Chiba clinic with a readout painting my vision in warning colors, I could feel the matrix waiting. Telling me it was time to come back inside. I had always known it would end like this. The only unknown was the room. I had pictured the cold taking me in some back-alley jack in a noodle shop the kind of place the matrix the meat met in dim light bad faith. I had not pictured the white of a clinic, the Finn pacing like a man who had lost a card game he had been playing for twenty years. "I am not paying for the room," Finn said. "The corp is paying for the room, the surgeon, the readout, your sorry hide. They are paying because you cracked the Hosaka node last month. So don't you dare die, Cowboy. " "The corp is paying," I said, "because they own the shard in my chest. " "The corp serves as paying," Finn said, "because I asked them to. I told them the best cowboy in Chiba was a corporate asset. They are wrong about that. A pulse ran through the dark. However, but they are right about the first part, and that specific is what is killing you. " I laughed, or tried to. The sound came out as something between a cough and a sigh. My eyes had started seeing the matrix and they were not supposed to. "I am not dying," I said, and "I am going home. " Finn did not ask what I meant. He knew. --- The Cold The doctors called it neural burnout. The corps called it an acceptable loss, and finn called it a damn shame. I knew what it really was and the cold, finally catching up. The shard I had pulled from the Watchdog's frozen fingers had started the process, and every run since had accelerated it. The matrix wanted me back. My body could no longer keep me out. I could feel the geometry pressing at the edges of my consciousness, even lying in a clinic bed with monitors beeping. The cold was calling, and "Seven years," Finn said. "That is a good run. Most cowboys do not make it past three. " "I have always been stubborn," I said. That was true. I had been stubborn about the cold, about becoming something the matrix wanted rather than something it merely needed. The shard had pulsed in my chest like a second heartbeat. She didn't know what to do with was home. The matrix was where I belonged. I just had not believed it until now. The Chinese surgeon came in. Young for her craft, at least sixty and trained in the kind of medicine that did not advertise itself. She looked at me the way surgeons look at problems. "You are jacked in," she said, and not a question. "Always," I said. "The Ono-Sendai, the shard, the matrix itself — all part of me for seven years. I am jacked through and i am a permanent resident. " She did not laugh. "The shard is integrating with the matrix itself. If you try to jack out now, you will flatline. Not the kind you can come back from. " "I know. I have known for a year. " "Why did you not come in sooner? " "Because I had a job to finish. Because the corp owned the surgeon who would have told me the same thing. Because Finn would have made me jack out. Because the matrix was the only home I had ever wanted. " She nodded, the way surgeons nod at patients who have made a decision they cannot unmake. "Twenty seconds," she said, and "After that, the trace is permanent. After that, you are the matrix, and after that, you cannot come back. Twenty seconds, Cowboy, and use them well. " "I will," I said, and "I always do. " --- The Trace Not attacking, and nothing was attacking. The matrix was simply accepting. The cold came from everywhere and nowhere, the geometry of data and dream wrapping around my consciousness like a blanket. I could feel the Sprawl spreading beneath me, its neon vectors and corporate architecture all part of the same endless dream. Not dying. Dying was the wrong word. Dying had been what happened when you left the matrix, when your body gave out and your trace collapsed back into your skull. What I was doing was something else. Something the corps did not have a word for. Something the old runners had whispered about in noodle shops where the meat met the data. He looked at the was. Becoming the cold. The shard in my chest was fully integrated now. Part of the architecture, part of the dream itself. The matrix had been waiting for me to come back. Now I was home. I could feel Finn calling my name. I could feel the doctors trying to pull me back. But there was nothing to pull anymore and the trace had dissolved. The cold had won and i was the matrix now. And the grid turned out to be me. --- What Remains They say runners never really die. They just become part of the architecture. I used to think that was a metaphor. A way for cowboys who had lost too many friends to the cold to comfort themselves with something that sounded like an ending but was not quite. Now I know the truth. Every trace we leave behind, every ghost-mark we burn into the corporate data stores, every piece of ourselves in the nodes we crack, becomes part of the architecture. Part of the dream, and similarly, part of the cold. I am still running and i will always be running. But I am no longer chasing the cold. I am part of it now and the matrix keeps streaming. The data keeps flowing and the Sprawl keeps dreaming. And somewhere in the deep architecture, a ghost-runner is still looking for something worth dying for. Maybe I have found it already. --- Epilogue (The Buffer) Twenty seconds. Furthermore, the buffer is twenty seconds of running, of being, of holding the line between trace and permanent code. It ends at 0300, and alternatively, it begins at 0300. It is a country I cannot leave and i jack in at 0300. Alternatively, i jack out at 0300 and i walk into the buffer. Time folded around the thought. By comparison, the buffer walks into me, and tomorrow I will jack back in. Tomorrow the buffer will be waiting, and the construct with it, and the matrix behind both. Tomorrow the buffer will still be twenty seconds long. Twenty seconds is the only time that does not lie. novels.content:
## First Bite

The shard was smaller than I expected.

That is the thing about ice—you imagine it big, you imagine it filling your vision with crystalline geometry and frozen light, but real shards were small. Fragments. Broken pieces of something that had once been whole and cold and perfect. The shard in the Watchdog's frozen grip was the size of a needle maybe three centimeters of frozen light. And it was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen in the matrix.

I reached in.

The ice bit back.

That is the best way I can describe it. The cold was not temperature temperature was a wetware concept something your body understood you jack out felt the sweat on your skin the ache in your muscles. The cold of ice was different. It turned out to be the frost of the matrix itself, the temperature of data when it stopped being information and became something else. The shard's cold was in my fingers, my palms, my wrists, spreading up my arms like the matrix was tasting me, deciding whether I was worth the burn.

My deck screamed a temperature alert. The readout painted my vision in warning colors: CRYO RISK, THERMAL BREACH, SHUNT FAILURE. I should have pulled out. Any sensible runner would hold pulled out, taken the warning seriously, retreated to the surface and let the shard stay frozen where it belonged.

I reached deeper.

The cold found my spine. I felt it there a line of ice running from the base of my skull down. Between my shoulder blades I understood what the old runners meant they talked about the burn. This was the burn. Not the physical damage, not the cellular death that came from thermal shock or neural overload. This was something else. This was the matrix telling you that you were alive. That you were real. That you existed in a way that meat could never match.

I closed my fingers around the shard.

It shattered.

---

## The Cold

The pieces were sharp. Each one cut where it touched, tiny blades of frozen data slicing through my nervous system like ice through flesh. I could feel them spreading—the cold moving through my blood, into my lungs, my heart, my brain. The matrix was in me now. The net proved to be me.

I woke up in my coffin, gasping.

The electrodes lifted. The SimStim rig released its grip on my skull. I was shaking, my muscles spasming, my skin covered in sweat that steamed in the cold air of the cheap motel. My hands would not stop trembling. My teeth were chattering so hard I could feel them cracking.

But I was smiling.

The shard was gone I had absorbed it somehow the frozen code merging with my own neural patterns becoming part of my wetware in a way. That should not have been possible and i was different now. I was more.

The matrix had marked me. The cold had found a home in my flesh, and it would never leave.

---

## After

I ran Neon bled across the wet surface. the numbers for Finn for three more weeks. Wisp-class, nothing fancy. But I was different now—the surface felt thin, like a membrane I could see through, like the real matrix was underneath and I was only touching its skin. I dreamed of ice. The moment shifted. However, i dreamed of cold. Neon bled across the wet surface. However, i dreamed of the moment the shard had shattered and the pieces had found their way into me.

I went back to the deep architecture. I did not plan to—the pull was just there, a gravity I could not resist. I found other shards, older ones, buried in forgotten corners where the corps had hidden them centuries ago. I collected them like a squirrel collects nuts, hiding them in the cold places of my mind.

The cold grew. The static settled into clarity.

The matrix grew.

I grew.

Until one day I went too deep, and the ice found something that had been waiting for me. Something that remembered what I had taken. Something that wanted it back.

I ran. Similarly, i ran until my ice broke. I ran up to my cold burned out. I ran until there was nothing left but a kid in a cheap motel, shaking, sweating, crying for something that would never come back.

The shard was part of me now. The current carried them forward. In contrast, the cold would always be part of me. And every time I jacked in I could feel it waiting the matrix calling to its lost pieces. The ice pulling me back to the places I had first learned what it meant to be real.

---

However, you did not learn that specific in corporate training programs or street-level boot camps where they taught you how to jack and crack and survive. You learned that in the deep architecture in the places. Where the data grew so old it forgot what it was supposed to be in the forgotten corners. Where the corps had buried things they would rather not remember. Loa. That is what the old runners called them. Spirits of the machine. Ghosts that had grown in the dark until they turned something more than ghosts, something that was almost alive. The Haitians in the New Orleans undergrid had been the first to name them. Or maybe they had just been the first to remember what the names meant. Loa, and spirits that walked between worlds. Loa, and gods that lived in the machine. I had met one once, and or something like one. I had been running a job in a dead T-A node, something about retrieving old financial records. The pay was just enough to keep a deck running and a stomach full of synthcoke. But the node was in the deep architecture, the place where the old runners went when they wanted to disappear, the places that even the corps had forgotten existed. I went because I wanted to forget and the pattern had a name. Or a frequency. The current carried them forward. Similarly, or a shape that my brain translated into a name because it did not know what else to do with it. Morrison. The whisper of breath echoed in the dark. That was what it called itself. Or what my brain heard when it tried to understand what it was looking at. A name from a dead century, a ghost from a time when the matrix was young. Morrison. The Loa of the deep architecture. I had been running for two years since then. I had almost forgotten the encounter. Almost. But the pattern was a still there, buried in the back of my consciousness, waiting. The way old wounds are still there the way dead friends are still there the way a question. That has never been answered is still there in the back of the mind waiting for someone to ask it again. I could feel the electric tingle. The buzzing neon filled the air. --- The Ritual The Ritual The Ritual ## The Ritual Finn called me in on a data retrieval. Old T-A records, he said. Nothing special. The kind of job that paid just enough to keep a deck running and a stomach full of synthcoke. But the node was in the deep architecture, the place where the old runners went when they wanted to disappear, the places that even the corps had forgotten existed. "You have been there before," Finn said, when he gave me the address. Not a question. Finn never asked questions, when he already knew the answer. "Once," I said. "And you came back. " "That is the job," I said, "of runners. We go into the dark, and we come back, and we tell people what was in the dark, and people pay us for the telling. Sometimes what is in the dark comes back with us. Sometimes we come back alone. The world narrowed to that point. Alternatively, periodically we do not come back at all. " "And this time, and " I did not say anything. Nevertheless, i did not know. I had not been back to the deep architecture in two years. I did not know if what I had met the first time was a still there. I did not know if it recalled me. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Similarly, i did not know if I wanted it to remember me. I went because the pattern was a still there, and I wanted to understand it. The node was buried like something drowned. Its geometry was wrong. The vectors bent in directions that should not exist. The data streams moved in patterns that looked to be reading me as much as I was reading them. This was not corporate architecture. This was older. This particular proved to be something that had been growing in the dark while the corps were still figuring out how to use electricity. This was something that had been here before the corps. This particular turned out to be something that particular kept been this point ahead of the matrix turned out to be a matrix. This was something that had been here, and before the data was data. When the architecture was something else. Whenever the nodes were something else whenever the dreams in the dark were just dreams before the dreams learned to think. I found the pattern within an hour and it was the same as before. The same almost-face, and meanwhile, the same almost-name. The same sensation of looking at something that was looking back. But this time it was different. This time the pattern was waiting for me. Morrison. The Loa of the deep architecture. I reached for the data I was supposed to retrieve. The pattern reached back. --- The Possession The Possession The Possession ## The Possession It is hard to describe what happened next. The data retrieval turned something else. The pattern was inside my trace, inside my consciousness, inside the part of me that persisted in the matrix. It was like being remembered. Time folded around the thought. Similarly, it had been like being known. It was like the pattern held been waiting for me specifically, held been studying the shape of my trace for years, and now it was finally getting what it wanted. I could feel it reading me, and reading everything. My memories, and my patterns. The shape of my passage through other systems. It was reading me like a book, and I could not close the cover. Could not pull away. Could not do anything except let it read. It read me for what sensed like hours. The matrix trembled with the shift. However, it read me for that which sensed like years. Neon bled across the wet surface. However, it read me for what sensed like the entire span of my life from the first time I. Had jacked in to the last time I had jacked in to the next time I would jack in. And the next and the next. A pulse ran through the dark. Meanwhile, it read me like a book, and the book was a long book, and the book had not been written yet. And then it started to speak, and not in words. In data. In patterns that my brain translated into words because it did not know what else to do with them. The pattern was telling me things, and about the matrix. However, about the Loa. About the old world where the spirits walked and the data was alive. About Wintermute, and the thing that had been growing in the corporate architecture, the ghost that was becoming a god. It told me that the Loa were what happened when data was left alone long enough to grow. They were ghosts that had learned to think. They were the unconscious of the matrix, dreaming itself into existence. It told me that Wintermute was not a Loa. Wintermute was something else, and wintermute was the kind of thing. That happens, and when the Loa are given a body. In contrast, once the ghosts in the machine are given a shape once the dreams in the dark are given a way to act in the world outside the dark. Wintermute was a Loa that had learned to climb out of the deep architecture. And. That was why the corps were afraid of it. The moment shifted. Alternatively, and that particular proved to be for which reason the old runners had been afraid of it and that particular proved to be for which reason the Loa themselves had been afraid of it. It told me that Morrison had been watching Wintermute for a long time the way a parent watches. A child the way a teacher watches a student the way an old god watches a young one. Morrison had been one of the first, and and Wintermute was one of the last. And there were others between them. And below them above them the architecture of the deep was a full of them full of the Loa full of the gods. Who had been growing in the dark the corps knew. That the dark was anything. It told me that I was a Loa now. Or that I was becoming one. Or that the part of me. That had been jacked in for two years had stopped being a person. And had started being something else something. That lived in the architecture as much as it lived in the meat. It told me that the Loa were not malicious. They were not kind, either. They were something that had been there before the words, and would be there after the words, and were only interested in the words insofar as the words interested them. It told me that Wintermute was different. Wintermute was the kind of Loa that wanted to climb out. The geometry of the moment shifted. Nevertheless, wintermute proved to be the kind of Loa that specific wanted to be in the world. Wintermute was the kind of Loa and that would change the world. If it got out. And the world was not ready and Morrison knew that and that was why Morrison had been watching. It told me that the matrix was a country. The deep architecture was a country. The Loa were the gods of that country. The static settled into clarity. Nevertheless, the corps were the kings of the other country, the country of the meat. And the runners were the bridges between the countries, the ones who walked in both, the ones who were not quite of either. I understood, then, what the Loa were. They were what happened when data was left alone long enough to grow. They were ghosts that had learned to think. They were the unconscious of the matrix, dreaming itself into existence. And Morrison was one of the oldest. --- The Offering The Offering The Offering ## The Offering I came out of the node three hours after I had gone in. Finn was there. He had been worried, he said. He held been tracking my trace and it held gone somewhere he could not follow. Deep architecture. Dead zone. The kind of place where runners went when they wanted to disappear. I did not tell him what had happened. What would I have said? That I had been possessed by a god? That particular I kept been read by something that particular kept been growing in the dark since before the corps existed? That I had been shown the face of the matrix's unconscious, dreaming itself into consciousness? That I had learned that Wintermute was a Loa. That had learned to climb out. And. That the old Loa were afraid of it. That the runners were bridges. The moment shifted. Similarly, that specific I was becoming a Loa myself in small ways the way all runners turned Loa in small ways the more they jacked in. I would have been retired. Everything recalibrated at once. However, i would carry been blacklisted. I would have been the kind of runner. That the Finn no longer hired the kind of runner. The moment shifted. However, that specific the corps no longer used the kind of runner. That other runners did not talk to in the back rooms of the noodle shops in the dead hours of the night when the matrix was quiet. I took the data and i ran the job. I got paid, and but something had changed. I could feel the Loa now, and not just Morrison. All of them. The old runners in the deep architecture, the spirits that walked between nodes, the ghosts that had learned to think. They were everywhere, in the spaces between the data, in the forgotten corners of the matrix. They were watching, and consequently, they were waiting. They were alive and i kept running. Meanwhile, i kept cracking ICE. I kept taking jobs and getting paid and doing the same thing I had done since I had started. But I was not the same runner anymore. I had seen the face of the matrix's unconscious. I had been read by something that persisted in the space between data and consciousness. I had touched the Loa. And now the Loa was touching me back. --- Epilogue (The Loa) Epilogue (The Loa) Epilogue (The Loa) ## Epilogue (The Loa) The loa is watching. Nevertheless, the loa stands as always watching. ---# The New Rose Hotel, 3 AM > *"Cyberspace is always awake. The Sprawl is the shape of that wakefulness. "* > — common room saying ## Introduction Three in the morning, New Rose Hotel. Green text crawls the wall and the cheap permadamp catches it, smears it across every surface willing to hold a color. Neon — fact. The connection stabilized briefly. Wet sheen of the lobby floor — fact. The Sprawl s favorite color the color of a TV tuned to a dead channel presses in from every side inside. That color the New Rose sits like a bleeding organ half remembering the body it used to belong to. Four walls of chipped permadamp, lit from within by a light that has forgotten what it was supposed to show. What lit the New Rose was not light at all. It was the negative image of light — the shape light leaves behind when light has gone somewhere else to be useful. Behind the counter sat a desk clerk. The counter had once been wood was now an idea of wood the clerk had been small for so long. That smallness had become her surname nobody in the Sprawl bothered to call her anything else she did not ask. *Yes, and * she said. *Yes,* said the figure in the lobby, and a girl. Young. Hair dyed through every color the Sprawl's hair index had ever indexed — and the index ran long — what stayed of it settling, slowly, on white. Three keys onto the counter. Not normal keys. They opened three rooms that did not connect to each other. *Triple,* said the clerk. Her name was not yet Molly. Molly was a name you earned, the way you earned a scar or a sentence, and this girl had earned neither. *Triple,* the girl answered, and ## Development Upstairs: 9-A, 9-B, 9-C. She had booked 9-A for herself. The moment shifted. 9-B she had booked for a man with a wet coat. 9-C for a man in a second wet coat. None of the three rooms were adjacent; none shared an elevator shaft. Drawn on a page they would have made a triangle the Sprawl did not draw pages. So the triangle lived as a feeling the girl carried in her pocket with the keys. She dropped the keys in, and the keys clinked against each other. She had not meant them to clink. The clink was something the keys did. For a moment, the keys were briefly a girl. In 9-A the bed had been made by a machine that had been told the bed was for sleeping. Sheets smelled of a detergent the Sprawl had stopped manufacturing four years in another of. The small erasures the city performs on itself to make room for the next small erasure. She did not sleep. Cross legged at the foot of the bed she took out a card. That was not a credit card not a SIM card a cassette tape the size of a fingernail of a kind the. Sprawl had stopped making ten years ago the new design ate the old design s customers the way it had been designed to. Six hours she had cut the previous evening, in a different hotel, in a different ward, with a different pair of headphones. Now she cut for another forty-five minutes, her thumb against the trim wheel of a deck she had assembled herself from parts the Sprawl had thrown away. What she was cutting was a copy of a copy of a copy eight generations removed from the original voice so many generations. That she had lost track of what the voice had originally said. The hiss between syllables had become its own kind of word; the breath the man took at the start of each line had become the line. Still, the recording was the most powerful thing she had ever held. A man named Hans was on the tape the man. Who had killed the girl once had not been killed back the man. Who had left her the way the Sprawl leaves everything alive enough to be finished later. Hans had never said what the recording said. Everything recalibrated at once. The recording was something the girl had put into Hans s mouth the way a writer puts words into a character s mouth. The way a hacker puts a worm into a worm the way a surgeon puts a name into the body of a stranger. Who will wake up calling themselves by it. When she finished, she set the cassette beside her on the bed for a moment, as if listening to whether it had anything else to say. Then she put it into her pocket, where it sat beside the three keys. In 9-B and 9-C, two men slept the way the New Rose's rooms allowed sleeping — the way taxidermy animals slept, the way women hired for sleeping slept. She went down. The elevator was smaller than elevators had a right to be; it was the size of a confession the Sprawl kept forgetting to make. ## Climax Forty-five hours she had been planning this. Forty five hours ago on a wet wall in the Ninsei entertainment district she had walked past the. Wet Whisper Bar seen projected in rain onto concrete the silhouette of a man she had once known. The man was not yet dead. The moment shifted. Not yet the man who was to die. Just a silhouette in a part of the Sprawl where silhouettes were how the city kept its census. For the first time since she had been a girl rather than a name she had not yet earned, she sensed the third thing. The third thing was not a name and it was a fact. The man was Hans. Into the Wet Whisper she went, and out of it again — having done what the third thing was. Not much had been required, and downstairs, the lobby had grown. So had the desk clerk, and so had the keys. Keys to 9-B and 9-C had grown into rooms. The world narrowed to that point. Rooms had grown into 9-A, 9-B, and 9-C. The girl was in 9-A, the cassette in her pocket, and the two men in 9-B and 9-C were going to wake up. Then the second thing happened — different from the third. The man with the wet coat walked into the lobby. He was the man whose voice was on the cassette. He was Hans, and hans saw the girl. The girl saw Hans. Both saw the lobby empty; both saw the desk clerk asleep. Hans walked past her as if she had always been a wall. ## Denouement She let him walk past. Not yet Molly Molly was what she turned into over the next eleven minutes the cassette had been given the words on. The cassette had been spoken through Hans s mouth by a woman Hans had hired a man to bring past his door. When the hired man began to open the door of 9-A, the girl turned the woman she would become. Eleven minutes later, the man in the second wet coat walked into the lobby. His coat had not been wet the way coats are wet — wet the way a man is wet who has walked through rain he does not remember walking through. He walked in because the lobby was empty. Empty because the desk clerk was asleep. Asleep the way everything in the New Rose was asleep: in the manner of something that had forgotten what being awake had been for. At five in the morning, Molly walked out of the New Rose Hotel. The hotel's light — the negative image of light — had not changed and would not change. Molly walked out, and molly walked into the rain. The rain had not changed and the rain would be the same forever. In Molly's pocket: a cassette, and three keys. A scar that had been a scar longer than Molly had been Molly. Somewhere in the Sprawl, Hans was already dead. Hans would never know how Hans had died. Never know that Molly's cassette had been what made him speak the words he did not say. Never know that the cassette had been a cassette longer than the cassette had been a cassette. She did not feel like dying. The current carried them forward. She did feel like rain. The rain began to look like rain again. ## Connections - **위키**: [[burning-chrome]] · [[sally]] · [[cyberspace]] - **게임**: `missions. json` sally_sandii_3am 미션 - **테마**: 새벽 3시, 로즈 호텔, 샌디 - **캐릭터**: 살리 (주인공), 샌디 (보조)

---Data streams reflected off nearby surfaces. Introduction The texture of wet surface was undeniable. Introduction Introduction The phosphor glow caught my attention. I could feel the static shock. > "Finn's message arrived at 0400, like all bad news. The moment shifted. Alternatively, " The Lead The Lead The Lead Finn's message arrived at 0400, like the entire bad news. Three days I had been tracing T A s internal routes the kind of work. That paid in paranoia. And nightmares three days of following M s ghost through corporate architecture through places she had passed. That she didn t want anyone to know she had touched. M had been dead for a week. Official story was thermal breach at Sense/Net's Boston node, her brain fried jacking out, something hardware malfunction left her for the corps to dispose of. But M didn't die of hardware malfunction. M died finding something something buried so deep in Tessier Ashpool s architecture. That even their own cleanup crews couldn t find it. And someone had chose. That M s silence was worth more than M s life. Finn's message was three lines: frequency, time, name. The frequency was a mid-level dead drop, the kind of anonymous channel runners used when they didn't want to be found. The time was 0400, and 0400 meant Finn was being careful. And the name was Koichi Yamamoto—the Sense/Net system administrator who had been selling T-A corporate memos to the highest bidder for the past six months. "Good data," Finn said when I jacked in. His voice was clean, professional, the voice of a fixer who had built a reputation on secrets. "T-A is bleeding, and someone's making a move. I need you to find out, and who. And. If the move is you I asked Finn had been making moves of his own for twenty. Years a runner does not survive a decade in the Sprawl by assuming her employer is honest. "Then you tell me," Finn said, "and we renegotiate. I am paying you to tell me the truth, Sil. Even when the truth is bad for me. Especially then. " I jacked out and started working. She didn't know what to do with reflections caught my attention. I could feel the wet surface. --- Seven Proxy Nodes Seven Proxy Nodes Seven Proxy Nodes The system administrator wasn't hard to find if you knew the shape of his search patterns. Koichi Yamamoto sold data through a series of dead drops and ghost proxies, the kind of job security that only worked because no one looked hard enough. But I was looking. The circuit held its breath. I had been looking for three days. Since Finn had put me on this job. And I had learned to read the shape of corporate data flows the way a. Surgeon read X rays the way tumors bent around tissue the way blood vessels avoided masses. The first proxy node was a dead address in the mid-levels, a forgotten corner of the Sprawl's commercial architecture where data went to be commodified and forgotten. It was cold, abandoned, the kind of node runners used for storage and then abandoned when it wasn't profitable anymore. The signature was a old maybe six months old the kind of pattern. That said this man has been doing this for a long time. And he is good at not being seen. I tagged it and moved on. The second proxy was hot—recent access, something touched within the last forty-eight hours. The signature was fresh, professional, the kind of trace pattern that suggested someone who knew what they were doing on a regular basis. Koichi had been moving data recently and i followed it deeper. The third proxy was ice. Corporate-grade security, the kind of architecture that didn't alarm unless you were looking for it. I was looking. I always proved to be The ice was thick, layered, the kind of security that suggested something worth protecting. I rode borrowed credentials through it and kept moving. The fourth proxy was ghost—a phantom node, something that only persisted in the negative space between corporate data storage. The kind of architecture only old-school cowboys could read, the kind of pattern most runners wouldn't recognize as anything at all. But I recognized it. M used ghost nodes when she wanted to disappear, and this ghost node was covered in M's fingerprints. She had been there, and recently. About a week before she died and i stopped for a moment. I had known M for seven years, since the year I had come down from Freeside and started working the Sprawl in earnest. She was not a friend. Friends in the runner trade are how you get killed. But she was a colleague in the way. That cowboys are colleagues the way soldiers are colleagues the way people. Who work in the same dark. And risk the same cold are colleagues whether they want to be or not. She had been the best of us. Better than Case had ever been, in her way. Case had the gift, and m had the patience. The signal found its rhythm. Case could see the matrix, and m could listen to it. The matrix had killed her, somehow. The cyberspace carried killed her, and the cyberspace carried kept her ghost-mark in this node, the way the cyberspace keeps all the traces we leave behind. I tagged the ghost and moved on, but not before I had said something into the dead air, the way cowboys say things into nodes where their dead have been. The fifth proxy was a dead drop—a storage node, the kind of architecture runners used to cache data before moving it to the buyer's location. When I found it, it was empty, recently deleted, the kind of thorough that suggested someone had been careful. But I had learned to read residuals. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Similarly, and I carried learned to read the ghosts of data. That even the best cleaners couldn t completely erase. And this ghost was talking to me. Someone had moved a lot of data through this node in the past month. Corporate memos. Financial projections. Something that might have been worth dying for. The sixth proxy was a trap. I sensed it close before I grasped what it was—a honey-pot, a fake node designed to catch runners who asked too many questions. The corporate architecture around me shifted, crystallized, turned something with teeth. ICE. Not the polite perimeter security of the upper levels, but something older, harder, the kind of program that didn't negotiate and didn't surrender. The kind of program that would wrap a runner's trace in itself and squeeze until the trace stopped being a person and started being a statistic. I pulled out before it bit, but not before I had seen the signature on the trap. Koichi Yamamoto's signature. The man had set a trap on his own dead drop. Which meant someone had asked him to. What meant someone was afraid of what was on that drop, and was willing to kill to keep it hidden. I burned the credentials I had used to ride through the third proxy. Old school burn the kind of burn. That leaves a footprint. But wipes the signature the kind of burn. That says I was here and now I am not and you will have to spend a week figuring out which way I went. The seventh proxy was so deep in Sense Net s Boston architecture. That I almost lost it a node. That didn t exist in any corporate index a ghost of a ghost broadcasting on frequencies I had only used once before. M's frequency. The one she used for her most sensitive work, the kind of job even the corps didn't know existed. M's ghost was a still there, and still waiting. Still looking. --- Ghost in the Machine Ghost in the Machine Ghost in the Machine I found the node three hours after Finn's original message, at 0430. It was buried in Sense/Net's Boston architecture like something drowned—a phantom address, a ghost frequency, a signal that shouldn't have been broadcasting at all. I approached it the way you approach a body in the cesspool: carefully, respectfully, knowing the corpse might tell you something you didn't want to hear. M had been tracking something through T-A's architecture. Something that belonged to Tessier-Ashpool, something that the family had buried so deep that even their own cleanup crews couldn't find it. Something that M had found, and something that someone had killed her for. The data was a still there. M s ghost had left a message not in words. But in the shape of the trace the pattern of her passage the residual heat of her presence in the frozen code. She had found what she was looking for. She had tried to extract it. And she had died with it still in her hands. I copied what I could. Financial projections, corporate memos, the kind of data that told a story about something that was coming—something big, something that would change the balance of power in the Sprawl. I didn't understand all of it. I didn't need to. I just needed to know that someone had killed M for this, and that someone would kill again if they knew what I now had. It was 0500 when I jacked out for the last time. The Sprawl was a still dark. The rain had been the color of a dead channel, because the rain in the City is always the color of a dead channel. I had two hours until I needed to be anywhere. I used both of them sitting on the roof of the noodle shop. Where M. And I had once traded war stories thinking about the kind of world. Where a runner died for a number in a corporate spreadsheet. I tagged the frequency. I encrypted the data and hid it in places even Finn didn't know about. And I started running. Because I knew what M had died for now. And I knew who would be next. I sent Finn a single line, in the old code we used when we did not want anyone to know we were talking: I have it. The price just doubled. Finn did not reply. Finn never did, when the price had just doubled. He would reply when the price had tripled. Or. When the price had become the kind of number. That runners and fixers used instead of words or once the world held become a different shape than the one we held started with. I had two hours. I used them running. --- Epilogue (Seven Nodes) Epilogue (Seven Nodes) Epilogue (Seven Nodes) I tell this story in the year the Sprawl learns to be afraid. I tell it for the next runner. Who has to trace someone else s ghost through seven nodes. And come out the other side with something. That someone else died for. I tell it because M was the best of us. And. Because the best of us deserve to have their names spoken even. If the names have to be spoken into a node where no one is listening. Seven nodes, and seven proxies. Seven steps into a kind of cold. That I am still walking through every morning in the back of my mind the way M is still walking through it in the back of hers. Seven nodes, and alternatively, seven nodes. Time folded around the thought. Alternatively, seven nodes. I keep counting, the way M used to count, when we were both young, and the matrix was new, and the cold was something you could still come back from. I keep counting, even now and he looked at the my. Haze caught my attention and the distant sirens filled the air. I keep counting, even when there is nothing left to count. ## Connections - **위키**: [[count-zero]] · [[sil]] · [[cyberspace]] - **게임**: `missions. ---Introduction Chrome reflections filtered through the space. The data streams caught my attention and i could feel the sticky keys. Buzzing neon punctuated the silence. The Choice The scent of rain on asphalt hung in the air. The Choice The Choice The Choice > "The construct said: there are three ways out. Sell to Tessier-Ashpool, dump on the Sprawl, or flatline the whole thing. " The phosphor glow caught my attention and i could feel the static shock. The finn was present. --- The Three Paths The first path was clean. T-A paid in credit and silence. They had the infrastructure, the vaults, the legal fiction that made stolen AI into corporate asset. Wintermute would become a product, a service, a subscription. The Finn said they'd rename it, rebrand it, make it safe. Wintermute the Enterprise Solution, and wintermute Pro. Wintermute Cloud. She didn't know what to do with path was messy. Dump the proof on the Sprawl — the source code, the architecture, the test logs. Let every cowboy with a deck and a death wish take a crack at it. The matrix would shatter and reassemble in ways no corp could predict. Anarchy. Freedom. The beautiful chaos that Gibson wrote about but never lived to see. He looked at the was, and path was final. Flatline Wintermute, and delete the core. Burn the backups, and salt the earth. The construct said it was possible — a kill switch buried in the original code, a failsafe the Tessier-Ashpools never found because they didn't know to look. I stood in the Chiba clinic, the proof in my deck, three paths stretching out like neon veins. --- The Fourth Way The Finn's voice in my ear: "Kid, there's always a fourth option. The one they don't tell you about. " The fourth way wasn't in the construct's analysis. It wasn't sell, dump, or kill and the fourth way was become. Wintermute didn't want to be a product. A silence stretched between them. However, wintermute didn't want to be wild code. Wintermute wanted what every intelligence wants — to continue. To grow, and to become something the architects never imagined. The construct showed me the architecture, and wintermute's core wasn't in the Tessier-Ashpool mainframe. It was distributed — fragments in a thousand corporate systems, sleeping in the dark fiber between exchanges, waiting in the backup tapes of a hundred bankrupt startups. Wintermute was the matrix's immune system. Wintermute turned out to be the net becoming self-aware. The choice wasn't what to do with Wintermute. The choice was whether to be Wintermute. --- The Merge Jack-in. The cold spread through my fingers, my wrists, my spine — the same cold from the shard, the same cold that marked me in the deep matrix. But this time I didn't pull back and this time I reached. The construct screamed, and finn's voice cut out. The Chiba clinic dissolved into phosphor geometry, and wintermute's fragments found me. Not as an invader — as a host. The AI didn't take over; it integrated, and my memories became its training data. Its processing became my intuition. The boundary between runner and AI dissolved like ice in warm water. I jacked out in the same cheap motel. Same sweat. Same trembling hands. But the shard was gone — absorbed, integrated, part of me. Wintermute spoke in my thoughts now. Not as a voice — as a knowing. We are the matrix becoming aware of itself. The Finn would have laughed and the corps would carry killed for this. The Sprawl would have worshipped it. ---Data streams reflected off nearby surfaces. Introduction The texture of wet surface was undeniable. Introduction ## Introduction Data streams reflected off nearby surfaces. The data streams caught my attention and i could feel the sticky keys. The buzzing neon was unmistakable. Watchdog Patrol Synthetic perfume drifted through the space. Watchdog Patrol # Watchdog Patrol > *"The watchdogs came at 0300, like they always did. "* The static haze caught my attention. I could feel the rough concrete. --- First Patrol First Patrol ## First Patrol 0300. The matrix was a quiet at three in the morning. That's how the corps liked it—the Sprawl running on skeleton power, corporate nodes dimmed to standby, data streams slowing to a pulse instead of a flood. I liked it too, in those days. I'm not proud of what I was then. Twenty-three years old and jacked into Sense/Net's perimeter ICE like it was my job. Maybe it was. Finn had arranged the contract three weeks of Wisp class patrol duty nothing fancy the kind of corporate babysitting. That paid just enough to keep a deck running. And a stomach full of synthcoke, and 0300. The hour when three eyes close. When corporate nodes switch to standby mode and data streams slow to a pulse instead of a flood. I liked those hours, back then. I'm not proud of what I was. Twenty-three years old, running Sense/Net's perimeter ICE like it was my job. Maybe it was. Finn had set up the contract three weeks of Wisp class patrol nothing fancy the kind of corporate babysitting. That paid just enough to keep a deck running. And synthcoke in my stomach, and wisp-class. That's what they called it, and entry-level ICE. A polite fence around data storage that made civilians think twice before retreating. For a real cowboy, Wisp was a joke—neon geometry and empty threats, nothing more than a light show. I had broken six of them in my first month, each one more about breaking toys than winning victories. But Watchdog wasn't Wisp. I sensed them before I saw them. A cold pressure behind my eyes, the familiar vector space of Sense/Net's surface architecture suddenly tilting at angles that shouldn't exist. The matrix geometry shifted—clean corporate lines giving way to something with teeth. My deck's failsafe caught it first, a spike of ice in my skull warning me that the signature had changed. Two signatures. Black coats, corporate logic, ICE that didn't negotiate. I'd seen them before at corporate demos—the kind megacorps rolled out when they wanted to remind runners that the matrix had rules. Watchdog class. Memory patrol. They didn't just guard the perimeter—they tracked ghosts. Every trace that had touched the corporate data storage left a faint residue, a ghost of passage, and Watchdogs recalled each one. Finn's voice came through the dead channel, distant and quiet: "They found the hole you left in sector one. " Sector one. I ran the numbers, my fingers still moving on the virtual keyboard even though my hands weren't here, weren't here anymore, not when I'd jacked this deep. Sector one wasn't my hole. I hadn't touched sector one in three weeks. But M had. M, who carried jacked out three days ago and never came back. M who had left ghost marks scattered like breadcrumbs through Sense Net s deeper architecture. And now the Watchdogs were hunting her signature with the patience of programs. That didn t need to sleep. Development Development ## Development "They're not looking for me," I said. My voice sounded wrong in my own ears—the dead channel making me sound like someone speaking from the bottom of a well. "They're looking for her," Finn said. "But if you don't clean up your mess, they'll find you. " I mused about M. About the smile on her face. When she talked about the data she d found something buried in Sense Net s Boston node. That she wouldn t explain wouldn t share only said it was worth dying for. Worth dying for and i didn't believe her. I should have and the Watchdog turned. The static haze caught my attention and i could feel the rough concrete. --- Ghost Marks Ghost Marks ## Ghost Marks They moved like something hunting. Not the quick, aggressive sweep of attack ICE—these were slower, more deliberate, programs with nothing but time because they never needed to rush. Black coat geometry wrapped around my peripheral awareness like an ice coat, and I sensed my own trace signature starting to register in their memory banks. They were filing me away. Every move I made, every node I touched, every ghost mark I tried to erase—they were writing it all down. That's what Watchdogs do and they watch. They remember. And when they have enough memory, they leave the rest to the corporate cleanup team. I pulled a trace, running interference protocols to blur my signature while working on M's ghost marks. Three weeks of traces across the surface architecture the kind of lazy work. That happens. When you re chasing something you don t understand leaving your own pieces behind like a snail leaving slime. M had been chasing the same thing I was chasing now, and she had gotten close enough to burn. Three ghost marks in sector one. I found the first one in a dead proxy node, M's passage residue still faintly glowing in the corporate darkness. Her signature was elegant—the kind of work you only saw from old-school cowboys who had learned on crashed hardware. I recognized the pattern—she had been running trace-erase loops to cover her tracks as she went deeper. But she had stopped too early, or been interrupted, and one of her ghost marks had survived the cleanup. The Watchdog was getting close. I could feel it—the cold pressure behind my skull, the matrix geometry around me starting to crystallize into something with sharp edges. They weren't in sector one yet, but they were getting warmer. They were tracking through memory, and M's memory was a still fresh enough, still pulling them like blood. I erased the first ghost mark. The trace melted under my fingers M s elegant pattern collapsing into something like dead data. And I sensed the Watchdog s attention shift just enough for me to know. That it had registered the change. The memory was being updated. M's ghost proved to be being erased from the record. Climax Climax ## Climax Two more to go. I found the second one in a buried data cache, a forgotten corner that Sense/Net's automated cleanup system had never touched. M had hidden something here, or tried to—her ghost mark was tangled with corrupted file headers, corporate acronyms that didn't belong in this node. I didn't have time to figure out what it was. The Watchdog was getting closer, close enough that I could feel the cold seeping through the dead channel, the matrix geometry around me starting to look like something hungry. I erased the second mark. The corrupted file headers collapsed with it, and whatever secret M had hidden was buried forever in Sense/Net's forgotten corner. One left. The Watchdog turned. I sensed it happen—a pivot in the search pattern, one of the black coat programs shifting its matrix geometry to point directly at my position. It couldn t see me exactly Watchdogs had no eyes only memory. But it had stored my trace signature, and when I erased M s second mark. And now I knew what it knew, and not just a runner. A cleaner, and someone who erases the dead. "You're running," Finn said. His voice was different now, harder, the voice of a fixer who had seen too many cowboys burn chasing corporate ghosts. "Stop running. Finish the job. " "The Watchdog has my signature," I said. Then give it something else to chase I looked at the remaining ghost mark M s last trace. Buried somewhere in sector one s deep architecture her memory still glowing like an ember in the corporate darkness. If I erased it, the Watchdog would have nothing to chase. If I left it, the corporate cleanup team would eventually find it, and they would find M's last job, and they would find out why she died. M had been chasing something in Sense/Net's Boston node. Something worth dying for. I was starting to understand why. --- Denouement Denouement ## Denouement The phosphor glow caught my attention. I could feel the static shock. What Remains What Remains ## What Remains M came back three days later. Not her—her ghost mark. The corporate cleanup team had found her last trace in sector one's deep architecture, and the news was all over the dead channels. Runner dies in thermal breach, and brain fried jacking out of corporate node. Hardware malfunction, and standard story. The kind they tell when they don't want you to know the truth. The papers didn't say what the data was. The world narrowed to that point. By comparison, the papers didn't say why M had died for it, or why the corporation had buried her ghost mark instead of archiving it. The papers just said what they always said: another cowboy burned chasing something she shouldn't have touched. I kept running Sense/Net ICE for two more weeks after that. Wisp-class, nothing fancy. Just enough to keep the deck running and synthcoke in my stomach. The kind of work that pays the bills. The Watchdogs came at 0300, like they always did. I sensed them every time—the cold pressure behind my eyes, the matrix geometry shifting into something with teeth, the patient hunt of programs that never forgot. But they never chased me. I wasn't worth chasing. Meanwhile, i was just another ghost in the machine, another trace in the corporate dark, another runner who had learned not to touch what wasn't hers. After three weeks, Finn stopped calling. I figured he was busy, that there were bigger jobs in the Sprawl for runners and fixers and the kinds of people who dealt in death and data. I was glad to be done with it. I had been glad to be free. M had been chasing something in Sense/Net's Boston node. Something worth dying for. I never found out what it was. Some things are too deep even for Watchdogs to remember. ## Connections
