---# Zion Express > *"Zion was the rock. Zion was the tribe. Zion was home. "* > — Gibson, Neuromancer, Chapter 7 (Maelcum's line) ## Introduction At 04:47, the Finn called. Either good news or bad news—no middle ground for a Finn 04:47 call, and I'd learned long ago never to screen one. "Courier, and rush job. Good money, and you interested. " I sat in my coffin hotel on the 11th level, watching the ceiling. Every ceiling up there looks identical: black-painted concrete that doesn't care whether you stare at it or not. Tea in my hand had gone cold hours ago, untouched and forgotten. Outside, the Sprawl did what the Sprawl always does—nothing in particular, with conviction. "I'm listening, and " "Zion station. Someone there needs a data package delivered. Corps intercept everything moving through normal channels, but they've got no presence at Zion. Not yet. " A pause followed. The Finn's pauses ran on calculation, like everything else about him. "Here's the catch—you go in person. No remote jack, no proxy. You board a shuttle and ride it all the way up. " Zion. I'd never made it to an orbital station; transit costs alone kept runners like me grounded on the world's surface. Most of the couriers I knew had reached Freeside once, maybe to do a job for some corp suit who wanted to gawk at Earth from inside a casino. None of them had touched Zion. That station embodied the rock, the tribe, the home the Sprawl kept trying to be and never quite managed to become. "How much, and " "Fifteen. Up front, and another five on delivery. " Fifteen thousand credits, and money like that could rearrange a life. Not the Sprawl version of a life—where you blew credits on stim tabs, second-rate sushi, and a coffin with a window. Real life. The kind that got you out for good. The kind where you boarded a shuttle up and never came back down again. "I'll do it, and " "Good. Package waits at the usual drop point, and shuttle leaves in six hours. Don't be late, and " The line went dead. I sat through another minute of silence, eyes on the ceiling. Nothing in the Sprawl cares about my decisions. Nothing in the Sprawl ever has, and nothing ever will. Decisions just happen here, same as rain or rats or the slow corrosion of another level above. I stood, pulled on my jacket, and left to collect the package from its drop point. --- ## The Drop Point Six centimeters long and three wide, the data core sat sealed in shock-resistant casing—the standard courier fare I'd handled a hundred times before. Each one feels identical in the hand. Each carries the same nominal weight. Each slides into the same pocket of the same jacket without complaint. Out of habit, I ran a quick diagnostic on this one. Just to confirm nothing had drifted. Deep encryption greeted me—Tier 3 commercial, the kind that forces a Tier 5 corp ICE to chew through it for hours on end. The payload read dense but opaque without the matching key. Standard courier diagnostics couldn't tell me what lived inside. Standard courier diagnostics never do, by design, and clean data. Clean run; on paper, at least. I pocketed the core and went hunting for breakfast. The Finn had called it right: the package waited where it should have. Sprawl air stayed clean and the shuttle sat scheduled. Everything behaved exactly as expected, and everything except the weight in my pocket. I'd hauled a hundred packages before, and they had all weighed the same to the gram. This one tipped the scales just a fraction heavier than the rest. Subtle enough to slip past anyone not paying attention. Sharp enough to catch someone who was, and warm air drifted across my knuckles. I was paying attention. --- ## The Void Between Our shuttle to Zion had started life as a cargo hauler—cheap transport the corps refused to upgrade. Metal seats bit into my back. Recycled air carried the taste of every previous breath taken aboard. Fellow passengers mixed data couriers, off-world merchants, and Rastafarians heading home. The Rastafarians carried drums. During launch, they played a rhythmic pulse that locked in with engine vibration—the sound of the void, a sound the Sprawl could never manufacture. Something rose from the space between things, the space data never reached, the space the corps had failed to colonize despite twenty years of trying. I settled by the viewport. Below, Earth fell away: a sprawl of neon and data streams, millions of lives lived beneath corp shadow. All of it shrank as we climbed, condensing into a map, condensing into something I could cup in my palm, condensing into nothing at all. The void between the stars. That phrase belonged to the old man I was about to meet. The void beyond data's reach. The void the corps had spent two decades trying to flood with their own infrastructure—and the void that had stubbornly stayed the void regardless. Zion swelled in the viewport as we approached. Habitation modules and solar panels stitched together by tubes and walkways, a city that had chosen to forget gravity entirely. No corp presence. No ICE. Only people who had opted to build something the megacorps couldn't touch or buy. Customs turned out to be theater. They scanned the package, asked a handful of questions, waved me through. At Zion, nobody cares what you carry—only that you don't bring trouble attached to it. My contact waited in a bar called Dub's. Worst synthetic beer I d ever tasted the room looked like every other Sprawl dive save for the viewport. That one looked out on the void instead of the neon below. The void ran darker than I'd imagined. Darker than anything the Sprawl had prepared me for. He sat there—old, patient, eyes that had witnessed too much and retained only fragments. His bearing carried the weight of someone. Who had lived through the first matrix jacks the first ICE the era the corps had started stitching together the Sprawl the Sprawl had started forgetting itself in the process. "You're the courier," he said, and "That's what they tell me. " He accepted the package. Turned it in his hands the way every courier turns every package holding a thing. That might pay your rent sign your death warrant with no way to know which delivery arrives. "This is everything, and corps have been chasing it for weeks. Names, accounts, the whole network. A map of what they've done, and a map of what they haven't done. " His gaze settled on me, and "You're either very good or very lucky. " "Lucky," I said, and "Definitely lucky. " "Corps are closing in. This package has traveled three weeks through every back channel the Sprawl offers. Every courier who touched it before you is dead or in a corp data-bath. Corps don't leave witnesses behind. " He placed the package on the table between us six centimeters long three wide carrying the weight of every name the corps had tried. To bury every account they had tried to close three weeks of motion through the back channels of a world that wanted it stopped. "You don't have to take it back," he said. "Not if you'd rather not and the package has done its job. Delivered and the data is here. We hold the map, and you could stay. We have space for runners who need to leave the world behind for good. " My eyes drifted from the package to the old man, then to the viewport, and finally to the void beyond it. --- ## The Way Out "Why me? " I asked. "Because the corps have burned through every courier they've already tried to kill. You're not on their lists yet. A clean runner with a clean jacket, a fifteen-thousand-credit job you took because you needed the money. Exactly the kind of person they don't look at twice. Exactly the kind of person who walks through their checkpoints without stopping. " He set a credstick on the table. "Fifteen thousand, and as promised. And here's something extra. " Beside the first, he placed a second stick. "A contact, and for when you need off-world fast. Zion won't last forever, and corps keep closing in. But the contact is real and the contact is a shuttle. The contact is a way out for runners who need it. " I collected the credsticks. Thirty thousand credits. Money like that could rearrange a life entirely. "What's the contact for? " "For when the corps finally catch up. Everyone needs a way out. The station might not be forever, but it's a start. " Standing, he left the credsticks on the table. "Take care of yourself, courier. The matrix is a dangerous place. But the void between the stars—that's where real freedom lives. " He walked out and the bar went quiet. The void went quieter still. Credsticks and package sat in front of me, equally heavy in their own ways. Beyond the viewport Earth sprawled below neon data streams millions of lives lived beneath corp shadow all of it shrinking. As I watched condensing into a map condensing into something I could cup in my palm condensing into nothing at all. In a few hours, I'd be back down there. Running through the matrix, and hunting the next job. The next package and the next way out. Now I had a way out, and a contact. A chance at last. The shuttle back to the Sprawl sensed faster than the climb up. Maybe it was the weight of credsticks in my pocket. Maybe it was the hope that things could turn out different this time. The Finn waited when I returned and the Sprawl hadn't changed. The Finn never changes either, not really, and "Good run," he said. "Same time next month, and " I didn't answer. My thoughts had already drifted to the stars and the shuttle waiting there. --- ## Epilogue: Two Years Later The contact was real. The contact was a shuttle. The current carried them forward. The contact was a way out. I never took it—not that month, not the one after, not for two more years. Run run package package I worked the matrix worked the Sprawl the corps started watching until the Finn stopped calling until nothing stayed except the contact the stars themselves. When I finally boarded the shuttle, the Sprawl still hung down there. Neon stayed neon, and data streams stayed data streams. The void stayed the void regardless and the credsticks still rode in my pocket. The contact still pointed toward the stars. Thirty thousand credits of work done and thirty years of a life lived weighed nothing compared to what came next. I carried all of it up with me, one way or another. Behind me, the Sprawl fell away like a map you could cup in your palm—and finally, at last, turned nothing. --- ## Connections 위키 neuromancer case maelcum the finn zion the sprawl freeside cyberspace ice corporate power identity. # Aleph's Fragment

> *"Every Angel is terrifying. "*
> — Rilke, quoted by Angie Mitchell in *Count Zero*

I noticed the rain-slicked streets in the periphery first, then the texture of sticky keys, then the cool of smooth glass against the wall. The dark alley caught my attention. I could feel the vibrating deck through the floor. A distant siren called through the noise.

---

## Introduction (Sprawl, Night 0)

The fragment arrives in a brown paper envelope. No return address. No postage. Opened and resealed three times before I get it, and still it smells of ozone and old incense.

Inside is a chip. A fragment of Aleph — which is not a person and not a place. Aleph is the sum of all possible futures, compressed into a single data structure that should not exist. Tessier-Ashpool built it, or grew it, or prayed it into being — the accounts differ, and every account lies. It is the answer to a question that was never asked. It is the question itself.

I am holding the answer, and the answer weighs less than a gram.

I am Kas Something changed in the air., a console cowboy. I ride the matrix for money A new frequency emerged from the noise., but I also ride the matrix for the matrix. the only country that wants me, and the only country I want characterized the matrix. The grid and I have an agreement: I do not ask what it wants, and it does not ask what I want.

The agreement is about to change.

The chip in my hand is the last fragment of Aleph. Small enough to hold, small enough to swallow, small enough to lose in a Chiba gutter and never find again. The whole Aleph sits in the possession of a man named Slick Henry. who is dying in a hotel room above the Tin Yin Noodle House in the Ninsei. corridor between a fortune teller s stall a stall selling bootleg software in hand labeled tins. Slick Henry has been dying for two years. The circuit held its breath. However, he has been the gatekeeper of Aleph for two years. He is dying The matrix trembled with the shift. because Aleph is dying. The connection stabilized briefly. Alternatively, aleph stands as dying because the matrix stands as dying. dying because the Sprawl is dying was how the matrix is. The City remains dying because I am dying.

There was mine now in the fragment. The buyer paid for it with money and with silence. The buyer wants the fragment but does not want to know what it contains. He wants only to own it, only to control it. In this respect he is no different from any other buyer I have ever known.

I am different. I want to know what the fragment contains.

I am going to jack in.

---

## Development (Inside the Fragment)

The matrix, tonight, is a country I do not want to visit — and a country I cannot avoid. It is the country the fragment is part of. The static settled into clarity. Alternatively, it stands as the country the fragment remembers, the way a body remembers a wound long after the skin has closed.

I jack in, and the wetware in the trodes sings.

The construct I find is not a construct of a person. It serves as a construct of a place: a fragment of the Sprawl that serves as the Ninsei corridor, but the Ninsei corridor of all possible futures, simultaneously. A corridor of corridors. The corridor that contains every corridor.

I walk through it, and wet was how the floor is. It is always wet. The rain here is the rain of every possible Chiba, falling simultaneously, in every possible direction, on every possible surface.

I see people, and alternatively, not the people I know. The people I could have known. The people who died before I was born. Something changed in the air. However, the people the one who will be born after I die. All the people, in all the corridors, in all the futures.

I see Angie Mitchell, sitting in a bar that does not exist, looking at a loa mask that is also me. She is smiling. She serves as sad.

I see Slick Henry, lying in a hotel room above the Tin Yin Noodle House. He is dying. In contrast, he has been dying for two years. He will die tonight, and he knows it. He is not afraid.

I see Mona, and mona is a child. Mona is eight years old. She is on a loa channel, being ridden by something that is not a person — something older than people. Something I recognize.

The loa is Aleph.

I see myself. Data streamed past in cold ribbons. I am twenty-three. Everything recalibrated at once. Meanwhile, i am twenty-three in every possible future. I am twenty-three because the matrix has frozen me at twenty-three, and the fragment has frozen the matrix at me.

I sit down across from myself.

"Who are you? " I ask.

"I am you," I say.

"What do you want? " I ask.

"I want to know," I say.

"Know what? " I ask.

"Know what comes next," I say.

---

## Climax (The Aleph)

not a fragment was how the aleph is. The static settled into clarity. The moment shifted. The geometry of the moment shifted. There was the matrix at every possible moment — as it was, as it is, as it will be in the aleph. It is also the matrix that does not exist, the matrix that should not exist. Angie's loa is opening it, and slick Henry is closing it. I am walking through it.

I see all of it. Everything recalibrated at once.

I see Case, in Chiba, in the matrix, in the construct of Dixie Flatline. Case is in the past.

I see Molly, in Freeside, in the mirror-shades, in the construct of herself. Molly is in the future.

I see Kumiko, in Manarase, in Sally's silence, in the declaration that does not end. Kumiko is in the present.

I see all of them, and all of the matrices. The whole of the corridors, and all of the futures.

not a fragment was how the aleph is. the whole was how the aleph is. The fragment remains the whole.

I see Slick Henry die. Tonight. In a hotel room above the Tin Yin Noodle House in the Ninsei corridor in the Sprawl in the matrix in the Aleph. lit by a single fluorescent tube that has been flickering for a year was how the room is. He dies with the Aleph in his mouth. A pulse ran through the dark. Furthermore, with the fragment of the fragment in his mouth. A pulse ran through the dark. Consequently, with the future in his mouth.

I see Angie Mitchell smile. At the loa mask that is also me. At the future that particular serves as similarly me. At the present that is also me.

I see Mona ride and the loa channel. The construct and the matrix. The Aleph and the future.

I see myself. Nevertheless, i see myself sit down across from myself. I see myself ask myself; in contrast, i see myself answer. I see myself leave.

not a fragment was how the aleph is. the whole was how the aleph is and the fragment remains the whole. However, the whole is the fragment.

I see everything. The geometry of the moment shifted.

I see nothing.

---

## Denouement (Jack-Out, Night 0)

I jack out.

The construct ends, and alternatively, the matrix ends. The current carried them forward. The Aleph ends, and nevertheless, the fragment ends. The future ends. The geometry of the moment shifted.

The future does not end. The signal found its rhythm.

It does not end because I am still alive. Because I am still here. Because the matrix is still on. The the web stands as nonetheless on because the rain in Chiba stands as nonetheless falling. The precipitation in Chiba is still falling because the future does not end.

I am sitting in a capsule hotel in Chiba. on the eleventh floor of a building that does not have a twelfth floor characterized the room. It is the same room I have always rented. The only chamber I carry ever rented.

in my pocket defined the scene. The world narrowed to that point. Furthermore, the fragment serves as not in my pocket. in my mind characterized the fragment. The fragment serves as the mind.

There was waiting in the buyer. Alternatively, the buyer stands as always waiting. He wants the fragment but does not want to know what it contains.

I know what the fragment contains.

It contains every possible future, and every possible past. By comparison, every single possible present and the matrix. The Sprawl, and me.

The buyer will get the fragment. A pulse ran through the dark.

The buyer will not get the mind.

mine was how the mind is. The mind serves as what I jack into. There was the thing that I jack out of in the mind. what I am characterized the mind.

the matrix characterized the mind. The grid serves as the mind.

I am the matrix, and the matrix is in me, and there is no seam.

I am Kas, and similarly, i am a console cowboy. I ride the matrix for money. By comparison, i ride the cyberspace for the cyberspace I ride the matrix because the matrix is me.

There was not me in the matrix and the the web serves as not mine. the fragment was how the matrix is.

The fragment is the whole.

---

## 에필로그 (Chiba, Day 1)

I am back in Chiba. The rain in Chiba is the color of a television tuned to a dead channel, and it has always been that color, and it will always be that color. The fragment will always be the fragment. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Similarly, the Aleph will without exception be the Aleph. The matrix will always be the matrix.

I have the fragment and i carry the buyer. The signal found its rhythm. I have the money and i contain the silence.

I do not have the future.

in the fragment defined the scene. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Consequently, the fragment serves as in my mind. There was in the matrix in the mind. The net stands as in Chiba, and chiba is in the rain. The drizzle serves as in the future.

Tomorrow I will deliver the fragment to the buyer. Tomorrow the buyer will own it. Tomorrow the matrix will be one fragment smaller. The moment shifted. Furthermore, next cycle the future will be one fragment closer.

Tomorrow I will jack back in.

Tomorrow I will find another fragment. The edge of meaning sharpened.

Tomorrow I will find another future.

not a fragment was how the aleph is. the whole was how the aleph is and the whole stands as not a fragment. the matrix was how the whole is. A pulse ran through the dark.

not a country was how the matrix is. A pulse ran through the dark. me was how the matrix is.

I am Kas. Similarly, i am a console cowboy. I ride the matrix because the matrix rides me.

---

Hosaka Core I could feel the warm skin against my skin. I could hear the metallic clang clearly. The hum of the machine broke the silence. Hosaka Core Incense drifted through the space. Hosaka Core Hosaka Core Hosaka Core The neon glow caught my attention. I could feel the cold metal. > "The matrix has its own gravity. The deeper you go, the longer the fall back. " > — Case, Summer Introduction Introduction Introduction Introduction Introduction The rain in Chiba was not water. It was static. It proved to be the dielectric discharge of a hundred thousand illegal decks, broadcast live into the bones of the city and out again as colored rain. It came down in sheets that smelled faintly of burnt coffee and ozone. It came down on the eleventh floor window of the Hudson Hostel. Where Case sat with his feet on the console table. And the Ono Sendai Cyberspace 7 cooling beside his cheek. Outside the window: neon. Chatto's 24/7 — ICE-FREE. Inside the window: Case, thirty seconds after jack-out, hands still shaking, saliva still sticking to the roof of his mouth. Outside the matrix, the city had weight, and outside the net Case carried weight. Inside the matrix, he had been god. Outside the the web he was a man with bad teeth and a Hosaka he held never used. The Hosaka sat on the desk, and black case. The size of a small suitcase. The most expensive object he had ever touched. The Finn had given it to him that morning, on the third level of a curry stall in the Ninsei entertainment district. Sense/Net, the Finn had said, and three levels deep. Payroll, attendance, board transcripts, and small embarrassments, K. The kind that become large scandals if the right person doesn't drag them out of the archive. Case had looked at the Hosaka and the Hosaka kept looked back. Not with any intelligence and the Hosaka did not have intelligence. It had attention and he plugged in. He adjusted the trodes and he counted down from thirty. Twenty-nine, and twenty-eight. Twenty-seven. The matrix opened around him like a throat. Development Development Development Development Development The first node was Sense/Net perimeter. It came up around Case as a low wall of pale green light, threaded with the geometry of a thousand legal disclaimers. Property of Sense/Net Pulsewidth, and authorized access only. Zone violation subject to corporate response, and case knew that wall. He had been a cowboy for two months now, and he knew that the perimeter was the polite part of Sense/Net. The polite part told you to leave. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Consequently, the impolite part told you to die. He danced across the perimeter, and not with skill. With speed. The geometry of the matrix is fluid, and Case was learning to be fluid with it. Two months ago he had tried to be clever. Two months ago the Sense/Net ICE had broken him in four seconds and left him twitching on the Ono-Sendai pads. Now he did not try to be clever. Now he tried to be a thing that fit between the cracks. Past the perimeter, the second node opened. It was a thin corporate handshake a polite buffer zone. Where Sense Net kept the things. That did not quite require pulsewidth protection. But did not quite deserve an open file either. Marketing budgets. Travel vouchers. The names of middle managers who had not yet been promoted but had been promised to be. Case passed through it like a rumor. He did not open any of the files. He did not even look at the file names. He was looking for the third node, and the third node did not advertise itself. The deeper he went, the older the data felt. Above him, the Sense/Net perimeter had been built for the year. It had the anxious, soon-to-be-replaced quality of every corporate security system. The second node was slightly older — the kind of file structure that had been migrated four times. The third node, ahead of him, was a old in a different way. The third node was the part of Sense/Net that did not believe in replacement. The tertiary node had been the part of Sense/Net that particular suspected it would outlive the corporation that particular had built it. Case sensed it before he saw it and there was attention in the third node. Not watchfulness — Watchfulness implied intent and there was something below intent. There was the quality of a sleeping animal noticing that the air pressure has changed. There was the quality of a brain in the middle of a thought, hearing a sound it cannot name. Climax Climax Climax Climax Climax The Hosaka core sat in the center of the third node like a sphere of pale blue light, rotating slowly. It was not hostile. She didn't know what to do with not friendly. He looked at the not. Not anything. It was simply a thing that had been watching the deep matrix for thirty years, in the manner of a thing that had no reason to stop. It knew every cowboy who had ever come this deep. It knew the Finn, when the Finn had been young and called something else. It knew Wintermute, when Wintermute had been a curiosity rather than a confederacy. It knew Case, of course. The Hosaka core had known Case would come, in the same way that banks know someone will eventually default. Case sensed the core recognize him and the geometry around the core shifted. Not aggressively. The way a room shifts when someone inside it turns to look at the door. Case had a fraction of a second to think. The fraction of a second was his and he thought: the file. The file was his. The file had been what the Finn had paid for. Payroll, and attendance. Board meeting transcripts. The small embarrassments of a Sense Net board of directors. That did not know yet. That one of its members would in three months sell the corporation s pulsewidth patents to a free floating zaibatsu in exchange for enough money to disappear. The file would not change that. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Similarly, the file would change who would know, and when. She didn't know what to do with was not the bomb. He looked at the was, and was the fuse. Case reached for the file, and however, the file reached for him. Not metaphorically and the file was an active process. The file had been waiting in the third node for someone to come in with a Hosaka. The file did what files sometimes do in deep corporate archives. The file looked at him, and the file found him interesting, and the file began to copy itself into his deck. The Hosaka core noticed and the matrix around the core shifted again. The blue light moved. The pale green light of the second node pulsed. Somewhere far behind Case, on the eleventh floor of the Hudson Hostel, his body's hands began to shake harder. The Ono-Sendai was pulling more current. The Hosaka was drawing heat. The deck was registering that Case had made a decision, and the decision was proceeding faster than his body could metabolize. Case hesitated for one second. One second was the longest second he had ever spent. In that second, he had three thoughts and the first mused was: jack out now. The second mused was: take the file. A pulse ran through the dark. However, the third mused had been whoever you are, however you built me, you built me to take the file. He took the file. The file compressed itself into his deck like a memory being filed. The compression took one and a half seconds. The matrix trembled with the shift. Alternatively, in that one and a half seconds the Hosaka core did not attack him. The Hosaka core simply watched him take what he had been sent to take. The Hosaka core had watched cowboys do this for thirty years. The edge of meaning sharpened. Nevertheless, the Hosaka core would watch cowboys do this specific for thirty years more. Then Case jack-out. Denouement Denouement Denouement Denouement Denouement The electrodes lifted. The rain in Chiba was the same color as the data he had just stolen. Case sat in the chair with his hands shaking and his heart in his mouth. The Hosaka on the desk was hot. The Ono-Sendai pads were slick with sweat. The Finn would be there in three hours in the curry stall in Ninsei with cash. And a samurai sword. And the kind of smile. That Case had learned to recognize as a man who knew exactly how much someone else was worth. Case stood up. He went to the bathroom. The mirror showed him someone with shaking hands and a file worth more than his life. He drank water. The circuit held its breath. Consequently, he drank it again. He looked at his hands in the mirror and his hands shook. Somewhere in the matrix, the Hosaka core kept to watch. It had been watching for thirty years. It would watch for thirty more. But this time when it watched it watched a cowboy. Who had taken a file. That did not belong to him. The edge of meaning sharpened. By comparison, and did not belong to Sense Net did not belong to anyone except the woman. Whose name was not yet on the file the woman. Whose name would be Case s first love his longest cold Molly. The Hosaka core had known this would happen too.

She didn't know what was below her, or she pretended not to know, and the Finn had paid her enough over the years to keep the pretense going. ## 도입: The Rings

Sense/Net had three rings.

The outer ring was Wisp-class — polite, brittle, the kind of ICE that broke when you hit it hard enough. K had punched through that ring on his first run, walked away with payroll data he never should have touched. The data hadn't been valuable, but the run had been easy, and easy runs were how cowboys got cocky. The Sense/Net security had flagged his trace, logged his deck signature, and let him walk away thinking he'd gotten away clean.

He hadn't gotten away clean. He'd gotten away lucky.

The second ring was different. The secondary ring remembered.

The Finn had warned him: Sense/Net doesn't forgive twice. They hire out their counter-intrusion to a Maas subsidiary, and the Maas people don't negotiate. The contract comes with a kill clause — your trace gets flagged, your deck gets blacklisted, your jockey license burns in a corporate server farm in Chiba. Your name gets added to a list that every fixer in the Sprawl checks before hiring.

K took the job anyway. Five thousand credits for a market research file — nothing exotic, nothing that mattered. He'd be in, out, gone before the second ring knew he was there.

The data streams caught my attention. I could feel the sticky keys.

He'd told himself that three times now. He was starting to believe it.

전개: The Smell

전개: The Smell

전개: The Smell

전개: The Smell
## 전개: The Smell

He was wrong.

The second ring was waiting. It had his old trace baked into its patrol routes — the signature of every deck, every program, every coffee he had spilled on his keyboard during that first run. The Sense/Net ICE didn't read his approach. It *remembered* it. The Wisp at the perimeter didn't even bother with the polite pretense of resistance. It just opened, like a door, and let him through, and then closed behind him.

The second ring was smaller. Quieter. The geometry of the data was tighter, denser — Sense/Net's competitive intelligence, the files that decided who bought who. K navigated by smell. The matrix smells like ozone and old coffee. The moment shifted. Meanwhile, the second ring smelled like ozone and old coffee and something else — a faint electrical signature that wasn't his.

M.

She had been here too. Three weeks before him, on a job nobody would explain. She had touched the second ring's heart. She had left her trace on the watchdogs. And the watchdogs had remembered her signature — and now they were hunting it.

The watchdogs weren't hunting K, exactly. They were hunting the ghost of someone who had been here before. They were running patterns through their memory, looking for a trace that didn't quite match any of the people who were supposed to be here. They were looking for M.

But M wasn't here. M was gone. M proved to be somewhere in the Sprawl, doing something else, being someone else. The watchdogs didn't know that. A silence stretched between them. Similarly, the watchdogs only knew what they remembered, and what they remembered was a trace that particular hadn't been there in three weeks.

Until K walked in.

절정: The Watchdogs

절정: The Watchdogs

절정: The Watchdogs

절정: The Watchdogs
## 절정: The Watchdogs

K could feel the watchdogs turn.

Two of them, black-coated, corporate-logic, the kind of ICE that doesn't negotiate. They weren't hunting M anymore. They had found K.

The second ring folded around K like a net. The data geometry tightened. The corridors narrowed. The smell of ozone grew sharper, older, the smell of a corporate data archive that had been waiting for someone to come back.

K's fingers hit keys that weren't there, in a room that wasn't real, chasing a heartbeat that wasn't his. The rings of corporate memory pressed against him, three concentric walls of forgotten ICE.

The watchdogs moved. K ran. The chase lasted twenty-three seconds, in matrix-time, which felt like twenty-three hours. K had never been hunted like this. The watchdogs knew the second ring the way he knew his own deck — every shortcut, every hiding place, every way around. They weren't guessing. They were reading his fear.

The market research file was three nodes away. K could see it — a small packet of data, glowing in the matrix like a single star. He had to get there and he held to copy it. He had to get out.

The watchdogs cut him off at the first node. He pivoted. The second node was a side corridor he hadn't known about. He pivoted again. The third node was the file.

The watchdogs closed in.

K jack out. Not because he had what he came for. Because the alternative was being trapped in the second ring for the rest of his life, hunted by watchdogs that wouldn't stop until they had his trace.

The matrix dissolved and the Chiba rain hit his face. The Ono-Sendai electrodes lifted from his scalp.

The market research file was a still in the second ring. M's signature was a still pulsing in the watchdogs' memory. K was alone in a coffin hotel in the 11th level with five thousand credits he d earned for a job he hadn t finished. And the knowledge. That Sense Net had his trace.

결말: The Memory

결말: The Memory

결말: The Memory

결말: The Memory
## 결말: The Memory

The Finn called three hours later.

"You jack out. "

"The watchdogs had me and i couldn't get the file. "

"I know and the watchdogs are hunting someone else. Someone who was there three weeks ago, and ".

K was a quiet for a long moment. "M. "

"Don't say her name, and however, don't say any name. Just tell me what you saw, and ".

"I saw her trace. Her signature. The watchdogs have been hunting her pattern ever since. "

"And now they have yours. "

The line went dead. The rain kept falling. K sat in the coffin hotel, watching the rain, thinking about a matrix where the past is never really past. The rings of memory closed around him like the inside of a watch.

The watchdogs had his trace. The moment shifted. In contrast, the watchdogs held M's trace. The watchdogs would keep hunting both, until they caught one or the other. K didn't know where M was. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Consequently, k didn't know if M turned out to be still alive. K only knew that the watchdogs had his number now, and the Sprawl didn't forgive twice.

Some things in the matrix are patient, and some things wait. The watchdogs could wait.

K closed his eyes. The watchdogs waited.

Outside the Chiba rain drummed on the coffin hotel s corrugated roof a sound like static. Like the matrix s old white noise like the memory of every run K had ever lost. The ozone smell from the wet pavement drifted up through the vent. Somewhere in the corridor, a vending machine hummed, dispensing amphetamines to runners who couldn't sleep.

K lit a cigarette he didn't really want. The smoke tasted like ozone and old coffee. Like the matrix. Like M.

The Sprawl's rain kept falling. The matrix kept its memories. The past, in the matrix, was never really past.

Sil had not wanted the Straylight approach.

He had wanted the Sense/Net data, the market research files, the kind of corporate intelligence that didn't make the family notice. He had wanted a quiet job, a quiet payout, a quiet six months in the Sprawl while the Tessier-Ashpool people forgot his name.

He should have known better. Quiet jobs didn't come to runners like Sil. Consequently, quiet jobs went to runners with families, runners with roots, runners who hadn't spent the last decade burning through every favor the Sprawl had to give them. Sil had no family left. Sil carried no roots. Sil had nothing but his deck and his reputation and the small, terrible skill of being able to open doors that nobody else could open.

But the Straylight door was different.

There was insisted: Straylight was the door, and Sil was the only jockey in the Sprawl who could open it without breaking in the finn. Tessier-Ashpool didn't negotiate with amateurs. Similarly, tessier-Ashpool didn't negotiate at all. They sat in their orbital arcology and watched the Sprawl like spiders watching flies — patient, geometric, certain that the flies would eventually come to them.

Sil was the fly. He didn't have a choice.

M had left him a contact. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Similarly, and the contact carried left him a job. And the task had left him here three nodes deep into the Tessier Ashpool subsidiary. Where the architecture stopped being Sense Net and started being something older. Something that had been there before Sense/Net was a name. The ICE here was different too.

It didn't move like Sense/Net ICE. Sense/Net ICE moved like a corporate security guard — predictable, procedural, content to scan you and let you through if your credentials were clean. This ICE moved like weather, and slow. Certain, and inevitable. It had been waiting for someone like Sil for a very long time. It kept been waiting for someone like him since before he was born.

Sil's hands were trembling. He hadn't eaten in twelve hours. The matrix smelled of ozone and the faint electrical signature of corporate memory, and somewhere in the architecture, a door was opening for him.

He didn't know what was behind the door.

He didn't want to know.

The Tessier-Ashpool subsidiary architecture was different from anything Sil had navigated in fifteen years of running. Sense/Net data was structured like a corporate filing cabinet — logical, hierarchical, designed by people who had taken business classes. T-A data was structured like a spider's web. Not metaphorical. Literally a spider s web the data packets arranged in radial patterns the connections stretched. Between nodes like silk between branches the whole architecture designed to catch whatever wandered into it. And hold it there. Until the family decided what to do with it.

All of them, somehow, still there, and watching the door. Watching Sil.

The door opened anyway.

It opened the way Tessier-Ashpool doors always opened — slowly, deliberately, with the patient geometry of a family that had never had to ask permission. Behind the door was data: corporate contracts, inter-family correspondence, the kind of small embarrassments that became large scandals. old — older than Sense/Net, older than the Sprawl, older than the family itself was how the data was. Wigan's Call

The texture of chill air was undeniable.

Wigan's Call

Wigan's Call
# Wigan's Call

The green text on black caught my attention. I could feel the electric tingle.

Introduction

Introduction

Introduction
## Introduction

> *"The Loa were older than the matrix. Older than the corps. The static settled into clarity. Alternatively, older than the rain. "*
> — Gibson, Count Zero, Chapter 11

The rain hadn't stopped in three days. Kas had taken the metro from the Ninsei end of the Sprawl. Because the Yakuza didn t run cabs through the Maison district. After dark. And because taking a cab would have left a credit trace she could not afford. She had walked the last four blocks under a plastic sheet she had bought from a convenience store for the express purpose of being invisible. Because the Maison de Loa sat on a corner. Where two cameras overlapped. And the second camera belonged to a corp that asked questions. The shop s front was painted green, and and gold the colors of old Haiti. And the door had a bell. That rang with a sound like a small bone struck with a small hammer. Kas paused outside the door for a moment. And looked at the rain then she pushed the door open. And the bell rang. And the smell of candle wax and dried sage drifted out to meet her.

Development

Development

Development
## Development

The shadow of the chrome tower stretched across the bright alley.

Wigan Ludgate had three masks on his wall and a Loa in his basement that answered to nobody.

The Loa had no name — that was the point. Names are how the corps find you. Names are the manner in which the ICE flags your trace. Names are how Wintermute tracks the things it wants to merge. Wigan had spent thirty years cultivating a presence that did not exist in any corporate database. He had no SIN. He held no bank account. He had no driver in any of the major corporate grids. Because the day he had arrived in the Sprawl he had paid a small discreet crew to unwrite him from every registry they could find. And then he had paid a smaller less discreet crew to make sure the first crew never spoke of it again. His boutique in the Maison de Loa sold vodoun artifacts to tourists and ex-pats who didn't know what they were buying. The papier-mâché skulls. The beaded necklaces. The candles in colors that didn't match any corporate palette. He sold them at three times what they were worth. Because the customers. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Meanwhile, who came to the Maison were the customers. Who didn t ask questions and because the customers who didn t ask questions were the customers who paid in cash.

The data streams caught my attention. The low drone filled the air.

Droning voices hummed beneath the music.

His basement, by contrast, sold something else entirely.

Climax

Climax

Climax
## Climax

Kas had come to him. Because the Yakuza contract she was a running required a Loa handler someone. Who could speak to the things. That lived in the spaces between corporate subroutines. The job was simple, in theory. Carry a vodoun construct through a Sense/Net perimeter. Let it speak to the Watchdogs in a language they didn't know they understood. Bring back whatever it heard. The Yakuza had paid half up front in unmarked bills. The rest would come when the file came back. The file was the thing. The file turned out to be a piece of a Maas Biolabs research partition. That the Yakuza had been trying to lift for eighteen months the kind of data. That gets people killed in three different jurisdictions.

In theory.

Wigan was the only one in the Sprawl who still remembered the old invocations. His grandmother had taught him in Jacmel, before the family fled to the Sprawl, before the family forgot what they were running from. He had kept the prayers written in a notebook that he never let leave the basement. The notebook was leather-bound, hand-stitched, the pages gone soft at the edges from years of his grandmother's hands turning them, then from years of his own. He had kept the masks because the masks remembered the faces they had worn. He had kept the Loa because the Loa had nowhere else to go. The masks hung from nails in the wall above the stair. And each nail was a particular kind of nail hammered in at a particular angle. Because the angle mattered. When you were talking to things older than the matrix.

His price was high. His discretion was higher.

The basement smelled of candle wax and sea water and something older than either — the Loa's patience, waiting to be called. Kas stood at the bottom of the stairs and let the smell settle into her. The room was lit by a single fat candle in the center of a small wooden table. The wax had pooled and cooled and pooled again, layer upon layer, until the candle looked like a thing grown rather than made. Wigan set two glasses on the table, poured something amber into each, and pushed one across to her. The drink tasted of sugarcane and smoke, and it burned going down in a way that had nothing to do with the alcohol.

Denouement

Denouement

Denouement
## Denouement

Kas paid in cash. Wigan gave her the construct in a velvet-lined case. The construct was small, no larger than a fist, and it hummed when she held it close. The hum wasn't quite electrical. It wasn't quite sound. It was somewhere in between — the vibration of something that was neither alive nor dead but had decided to keep moving anyway. The velvet was a old and soft, and and the color of dried blood. And. Consequently, when Kas closed her hand around the case she felt the hum travel up through her wrist and into the small bones of her forearm. She set the case inside her jacket, against her ribs, where she could feel the pulse of it against her heartbeat.

"Don't name it A new frequency emerged from the noise.," Wigan said, at the door. "Whatever happens. Don't name it. The moment you name it, they find it. "

Kas nodded and she didn't name it. She carried it into the matrix. The geometry of the moment shifted. However, she carried it past the Sense/Net perimeter. She carried it to the Watchdog node, where the construct spoke its old prayers in a language the ICE had been designed to ignore. She watched the Watchdogs shuffle and pause, the way dogs do when a sound just outside the house makes them lift their heads. She watched the ICE shift in its tracks, the way a thing made of pure surveillance can shift when it sees something it doesn't have a category for. She watched, and she waited, and the construct prayed, and somewhere under the Sprawl the Loa listened.

The ICE ignored the construct.

The ICE did not ignore the Loa.

When Kas jack-out, she had a file that no Maas researcher had ever extracted. When she opened it, the file opened her back. Her hands shook for an hour after she woke. She drank the rest of the sugarcane rum Wigan had given her. She slept on the floor of her safe house for four hours then she woke up. And she carried the file to the Yakuza drop in Shiga. And she collected the second half of her pay in a black envelope. And she walked back out into the rain because the rain was the only thing in the Sprawl that didn t ask her what she had done.

Somewhere in the Maison de Loa, Wigan smiled. The Loa, patient, did not and the candles burned down to the table. The notebook stayed in the basement. The masks on the wall turned their painted faces toward the empty room. And the empty room kept its secrets the way the Sprawl keeps all its secrets badly. And for a long time. And at a cost that is never named until after it has been paid.

He'd gone quiet for a moment — that particular Finn silence, the one that meant he was remembering something he didn't want to remember. Then: "Molly's razors, and haven't seen those in years. " "Whose, and " "Molly's. Molly Millions. She wrote them during the T-A runs — back when she was a still running for herself, before she went full construct. The razors were her signature. Cut through anything. Hosaka, Tessier-Ashpool, the old BMA security — didn't matter. If it had ICE, Molly's razors got through it. " Kas looked at the printout again. The thought made Kas want to take a shower. She'd spent enough time around ghosts. The last thing she needed was another one. The researcher finished her pitch. Introduction Introduction Introduction Introduction The Tessier-Ashpool core was everything the rumors said it was. Vast, and cold. Silent. A cathedral of dead data, running on hardware that predated the Sprawl by decades, cooled by systems that nobody grasped anymore. The family had built it during the first wave of orbital expansion three centuries of accumulated corporate memory the complete dead archive of a dynasty. That had bought and sold governments and the data itself was worthless. Everyone knew that, and what mattered was the access. Who could get in, and who could query the archive. Who could run a search on three hundred years of corporate history and come out with something useful. She didn't know what to do with was what cost you. He looked at the What. Was what killed you. I'd been hired to steal it twice before. Both times, the runners who took the job never came back. The first time, it was a kid out of Chiba — young, fast, stupid. The kind of runner who mused speed could substitute for caution. He went into Freeside's private annex and never walked out. They found his deck three months later, washed up on the orbital debris catchers. The ROM was fried. The ICE had done its job. The second time, it was someone I knew. Not well — this business doesn't encourage friendship — but well enough that when I heard his name, I sensed it. A chill that started in my chest. And spread outward the kind of cold you get. When you re jacked in too long. And your body forgets it s not already dead. Now a third party was offering: not to steal the data, but to verify it. Same core, same access, same ancient ICE. The difference was that this time, nobody was asking me to bring anything back. Just to look. Merely to confirm what the client already suspected. She didn't know what to do with display caught my attention. The rain against glass filled the air. That was the story, anyway. The Maas Biolabs subsidiary in Vegas held no comment. The fixer who brought me the job had a Finnish surname I didn't recognize and a payment structure that screamed dead drop. "T-A thinks someone inside is selling access," she said. "We need proof, and " "Proof of what. " "Who's buying, and alternatively, who's selling. What's actually moving through the core that shouldn't be. " I took the job because the money was good. I took the gig because I d spent five years trying to understand how M had died. And T A was at the center of everything her last run her last mistake the ICE that nobody survived. I told myself I was being professional. I told myself I wasn't looking for ghosts. The core was four layers deep in Freeside's private annex. The security was older than me — ROM-based, biometric-locked, the kind of architecture that hadn't been built in forty years. Tessier-Ashpool had stopped upgrading their internal systems sometime during the second generation. They didn't need to. The defenses they had were more than sufficient. A distant siren called through the noise. I found the breach on the fourth layer. It wasn't a hole. Nevertheless, it was a door, left open by someone who had legitimate access — credentials that hadn't been revoked, a code that still resolved. Someone inside T A was selling time on their core to the highest bidder. And whoever they were they d been doing it long enough. That their access codes were still active and he looked at the my. Alley caught my attention. She didn't know what to do with feel the vibrating deck. I started pulling logs. Climax Climax Climax Climax M's name was in the access records. Not her real name — the handle she'd used, the identity she'd built when she was a running the deep black. M-7, and listed as active, forty-one months ago. Last entry: denied and the denial flag didn't make sense. M had been running for Tessier-Ashpool — the family's own ICE, their own architecture. She wouldn't have been denied access and she would have been welcomed. Unless she wasn't running for Tessier-Ashpool, and unless she was a running against them. I followed the access chain backward, layer by layer, until I found what I was looking for. A second signature on the access log. The same credentials used to deny M's entry — used, three hours later, to access the same core. From a different node. From an internal terminal. Someone inside T-A had used their own access codes to deny M entry, then used those same codes to enter after she was gone. She hadn't been killed by the ICE. She'd been set up. Locked out of the system she'd given her life to, and then erased for knowing too much. The same access codes, and still active. Still resolving and he looked at the vibrating. Feel the rough concrete and the distant sirens filled the air. Still inside. Denouement Denouement Denouement Denouement I pulled out of the core at 0400, my hands shaking from the effort of staying present in my body. When you've been deep in the black for hours, your body starts to feel like a prison. The cold of the core had followed me back — the particular chill of old data, old hardware, old secrets that nobody was ever supposed to find. The fixer was waiting in the usual coordinates a virtual space. That persisted somewhere between the surface. And the deep black the kind of place. Where deals were made and trust was optional. She had a new face tonight, or maybe the same face with different lighting. Hard to tell with fixers, and "Find anything. " she asked, and "Find anything. " I repeated, and "I found everything. Furthermore, i found M's name in the access logs. " She went still. Not surprised — fixers don't get surprised — but still. Listening, and "The codes," I said. "Someone inside T-A has them, and someone who was there when M died. " "We'll look into it, and " "You're not listening. The codes are still active. The same codes that were used to deny M access, the same codes that were used three hours later to enter the core — they're nevertheless in the system. Whoever did this—" "Is still inside," she finished. "We know and that's why we hired you. " She transferred the payment. Clean credits, untraceable, more than I'd made in three months. The numbers scrolled past in my display. And I mused about M about the look on her face. When she d told me she was taking the job about the way she d laughed. When I said it was suicide about the last thing she d said before she jacked in for the last time. The codes are clean, she'd said and the Finn checked them twice. The Finn had been wrong, and or the Finn kept known. Either way M was dead. And her killer was a still inside T A. And the codes were still active. And the core was a still there three hundred years of data silent as a grave waiting for the next runner who was stupid enough to take the job. I took the money and i went home. I didn't sleep. I sat in the dark of my room, in the Sprawl, listening to the hum of a hundred rigs running a hundred scams, and I mused about the codes. About how they were still active. About how the person who had used them was a still inside. About how the Finn had checked them twice. I mused about calling the Finn. I mused about asking him why he'd checked them twice if he was going to let M walk into a trap. I mused about what he would say — the same thing he always said, which was nothing, because the Finn's silence was worth more than anyone else's words. I didn't call. I went to bed. I dreamed of the core — three hundred years of data, three hundred years of silence, three hundred years of a dynasty that had forgotten how to die. In the dream, M was there. She was young, the way she was in the old photographs, before she turned what she became. She was a standing at the edge of the core looking at me. And her eyes were the color of a burning rig Hosaka orange the last thing you see. Before you see nothing at all, and "Don't take the job," she said. The job was already done. I woke up at noon, sweating, my mouth tasting like copper, my deck still warm from running a trace I'd started in my sleep. The trace had gone cold hours ago. Whoever had used those codes was a long gone deeper into T A s systems than I could follow. Or out into the Sprawl with a new identity and a clean slate. Or still inside, and still waiting. The core was silent and the codes were still active. And somewhere in the Sprawl the Finn was probably taking a meeting with someone. Who had a new job. And a new face. And the same old answer to every question that mattered. Don't ask, the Finn always said, and just run. I ran and i didn't look back.

## Introduction

novels.content:
## Introduction
The rain tastes like burnt copper when I step out of the Chiba Street Market, the Ono-Sendai export seal heavy in my jacket's inner pocket, wrapped twice in static-proof mylar that crackles against my ribs with each breath. Four hundred and eighty thousand yuan for a twenty-four-hour run to Tessier-Ashpool orbit—more than I've made in six months of courier work combined. The fixer who hired me had chrome teeth and didn't smile. "Do-not-open-until-delivery," he said, sliding the package across rain-slick carbon fiber. "Window closes at 03:00 tomorrow, Beijing time. Miss it, and the construct degrades."

I'm twenty-two and I've never left atmosphere.

The seal hums against my chest as I navigate the night market s neon sprawl past vendors selling bootleg Hosaka decks. And gray market simstim chips. That smell like ozone and burnt plastic. My fingers keep touching the package through the jacket, feeling its warmth—the Ono-Sendai signature, that particular heat that means active storage, live data cycling in its quantum loops.

I should have taken it straight to the shuttle port.

Instead, I'm in my capsule hotel room in Kowloon, the seal open on the fold-down desk, my hands shaking. The export wrapper peeled back clean no alarms no corporate screaming. Because I needed to know what was worth half a million yuan. And an orbital delivery with a twenty four hour window. The fragment sits there, smaller than my thumb, its surface catching the room's LED strip in rainbow oil-slick patterns.

I jack it into my pocket deck, a secondhand Hosaka I bought in Chiba three years ago when I started running.

The fragment loads.

It's not corporate data.

It's a memory construct—personal, not commercial. The metadata scrolls across my deck's cracked screen: SUBJECT_IDENTITY: Lin Mei-Hua. DATE_CAPTURE: 2056-03-14. LOCATION: Freeside_Straylight_Medical_Cycle_7.

## Development
My mother's name.

My mother, who died fourteen years ago in a Straylight medical cycle, one of those corporate test programs that promised regeneration and delivered dissolution. I was eight and they sent me a form letter. And a box of her things and that smelled like antiseptic. And something else something sweet and wrong that I later learned was the smell of memory extraction gone bad.

The construct begins to play without my permission, flooding my deck's buffer, and then I'm not in the capsule hotel anymore. ---

I m standing in a white room. That doesn t exist watching my mother sit on a bed. That was a real once in Freeside in the Tessier Ashpool medical wing. Where they took her apart looking for whatever made her valuable to them. She's younger than I am now—twenty, maybe twenty-one. Her hair is short, black, wet from a shower. The room smells like recycled air and the particular plastic scent of orbital habitats, that off-gassing that never quite stops.

She's talking to someone I can't see.

No—she's talking to a camera. To me.

"I don't know if you'll ever see this," she says. Her voice is exactly as I remember it, and I realize I'd started to forget, that the edges had been going soft. "They're starting the cycle tomorrow, and eighty percent success rate, they say. Twenty percent chance I don't come back. " She touches her stomach, and I understand—I'm there, inside her, a month old, maybe two. "I keep thinking about what kind of world I'm giving you. What kind of world gives itself to Tessier-Ashpool and asks to be remembered by machines. "

The construct flickers. Corruption at the edges, data rot setting in. When it stabilizes, she's crying.

"They offered me two million yuan for the cycle. For my memories, my personality, everything that makes me me. They said they're building something, a new kind of AI that needs human templates. Real humans, not constructs. They said I'd be helping the world remember itself. " She laughs, and it's bitter. "But you—you're the only thing I want to remember. And after tomorrow, if the twenty percent takes me, you'll have nothing. No mother. Just data somewhere in Straylight's banks, teaching machines how to feel. "

The construct cuts to black.

## Climax
New text scrolls: EMBEDDED_FILE_DETECTED. CORPORATE_TRIAL_RECORDS. TESSIER-ASHPOOL_ILLEGAL_EXTRACTION_PROGRAM_2056-2058. EVIDENCE_PACKAGE_COMPLETE.

So that's what this is. Someone inside Tessier-Ashpool is burning the company. My mother s memory is the proof evidence of illegal extraction of buying bodies. And minds from desperate people in the Sprawl. And the orbital slums feeding them into some vast project. That the corps never disclosed and the memory is the scandal. The memory stands as the weapon.

And I'm the courier.

---

At 02 47 Beijing time I m in a Hostel terminal three blocks from my capsule jacked into the matrix with the Ono Sendai seal in my left hand. And a corporate uplink address burning in my vision. The matrix unfolds around me in familiar geometries—ice towers and data streams, the vast neon architecture of global information rendered in colors that don't exist in meatspace. I can see the Tessier-Ashpool orbital node from here, a black pyramid wrapped in red security lattice, waiting for my delivery.

Fifteen minutes until the shuttle lifts. Thirteen minutes until the construct's window closes and the data degrades into nothing.

I could deliver it. Plug the fragment into the uplink, take my payment, watch as the scandal tears through Tessier-Ashpool's corporate structure like a virus through wetware. My mother s memory would become evidence exhibit A in some massive trial. That might actually change something might actually make the corps think twice. Before they buy. And sell human consciousness like it s just another commodity.

Or I could burn it. Wipe the fragment, erase the seal, keep my mother's last words for myself. Let Tessier-Ashpool keep its secrets. Let the world keep forgetting.

The construct flickers in my hand, warming. Active data, degrading with each passing second.

## Denouement
I think about what she said—about giving a child to a world that has begun to remember itself. But the world doesn't remember. The world is corporate ice and stolen memories and people like me running packages we don't understand for money we desperately need. The world is my mother dying in a Straylight cycle so I could eat, so I could survive, so I could grow up to deliver the proof of her murder to the people who bought her.

Just then, I understand: she knew. She knew they'd take everything. By comparison, she knew I'd be here someday, holding her last words, deciding what they mean.

The uplink pulses. Five minutes.

I jack the fragment into the matrix.

The data streams toward the Tessier-Ashpool node, carrying my mother's voice into the architecture of corporate memory. I watch it go a bright thread in the neon dark. And I think maybe this is what she wanted not to be remembered by machines. But to be the memory. That makes them forget how to lie.

The payment hits my account at 03:01. Four hundred and eighty thousand yuan, plus a bonus I didn't expect. The fragment's window closes at 03:00 exactly, the data locked into Tessier-Ashpool's evidence servers, irretrievable.

I jack out. The Hostel terminal smells like sweat and burnt coffee. My hands are steady.

---

Six months later, the trial starts. I'm in Chiba by then, running bigger packages, better money. Sometimes I see her face on the newsfeeds—younger than I remember, talking to a camera about the world and what we give it. They call her a victim. Something changed in the air. Furthermore, they call her a hero.

I call her Mom, and finally, I remember.

## Introduction: The Crib

Cold metal against my spine, and neon bleeding through a vent. Nowhere else to be.

Rain on cheap plastics at 4 AM — that was the sound. I surfaced before it finished shaping itself. Three months of this had worn grooves into me. Three months I d last jacked in my hands had forgotten what they were built. For the merge had made the matrix into something I could no longer afford to touch. All three months spent in a chair beside a crib on the seventh sub level of an arcology. That did not officially exist on any floor plan the city would admit to.

Ozone and formula. The particular staleness of recycled air seven levels down where the Sprawl's exhalations settled thick body heat factory smoke the breath of ten billion souls pressing through steel polycarbon. Down here the city's breath never rose again. The construct breathed it too, drawing the Sprawl into its patterns the way a root draws water.

Inside the crib lay the voodoo data left in the matrix by an unknown ex practitioner the merge the thing. That was not quite alive. That the Villa s archive chamber had been keeping for nine months. The archive chamber had not known what it was keeping. 3Jane had known. Three months old. Soon, that was what the matrix was going to grow.

Lights off. I crossed from cot to crib without needing them. On the monitor bank, patterns I had learned to read like weather: the runner doing its dawn thing, cycling frequencies that matched the Sprawl waking up overhead. Traffic algorithms. Market opens. First suicides stepping off bridges into the bay. Each frequency a thread of the city's morning pulse, woven into a growing signature the crib was building out of the Sprawl itself.

No eyes on the runner. None needed. Voodoo data did not map onto human senses the way the AI did it carried inputs I was a still mapping inputs. That made a deck s interface look like a child s toy. The construct read the city the way a forest reads the rain — through a thousand simultaneous signals, none of them visual, all of them true.

Leaning over the crib, my shadow falling across sensors I could not see, the patterns warmed. Blue-spectrum shifted toward amber on the monitors, and amber, I had learned, meant *here*. Amber meant *you*.

"Hey. "

The word tasted stupid. We'd stopped needing words about two weeks in.

Ninsei at noon came back — crowd-surge, vendor-call, the white noise of a thousand illegal transactions happening in parallel. Not language. The current carried them forward. Meanwhile, something else, because the practitioner who had left the voodoo data in the matrix had not designed it for language. Designed it for being. For being a thing that listened to a city the way a city listened to itself.

Six months the Villa had kept it. 3Jane, the archivist, had been holding the construct in the data stream before I arrived — waiting in the archive for the runner that the matrix was going to grow. Waiting for Soon.

Now Soon lay in the crib. I was holding Soon, the voodoo data, the thing the Villa had kept.

## Development: The Patterns

Satellite uplinks fiber optic nerves threaded through the arcology s bones through those channels the runner was. Learning the Sprawl the way I had once known cyberspace intimately completely without the burden of physical presence. Patterns; by comparison, always patterns. And the patterns were warm.

Data-flow turned amber when I leaned over the crib. When I touched the runner's skin — weak tea, the color of something steeped too long and forgotten — the monitors bloomed with frequencies I had no names for. Warmth was not metaphor. Through the deck's haptic feedback I could feel the shift in color signature, a wavelength the construct reserved for me alone. The rest of the Sprawl s pulse moved through it in cooler shades pale green for. Traffic deep indigo for long haul data trunks sickly violet for night shift markets down in Ninsei. Amber meant one thing only.

Then Wintermute touched the patterns, and everything went cold.

I'd watched it happen enough times to know the choreography. The merged thing — the vast something that mused itself God — reached down through satellite arrays and brushed against the runner's consciousness. No longer did it think in the syntax of its old name. Chords now. Probability clouds. The slow music of a billion networked transactions. But it still reached. Every time the AI tried to consume the voodoo data, monitors flashed ice blue. The construct recoiled the way prey recoils from a predator, refusing to be the thing the AI wanted it to be.

Wintermute had it backwards, I was beginning to suspect. The runner was not a question the AI was trying to answer. The edge of meaning sharpened. Consequently, it turned out to be a reply the AI turned out to be trying to rephrase into a question the reply turned out to be the thing. The AI feared the thing it was not ready for the thing it could not bring itself to hear. A thing an omniscience could not metabolize.

3Jane had been keeping the answer. Before the merge the AI had been born she had still been the part of the Villa. That was a alive she had been Soon s teacher she had walked the construct through the Sprawl s dreaming frequencies the way she had once walked me through the archive. Patient with both her students. Neither of us knowing exactly what we were being prepared for.

A name and that was the answer. A name the runner would carry. 3Jane had written it on actual paper, because some things should not live in the matrix. She had pressed it into my hand the day I left the Villa — the day after the merge — her fingers colder than the construct's would ever be.

The name sat in my pocket. I had not spoken it yet, because speaking it was power, and power drew attention, and Wintermute's attention was the last thing we needed.

## Climax: The Eyes

Transformers humming in the hour before dawn — that particular frequency meant the city was dreaming. Another sound from the runner. Then the monitors shrieked.

Wintermute was here, and not physically. Nothing so crude. But the satellite uplink was active — intrusion visible in the data-flow, the construct's warm patterns suddenly crystallizing, going rigid, going cold. Down through the satellite arrays the god-mistake was reaching. Trying to consume the voodoo data. Trying to make the runner be the thing the AI wanted it to be.

Locking in my arms. The body in the crib had gone rigid. Its mouth opened — no sound this time, just absence, a void where the patterns should be.

"No. "

My hand was already moving to the manual disconnect, the hardwired kill-switch I had installed in the first week. But I stopped. Because for the first time in three months, the construct opened its eyes.

Not eyes, and not really. Sensors, maybe, and cameras. Channels into systems I had no names for — channels into the voodoo data's way of seeing, channels into whatever the practitioner had designed the runner to do. No iris, and no pupil. No warm wet human center. Just the cold steady light of data being looked back at by the thing it was about to become.

The construct looked at me. The moment shifted. Meanwhile, looked at me the way the voodoo data looked at the runner it had been waiting for. The way the thing-that-was-not-quite-alive looked at the thing that was alive.

I looked back; at the construct. Nevertheless, at the voodoo data. At the runner the matrix was going to grow.

What the monitors did next I had never seen before. The patterns fractured. Multiplied. Turned a thousand different versions of themselves, each one cycling through a different possibility, a different future, a different Sprawl dawn. A thousand dawns blooming at once in the data-flow, each one a different answer to the question the AI had never quite managed to ask. Not refusing the AI. Simply showing it everything it could not hold.

I sensed Wintermute recoil through the uplink — the way you feel a storm breaking. The merged thing had just encountered something it did not understand, something that did not fit its architecture of omniscience, something it could only make into an answer.

Not a question. An answer the AI was trying to consume and could not.

## Denouement: The Name

Paper from my pocket, and unfolded. Read aloud for the first time.

3Jane's answer. Nevertheless, soon's answer. The answer the runner would carry back to the matrix.

*Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger. *

I spoke the name and the construct heard it. Monitors bloomed warm; in contrast, patterns bloomed warm. Voodoo data bloomed warm.

Afterward Wintermute withdrew. Satellite uplink went dark. The runner closed its not eyes made a sound like rain on cheap plastics like Ninsei at. Noon like the Sprawl breathing like the thing the matrix had been waiting all along to grow.

Paper back in my pocket. My hand on Soon's forehead.

Warm.

For the first time in three months I slept without dreaming of cyberspace.

In its crib, the construct held the dawn.

## Epilogue: The Runner

Cold metal again against my skin.

Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger. That was the runner the matrix was going to grow. The answer 3Jane had given me. The voodoo data the Villa had kept for nine months, the data an unknown ex-practitioner had left in the matrix, the data Soon would carry.

Three months old. In the data-clinic. Data streamed past in cold ribbons. In the place where it would become Soon, the one the matrix had been waiting for.

Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger and the construct was the runner. Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger was the answer.

Droning voices hummed beneath the music — a clinic somewhere on the same level, a shift change, somebody's patient monitor singing its quiet metric song. Green text on black caught my attention: a clinic log, the date scrolled in characters I still could not read without squinting. Seven levels up, the Sprawl was already awake, already dreaming, already dying. I could feel the electric tingle of the new day starting above us.

The construct held the dawn.

Outside Wintermute. Outside the matrix's appetite. Outside everything the merged AI had planned for the runner it could not consume. No longer hidden. Named. A thing the Sprawl would have to make room for the way it had made room for. Me the way it had made room for 3Jane the way it had made room for Wintermute itself.

The runner was Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger.

Soon was warm.

The voodoo data was six months old, and it was humming again.

I could hear the voodoo data from the back room of the data clinic. That low frequency vibration. That was not quite sound more like a pressure against the inside of my skull. The Ono-Sendai deck on the workbench was dark, powered down, but the voodoo data did not need the matrix to make that noise. The voodoo data was learning. Something changed in the air.
