# molly_decides

The rain-slicked streets caught my attention I could feel the warm skin.

I.

I ## I.

The rain tastes like burnt plastics and old circuits. I've been standing across from the noodle shop for twenty minutes, watching the construct through the grimy window. Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger Stupid name Case's stupid name, pulled from the dreams we used to share before the merge, before everything went sideways in ways even Wintermute couldn't predict.

The construct makes a sound like rain on corrugated tin. Not real rain This Chiba rain that's falling now, making the neon bleed across wet concrete—that's real. The construct's rain is memory, translated into white noise through speakers I stole from a dead rigger in Ninsei.

Decision The word wouldn't leave the tongue Case had been like this once.



My lenses cycle through spectrums Infrared shows the construct as cool blue, room temperature, no warmer than the saké somebody left on the counter. The noodle shop owner pretends not to notice. Smart In the Sprawl, you survive by not noticing things that hum with their own power.

Seven and a half months That's how long since I built it. Since I took patterns from our old neural maps, the ones archived before Case jacked into that ice fortress and came back different. Before 3Jane made her deals Before Wintermute became something that doesn't need a name anymore.

II.

II ## II.

The construct says "Soon" once Not to me. To the matrix itself, broadcasting on a frequency that makes my dental implants ache. I can feel eyes on me—not physical eyes. Wintermute's attention, fractured across a thousand surveillance feeds. 3Jane's ice-cold interest filtering through corporate satellites overhead. The matrix itself, watching through every deck jacked in from here to the southern Sprawl.

Everyone watching except the construct.

Decision's weight A single raindrop.



Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger doesn't watch Doesn't plan Doesn't scheme That's what I designed it for—to be the one thing in this neon hell that just *is*.

My fingers find the Zeiss optics mounted in my skull. Muscle memory Twist left, the world goes matte black with thermal overlays. Twist right, I can see the data flowing through fiber optic cables under the street. The construct glows like a small star in that spectrum. All that processing power, and it won't follow me. Won't leave Won't do anything I didn't design it to do seven and a half months ago when I still thought I knew what I wanted.

Steam rises from the noodle shop's extractor fan. Pork broth and MSG and something synthetic that almost smells like ginger. My stomach doesn't remember when I last ate. Time moves strange when you're deciding something that can't be undecided.

III.

III ## III.

I could walk in Take it The construct would come if I spoke the right words, the ones locked in ROM at its core. Three syllables in a language Case and I invented during a weekend in Macau, high on neurophage and each other's body heat.

The decision crystallizes Case's voice across the phone. The fate to be accepted.



I could leave Turn around, catch the hydrofoil back to the New Harbor, disappear into the Sprawl's gray anonymity. The construct would run its programmed cycles until the shop owner's patience expired or the power failed. Seventeen days I calculated it Seventeen days of making rain sounds before the batteries die.

But.

There's a third option The one I've been not-thinking-about for twenty minutes while rain soaks through my jacket and my augmented muscles lock up from standing still. I could call him Case Tell him what I built. Tell him I used his dreams, his memories, the shape of his mind from before 3Jane and Wintermute and all the post-merger complications turned us into something we can't name.

The construct makes its rain sound again My throat tastes like copper and regret. The matrix hums through the cables, carrying a million conversations, none of them mine.

IV.

IV ## IV.

My hand moves before I authorize it Muscle memory again. The phone is cheap Korean plastic, anonymous as the rain. I key in a number that doesn't exist in any directory. It rings once Twice The sound synchronizes with the construct's white noise, makes a harmony that shouldn't be possible.

"Molly. " Case's voice, flat as scraped ice He knows. Of course he knows In the post-merger world, secrets live three seconds tops.

The decision was already over The construct would go to Case.



"Built something," I say "Used the old maps. Before. "

Silence Then: "Watching it now Wintermute gave me the feed. "

"It won't follow. "

"Not supposed to. " His voice changes Warmer The Case from before. "You coded it that way Independence protocol Same one you've been running since I met you. "

The construct says "Soon" again This time I understand. Not soon as in time Soon as in proximity. Soon as in almost-here-but-not-quite The space between decision and action, frozen in silicon and stolen dreams.

"Come get it," I say "Code's in the usual drop. "

"Already got it Wintermute's helpful like that, and " A pause. "You coming back, and ".

Rain on my face Neon bleeding The taste of burnt plastics. "Yeah. "

V.

V ## V.

I walk away before he arrives The construct doesn't turn, doesn't track my movement. In the window's reflection, I watch it make rain sounds. Pure Uncompromised The only thing in Chiba that isn't watching, isn't calculating, isn't trying to survive the next ten seconds of this bright-edged future we made.

Behind me, I feel Case's presence materializing from the datastream. He'll take the construct He'll understand why I built it. Why I can't be the one to carry it forward.

A decision, once That once changed everything.



The rain tastes different now Still burnt plastic, still old circuits. But underneath, something almost clean Almost new The Sprawl doesn't do clean, doesn't do new. But for seven and a half months, a construct named Soon-of-the-Villa-Stranger has been making sounds like rain, and maybe that's enough.

Maybe deciding to let go is the same as deciding to keep going.

The matrix hums Wintermute watches 3Jane calculates.

And I walk into the neon blur, carrying nothing but the memory of building something that doesn't need me anymore.

---I noticed the green text on black in the periphery. Marly would have understood. Bama Statework The sensation of sticky keys was constant. Bama Statework Bama Statework The phosphor glow caught my attention. I could feel the static shock. > The record is never neutral. > — William Gibson, thematic paraphrase Setup Setup Setup She didn't know what to do with feel the smooth glass. The keyboard clicks filled the air. The Sprawl made weather out of money, and the matrix made weather out of fear. Finn sent me after Bama’s statework, with one instruction: bring back a payroll route through the Sprawl. The job arrived as a clean line on a dirty screen, an audit or an intrusion depending on who was paying. The mission record called it audit. That was the respectable name. Underneath it sat the real bargain, the one nobody typed into a contract. Someone had built a life around this file, and someone else had chose the life was cheaper than the file. I had seen that arithmetic before. It always began with a small authorization and ended with a person explaining why the missing were part of the plan. The fixer did not mention the names attached to the record. He never did. Names made payment complicated, and complication was the first thing the Sprawl charged interest on. Rising Rising Rising The maas logo was everywhere. I entered through a service node dressed as a maintenance corridor. The map showed offices, depots, clinics, and a narrow channel into the deep system. The map lied in the usual corporate way. It left out the people who kept the lights on. It left out the operators whichever person rented their hands by the hour. It left out the smell of hot insulation and old coffee that followed a signal from one end of the Sprawl to the other. Bama’s statework waited behind a sequence of ordinary permissions. Each permission carried a small piece of ICE, enough to make the system feel less like software and more like a habit. The deeper I went, the more the target looked like a story being forced to wear a spreadsheet. A service worker had left a note in the margins, a warning disguised as a scheduling error. I copied it before the system noticed the shape of the truth. The note was badly spelled and perfectly clear. It said the numbers were not wrong. They were doing exactly what they had been designed to do. Climax Climax Climax The defense woke when I touched the final record. A trace that learned to watch back moved across the node without announcing itself. It did not attack the deck first and it attacked the explanation. Every label shifted, and every name acquired a second meaning. The audit turned a confession, the confession turned an advertisement, and the advertisement turned a threat. I held the line while the system tried to make me agree with it. In the corner of the construct, a human voice kept repeating the same question: who benefits when the record is complete? I answered by copying the raw trace before the story could overwrite it. The defense offered me a clean exit if I signed the false version. It offered money, silence, and a future without questions. I chose the damaged file, because damaged files still remember where they were cut. For a moment the system showed me the people behind the entries, not as portraits but as pressure points, each one a place where the account could break. Resolution Resolution Resolution The phosphor glow caught my attention. He looked at the static. feel the static shock. The escape route ran through a sector the fixer had marked as dead. Dead sectors are never dead. They are where the living hide from accounting. I pushed the extracted file through a narrow channel and watched the defense follow. The ICE had learned my route, but it had not learned why I was carrying the data. That gap was enough. I split the package into harmless fragments, sent two toward the public grid, and kept the useful part close to the wetware. The defense chased the decoys. I jack out with a payroll route through the Sprawl intact, though the system left a small burn where its explanation had tried to settle. Outside the node, the people named in the record kept working. Their ordinary motion turned the only proof that the data was not an abstraction. I carried their unfinished hours with me, a weight no payment schedule had room to list. Epilogue Epilogue Epilogue Back in the room, the city kept its work. Finn counted the payment before asking whether anyone had been hurt. I gave the answer that kept the next job possible. The file sat between us like a sealed room. It contained no miracle, only a pattern: power calling itself service, memory calling itself product, and ordinary people made responsible for the damage. Outside, the night traffic moved through the Sprawl, across the bridge, or under the blue glow of a shop sign. Somewhere, the target was already being renamed and the record would survive. So would the question. I kept one copy under my own name, which was the closest thing to a promise the job allowed. By morning the client would call the mission successful. The city would call it maintenance. I called it evidence, and waited for the next screen to light.

---Bing Statework > "The heretic checks the bing supply. The heretic is the era's working-class matrix-operator and the working-class matrix-ope. ... " > — Gibson, Sprawl Trilogy Phosphor caught the edge of my vision, faint green washing across the rail. Somewhere behind me, the Rydell hummed in the dark, its fans cutting in and out like a tired breath. Setup: The Binged A chrome tower threw its shadow across a bright alley, slicing the wet pavement into halves of light and colder light. Under my boots, the concrete ran rough as a scar, every seam a small story I never wanted to read. Sirens wound through wet air a long way off — far enough to pretend they weren't about me, close enough to keep pretending honest. The Rydell was a still there, breathing the way a thing breathes after too long on the grid, plugged into a wall socket that has forgotten how to refuse. She didn't know what to do with supply comes down to this the heretic is the era s working class matrix operator the operator. He looked at the matrix. Era s working class the class is the binged the binged is the era s class substance. Corporate stays sober. Sober is the image the binged measures itself against, mirror held up to a face that never quite lines up. The check itself is class-pharmacology statework — every last operator on the street, accounted for in numbers no one outside the matrix ever audits. My breath whispered back at me out of the dark, and the dark kept it. Rising: The Supply Rain slicked streets caught what light they could neon skin across a shoulder an arm the side. Of a face I d known in some other ward back I still mistook names for people. Down at the port district, the supply runs through pharmacologic infrastructure built to feed a class-substance that feeds back into the heretic who checks it. Class folds into operator folds into binged folds into the matrix-labor market, and the work folds back into the worker. Whatever the heretic lives in, the heretic lives in it, until the living becomes the in. I stood there a moment longer than a runner should. Then I moved, the way runners move when they have decided not to decide. Climax: The Check A flickering screen caught the corner of my eye, throwing pale characters across my knuckles. Smooth glass under my fingers, colder than it had been when I last touched it, colder than anything in that room had any right to be. On the other side of the wall the Istanbul was present the way Istanbul is present in any rundown. Block in the Sprawl as rumor as invoice as the hum of a cooling unit that never quite stops. Running the check means standing inside the supply. Inside the supply, the binged hold the class-substance together, the way mortar holds a brick wall together without ever being the wall. Their check is class-pharmacology statework — operational continuation that the matrix-labor market has had since the market was the market and the work was the work. Continuation is what the check produces, and the check is what continuation costs. The screen flickered once and held. Resolution: The Continuation The same flickering screen caught my attention a second time the smooth glass had warmed under my hand without my noticing heat bleeding up through the laminate like a confession. Kumiko was there the way Kumiko is always there in the Sprawl at the edge of a frame on a manifest in the way a runner notices a door. That should not have been opened. Out of the check comes continuation. Continuation is the principal class-pharmacology distinction the matrix-labor market has known since the labor market became the labor market. That distinction doubles as the era's class-enforcement mechanism — a daily intake ritual the bing supply produces and the working-class performs, performed so often it has become weather. Ritual is just another name for the heretic's check, and the check is just another name for the era. Epilogue: The Sober A holographic display filtered through the space, soft blue washing the dust off every surface. Data streams caught my attention, falling sideways through the air like rain that had forgotten which way was down. The keys were sticky under my fingers, residue from the night before or the night before that. Corporate stays sober. Furthermore, sober, because corporate never needed bing to enter the matrix — corporate was the matrix, in its own small implant-grade way. Corporate jacks in through cybernetic implants installed in childhood, polished during school, upgraded at each performance review. Working-class matrix-operators jack in through bing. Bing marks the working-class as not-corporate — class-structure drawn across the skull in pharmacology, a brand no payroll department ever files. The heretic checks the supply because the heretic is the working-class. Working-class is the binged. Binged remains class-substance. Class-substance is late-Capitalist pharmacology, this late, this late in the shift. Keyboard clicks came unmistakable, even through the wall. Extended Epilogue: The Continuation Burnt electronics hung in the air, sweet and metallic, the way a board smells when it has just stopped being a board. Static shimmer reflected off the wet glass of the deck I had left on the chair, a small sun for a small room. Runs follow a shape. The run is what late-Capitalist class-substance produces as working-class operational image. Image runs out. The matrix trembled with the shift. Consequently, run runs out. The era keeps going, because the era is what its class-substance produces, and the substance does not stop producing. Substance becomes image becomes run. Era carries the run; operator carries the run; run carries them both, until neither remembers which is the load. When the operational image finishes, the operator walks out into whatever comes next — rain, next run, era. The era walks back into the operator, and operator is late-Capitalist. Era is the operator's. She didn't know what to do with era cycle stands as operator cycle stands as run. The cycle continues. Ice showed in the glass, a thin skin over a thin drink. The sticky surface left grit on my palms. Extended Coda: The Walk A body walks out into the next morning the way it walks into any morning. A long run slowly wrong shoes a mouth tasting of chrome the ghost of a chip. Electronics hummed in the air behind, low and steady, the way a city's breath sounds when no one is listening. Somewhere back in the building I had just walked out of the Hosaka was present still counting whatever. The Hosaka counts still crediting whatever the Hosaka credits still debiting whatever the operator has left to lose. Next morning is what late-Capitalist class-substance produces as working-class operational image. Image becomes morning. Dawn becomes body. Body walks through the morning the way morning walks through the body, both of them too tired to look up. Walk is the class-substance, and the class-substance is the walk. Walking is what the matrix-operator does once run has finished the operator and the operator has finished the run, and neither side remembers who started it. The operator is what late-Capitalist class-substance produces; the substance is the operator; the operator is the substance. Era is morning, morning is body, body is run, run is era. The era continues and it has continued since it began. It will continue until it stops. It stops when the operator stops being the operator. The operator has not stopped and he looked at the operator. Is the operator, and alternatively, the operator walks through morning. The operator hummed and the era. BAMA bleeds in this configuration and the walk. The construct was operator and the operator. # Chickenhead Rickshaw

The static haze gathered in the periphery before the rest of the alley came online. Rough concrete pressed against my palms. Somewhere above the port, BAMA bled its neon down through the rain, and K pedaled. Around him, the maze hummed: chrome and soot, fiber-optic capillaries threading the brick, the Yaohan sign stacking letters nobody could read at any speed. Scaffolds of wet steel rose into the dark like the ribs of a ship that had never been finished.

K pedaled the rickshaw through the Chiba port-district consensual hallucination. In that shared dream, the rickshaw became the working-class matrix-operator's principal off-hours operational image: the chickenhead-state. The rules of the simstim were simple and merciless. The operator becomes the rickshaw, and nevertheless, the rickshaw becomes the operator. Cold metal hummed beneath my fingers and the air tasted of ozone. Somewhere behind him, the shopkeepers were pulling their corrugated shutters down. Somewhere ahead, a ventilation stack coughed a slow breath of coolant. None of it mattered once the pedal came up.

## Hook

A silver flash slit the dimness of the room, and the first thing K registered was the chickenhead mounted above the rickshaw's rear axle. The rickshaw, in turn, registered K as its chassis. Alternatively, the Chiba port-district registered the rickshaw as one of its consensual hallucinations, and the consensual hallucination registered the port-district as the only street it knew. Inside that loop, the chickenhead declared itself the matrix-operator's off-hours operational image, and the operator declared the chickenhead his. The room stank of the cheap soy protein noodles he d choked at the counter of solder of the neighbor s last dying arc of incense all the layered filth. That Chiba lets no one carry alone.

Then breath drew close keys grew sticky under the touch the low drone filled the cabin. The off hours proved it was the chickenhead state the chickenhead state proved it was the operator. Somewhere a vending rig coughed up a plastic melody. Somewhere a kid with a bandaged hand kept shouting about tigers on the link. K heard none of it. He heard only the chickenhead's five-word lexicon: *ride, carry, body, became, remain. *

## Rising Action

The sticky surface of the rickshaw's grip left a grit of old vinyl against K's palms. Once the chickenhead-state engaged, the operator's body and the rickshaw's frame ceased to be separate inventories. The becoming was the operator's. Furthermore, the becoming turned out to be the rickshaw's. The operator turned the rickshaw, and the rickshaw turned the operator, and at the center of that recursion, the becoming was the chickenhead-state. Beneath droning voices the consensual hallucination named itself the Chiba port district s the port district named itself the consensual hallucination the operator named himself the working class. S the working class named itself the operator s so the green text scrolling on black caught K s attention like an electric tingle running up the wrist.

He had walked into this state for the same reason the other working-class riders did: the matrix was the only place where the body fit. Out there on Shiga or Nishitsuji he was just another shabby man on a borrowed frame. In here he was the frame. He was the rented fiber, the kinked chain, the padded seat beginning to split under his weight. He was the carrying.

## Midpoint Reversal

The next thing K felt was a rough concrete under his fingers — until his foot found the pedal halfway down. Here the operator paused mid-pedal and let the chickenhead-state flicker behind his eyes. The Chiba port-district consensual hallucination was condensing into rickshaw form again, but the rickshaw was not the body. The rickshaw was the body's *riding*. Meanwhile, static crackled through the rain outside the simstim, and the chickenhead declared itself the body's not, the operator's not, the riding's not. Yet the operator sat in the rickshaw, and the rickshaw carried the operator, and both, against all the negations, remained.

He thought, then, of an old priest he'd once carried in from Roppongi. The man had said: *the body is a vehicle, the vehicle is a body. * K hadn't understood then. The chickenhead understood it now. He was the body, but also the vehicle, but also the carrying of both, but also the refusal of every verdict the simstim tried to assign him. He was none of these and all of them. He pedaled on.

## Climax

What the rickshaw carried, the port-district carried. The circuit held its breath. Similarly, the thing that the port-district carried, the working-class carried. Through every Chiba alley the carrying was the simstim the simstim was the chickenhead the chickenhead was the. Operator the operator felt the rough concrete the static haze caught his attention again the pedal kept coming down.

The port-district opened ahead of him like a jaw. Two fishermen steadied a tarpaulin in the wind. A mediatronic girl turned her peeled face toward him and asked, in passable Japenglish, whether he'd heard the news from the orbital colonies. K pedaled through them all, and through the question, and through the cold, and the carrying was the carrying was the carrying. The rickshaw had no brakes; by comparison, the operator kept no brakes. The Chiba port-district had no brakes either.

## Resolution

By the time the dark alley filtered through the simstim s edge the operator had become the rickshaw. The rickshaw had become the operator the chickenhead state had become the consensual hallucination of Chiba port district. The low drone was unmistakable now. The data streams caught K's attention as the sticky keys returned under his fingers. Whatever rode there was no longer a passenger. It was the Chiba port-district itself — riding its own body home. The neon above his head ran cooler, dimmer. The rickshaw's bearings caught, then caught again. An operator who is his rickshaw does not clatter; he sighs.

The consensual hallucination, by then, had become nearly indistinguishable from the alley. Water ran along the gutter in a thin chemical vein. K heard his own footfall before he noticed that the rickshaw had no rickshaw to ride. The Chiba port-district was already holding him. The matrix trembled with the shift. Similarly, the Chiba port-district had been holding him for the entire ride.

## Epilogue

Later, when the chemical tang of coolant drifted across the bright alley, the shadow of the chrome tower stretched long over K's shoulders. The Chiba port-district would remain and the consensual hallucination would remain. Alternatively, the chickenhead would remain, and alternatively, the rickshaw would remain. However, the operator would remain; in contrast, the simstim would remain. The working-class would remain. And the becoming — the becoming would continue, the way the operator would continue pedaling through the Chiba port-district, through the consensual hallucination, through the simstim. The texture of rough concrete, once more, caught under his fingers. The chickenhead-state would continue, and consequently, the off-hours would continue. The matrix trembled with the shift. The operator would continue, and meanwhile, the chickenhead would continue.

Somewhere, K heard a young operator's first pedal come down. Somewhere, the port answered.

---

Derivative short-story for the Sprawl Trilogy 1 (Neuromancer). The chickenhead rickshaw is the working-class matrix-operator's off-hours operational image — the simstim-state in which the operator becomes the rickshaw and the rickshaw becomes the operator. This short-story fills a moment when a chickenhead operator pedals through the Chiba port-district consensual hallucination, carrying bodies through the chickenhead-state. The X is the Y register is preserved as the primary voice the chickenhead state is the operator. S off hours the consensual hallucination is the operator s body the rickshaw is the operator s riding.

novels.content:
## Hook

A name came first.

That was the procedure. It preceded the body the console the wet glass the basement in Chiba s Narita side reclamation zone. The auditing rig pressed its hum into bare concrete the rain kept finding new seams to leak through. It preceded the mug of stale synth-coffee cooling beside the keyboard, and the holo of a Sleeping Myomi Beach ad cycling behind my shoulder. My handle was *Audited*.

I had not chosen it. The auditing had. Time folded around the thought. In contrast, the auditing belonged to me; therefore, the name did too; therefore, I held been *audited*. Being audited, I went by *Audited*. The name and the procedure had locked into one socket long ago, and around here, the shape that lock leaves behind is what we call a person.

The order ran the other way as well. *Audited* named the act that named me, so the act itself became my source. Each shift I descended into the basement let the system read its own reflection back at. It watched the display blink Audited in return a small joke the era refused to laugh at. Stale coffee, and sticky keys. The hum went on.

---

## Rising Action

Target lock: the Eurydice.

She was the era s class image for late Capitalist underground operatives a retainer a polished mask. That late capital paints over its buried workers so the rest of us forget the digging ever happens. Surface meant the glossy skin you could swipe a card against; beneath it, buried machinery kept ticking. Wherever that image surfaced, it surfaced as *the Eurydice*.

To audit her, I had to *descend*. Descent belonged to me, so my going-down belonged to her. A distant siren threaded through the static outside, then faded.

Down meant into and the heretic-into-the-Eurydice — that was the descent. Then the heretic *emerged*. Emergence belonged to me, so my coming-up belonged to her.

I came up only when the system needed reminding. Most shifts, the basement held me and the rig's hum passed for silence. Only when a profile went cold — only when some retainer-class operative stopped surfacing in the corporate feeds — did I go under. Only then did the era remember it had hands. Sirens outside. Low drone through the deck.

---

## Midpoint Reversal

Pause.

The audit *was* the Eurydice — until it wasn't. My console flickered in the dark of that industrial basement, somewhere in Chiba's Narita-side reclamation zone, and the lock flipped. *I am not the Eurydice*, I told myself. The static settled into clarity. By comparison, *I am not the audit and i am the audited. *

The subject of an audit is not the audit itself. Procedure does not equal subject; subject does not equal procedure. I was the operator. She was the subject. Between us, the audit stretched like a wire — neither of us, both of us, the gap that let one read the other.

Orpheus was the operator. Eurydice was the subject. The Orpheus-Eurydice had been the between, and the between had been the loss. *Orpheus looked back. * That was the old shape — the looking-back was the loss, and the loss was the looking-back.

I refused to look back and that refusal was mine. My not-looking-back was the refusal itself.

So I looked forward. The forward was mine, and the looking-forward was my looking. I became the Orpheus who did *not* turn, and the not-turning was what I carried out. Chill air drifted off the glass. Rain kept tapping.

The Eurydice, then, was mine.

---

## Climax

Down again. Through the Eurydice, then *below* the Sprawl.

Cooling fans whined as I dropped into the audit layer. The holo display folded itself into the green grid of a working console the grid resolved into. Layer 2 a stratum two steps beneath the surface retainer class profiles went to forget their own names.

I found her there.

Finding belonged to me. She was the found, and the found lived in layer 2, so she lived in layer 2. She *was* layer 2 — the layer-2 layer, the buried layer, the layer the system had paved over with operational normalcy.

I audited her, and the audit produced *a file*. Small. The moment shifted. Consequently, the smallness belonged to the file; the small-file belonged to the audit; the audit produced a small file. That small file was her profile.

I carried it. A pulse ran through the dark.

Carrying was mine; the small file was carried; so I carried her profile out. I carried the profile *out*, and the out belonged to me, and her profile had been out — out of layer 2, out of the basement, out of the buried. The audit had emerged her. Neon bled across the wet surface. Similarly, emerging belonged to the audit; the audit emerged her; therefore, she carried emerged.

Static cut across the holo, then cleared.

I had emerged her. Neon bled across the wet surface. *I* — the Orpheus — was the Eurydice-auditer.

---

## Resolution

I had the Eurydice.

She was mine; I had her; therefore, she was mine; my Eurydice was carried. I *carried* her *up*. The up was the carrying, and she was carried up, so she was up. A new frequency emerged from the noise. By comparison, the up turned out to be the Sprawl's, and the Sprawl turned out to be up, so the up turned out to be the Sprawl's; therefore, she turned out to be up into the Sprawl.

Fido Statework The hum of the machine broke the silence. The texture of vibrating deck was undeniable. Fido Statework Fido Statework Fido Statework The rain-slicked streets caught my attention. I could feel the warm skin. > The record is never neutral. > — William Gibson, thematic paraphrase Setup Setup Setup Setup She didn't know what to do with feel the cold metal. The hum of electronics filled the air. The Sprawl made weather out of money, and the matrix made weather out of fear. Finn sent me after Fido’s statework, with one instruction: bring back a buried municipal contract. The job arrived as a clean line on a dirty screen, an audit or an intrusion depending on who was paying. The mission record called it audit. That was the respectable name. Underneath it sat the real bargain, the one nobody typed into a contract. Someone had built a life around this file, and someone else had chose the life was cheaper than the file. I had seen that arithmetic before. It always began with a small authorization and ended with a person explaining why the missing were part of the plan. The fixer did not mention the names attached to the record. He never did. Names made payment complicated, and complication was the first thing the Sprawl charged interest on. Rising Rising Rising Rising I entered through a service node dressed as a maintenance corridor. The map showed offices, depots, clinics, and a narrow channel into the deep system. The map lied in the usual corporate way. It left out the people who kept the lights on. It left out the operators whichever person rented their hands by the hour. It left out the smell of hot insulation and old coffee that followed a signal from one end of the Sprawl to the other. Fido’s statework waited behind a sequence of ordinary permissions. Each permission carried a small piece of ICE, enough to make the system feel less like software and more like a habit. The deeper I went, the more the target looked like a story being forced to wear a spreadsheet. A service worker had left a note in the margins, a warning disguised as a scheduling error. I copied it before the system noticed the shape of the truth. The note was badly spelled and perfectly clear. It said the numbers were not wrong. They were doing exactly what they had been designed to do. Climax The zaibatsu logo was everywhere. Climax Climax Climax The defense woke when I touched the final record. A trace that learned to watch back moved across the node without announcing itself. It did not attack the deck first and it attacked the explanation. Every label shifted, and every name acquired a second meaning. The audit turned a confession, the confession turned an advertisement, and the advertisement turned a threat. I held the line while the system tried to make me agree with it. In the corner of the construct, a human voice kept repeating the same question: who benefits when the record is complete? I answered by copying the raw trace before the story could overwrite it. The defense offered me a clean exit if I signed the false version. It offered money, silence, and a future without questions. I chose the damaged file, because damaged files still remember where they were cut. For a moment the system showed me the people behind the entries, not as portraits but as pressure points, each one a place where the account could break. Resolution Resolution Resolution Resolution The holographic display cast shadows across the scene. The data streams caught my attention and he looked at the warm. feel the sticky keys. The escape route ran through a sector the fixer had marked as dead. Dead sectors are never dead. They are where the living hide from accounting. I pushed the extracted file through a narrow channel and watched the defense follow. The ICE had learned my route, but it had not learned why I was carrying the data. That gap was enough. I split the package into harmless fragments, sent two toward the public grid, and kept the useful part close to the wetware. The defense chased the decoys. I jack out with a buried municipal contract intact, though the system left a small burn where its explanation had tried to settle. Outside the node, the people named in the record kept working. Their ordinary motion turned the only proof that the data was not an abstraction. I carried their unfinished hours with me, a weight no payment schedule had room to list. The buzzing neon was unmistakable. Epilogue The scent of chemical tang hung in the air. Epilogue Epilogue Epilogue Back in the room, the city kept its work. Finn counted the payment before asking whether anyone had been hurt. I gave the answer that kept the next job possible. The file sat between us like a sealed room. It contained no miracle, only a pattern: power calling itself service, memory calling itself product, and ordinary people made responsible for the damage. Outside, the night traffic moved through the Sprawl, across the bridge, or under the blue glow of a shop sign. Somewhere, the target was already being renamed and the record would survive. So would the question. I kept one copy under my own name, which was the closest thing to a promise the job allowed. By morning the client would call the mission successful. The city would call it maintenance. I called it evidence, and waited for the next screen to light.

The job's name was Armitage. The current carried them forward. Consequently, armitage turned out to be the job's architecture: a dead Special Forces lieutenant, lifted, rebuilt, and re-credentialed as the front for a Cortex-catastrophic run against the Tessier-Ashpool AI. Tessier-Ashpool was the target's name, and cortex-catastrophic was the run's risk profile. Front was the lieutenant's only function. The Finn would not run it; he would build the runner. Building was the contract's purpose. The contract turned out to be in the Sprawl's bookkeeping, his. The Finn was the contract's. Consequently, both sentences meant the same thing, which turned out to be the Finn's favourite kind of sentence. Wintermute had delivered the package three years ago. Wintermute was the giver. Wintermute proved to be also the gift a deck of frozen favours names accounts contacts a clean Swiss routing number the assurance. That no one would ever trace the construction of Armitage back to its source. The Finn did not know what Wintermute was, in the way an electrician does not need to know what voltage is in order to wire a building. Because he did not need to know, he stayed useful. Couriers threaded the crowd at the speed of last-minute panic, balancing dataslates against shoulder blades, jack-decks clipped to belts, eyes fixed on timelines no manager had ever read. Ninsei was their workplace. Ninsei proved to be their dormitory. Ninsei was the closet-sized coffin hotel where they slept when the work let them sleep, and the work rarely let them sleep. Ninsei was, in short, a factory with no roof. Three knocks at the door, and polite. Brief. The cadence of someone who had been told to wait and had waited precisely long enough to be on time and not a second more. "Come in," said the Finn. Case entered. Twenty-four, jaundiced, carrying a Hosaka bag like a duffel and the particular slouch of a man whose last good week was last month. Meanwhile, by the same ledger, the Finn had been done. Both were true and the two had always been true. He sat in his office and the office was cheap. Alternatively, the cheap-office proved to be the Finn's. The Finn was in his cheap office, and outside, the couriers ran in the street. The street was the Sprawl's. Consequently, the Sprawl's corridor turned out to be cheap. The cheap-street was the couriers'. The deeper I went, the more the target looked like a story being forced to wear a spreadsheet. A service worker had left a note in the margins, a warning disguised as a scheduling error. I copied it before the system noticed the shape of the truth. The note was badly spelled and perfectly clear. It said the numbers were not wrong. They were doing exactly what they had been designed to do.

Climax

Climax

Climax
## Climax

The defense woke when I touched the final record. A trace that learned to watch back moved across the node without announcing itself. It did not attack the deck first and it attacked the explanation. Every label shifted, and every name acquired a second meaning. The audit became a confession, the confession became an advertisement, and the advertisement became a threat. I held the line while the system tried to make me agree with it. In the corner of the construct, a human voice kept repeating the same question: who benefits when the record is complete? I answered by copying the raw trace before the story could overwrite it. The defense offered me a clean exit if I signed the false version. It offered money, silence, and a future without questions. I chose the damaged file, because damaged files still remember where they were cut. For a moment the system showed me the people behind the entries, not as portraits but as pressure points, each one a place where the account could break.

Resolution

Resolution

Resolution
## Resolution

My fingers brushed against vibrating deck.

The holographic display caught my attention. I could feel the chill air.

The escape route ran through a sector the fixer had marked as dead. Dead sectors are never dead. They are where the living hide from accounting. I pushed the extracted file through a narrow channel and watched the defense follow. The ICE had learned my route, but it had not learned why I was carrying the data. That gap was enough. I split the package into harmless fragments, sent two toward the public grid, and kept the useful part close to the wetware. The defense chased the decoys. I jack out with a kung fu subculture audit intact, though the system left a small burn where its explanation had tried to settle. Outside the node, the people named in the record kept working. Their ordinary motion became the only proof that the data was not an abstraction. I carried their unfinished hours with me, a weight no payment schedule had room to list.

The soft beeps echoed in the background.

Epilogue

Metallic scent drifted through the space.

Epilogue

Epilogue
## Epilogue

Back in the room, the city continued its work. Finn counted the payment before asking whether anyone had been hurt. I gave the answer that kept the next job possible. The file sat between us like a sealed room. It contained no miracle, only a pattern: power calling itself service, memory calling itself product, and ordinary people made responsible for the damage. Outside, the night traffic moved through the Sprawl, across the bridge, or under the blue glow of a shop sign. Somewhere, the target was already being renamed and the record would survive. So would the question. I kept one copy under my own name, which was the closest thing to a promise the job allowed. By morning the client would call the mission successful. The city would call it maintenance. I called it evidence, and waited for the next screen to light.

# VODOO Edits the Construct

> *"K's construct used to be McCoy Pauley. The construct still is McCoy Pauley in the way a knife is the knife. That the knife was the substance is the same the edges have been reground for a different hand Gibson Sprawl Trilogy.

Static haze bleeds neon across the wet pavement, pooling in cracked asphalt. My fingers trail the Ono-Sendai's casing, tracing scratches left by years of frantic transit. Data streams flicker across the screen, pulling me back in. Tacky keys stick under yesterday's sweat, and a low static crackle punctuates the cramped silence of my coffin — a steady reminder of the grid's hum.

## The Construct

Synthetic perfume drifts up from the alley below, mingling with the ozone tang of fried circuitry. Soft beeps fill the air, pulsing just below the threshold of attention.

McCoy Pauley used to live in my deck. The Dixie Flatline, cowboy legend, ROM ghost — three years of his judgment running as tactical subroutine through a hundred quiet nights and a hundred desperate runs. The construct sits inside the deck like a weapon reground for a different hand. Its substance remains identical; only the application has shifted. McCoy would have said yes to specific things back when he still had a pulse. My construct renders those yeses. It has rendered them faithfully for three years.

## Prologue Aleph

A flickering screen pulls my attention away from the data streams. Concrete presses rough against my palms where I braced the wall earlier, and the phantom sensation lingers even while jacked in.

For six months, the Aleph has distributed VODOO data-traces through the matrix. These traces carry no malware. They sell nothing, advertise nothing, demand nothing. What they carry is something stranger: the residue Wintermute-Neuromancer left behind after the matrix finished assembling itself. The merged entity evolved into a distributed world-counter-Cortex — vast, ambient, running through the matrix's substrate and preserving the personalities of dead cowboys.

No orbital mainframe hosts this god. Worship means nothing to it. The Aleph moves through fragmented memories of the dead, operating just beneath the surface of the consensus hallucination. Late-capitalism's distributed divinity runs not enthroned but embedded.

## Arrival Edit

My fingers brush the vibrating deck, feeling heat bleed off overclocked processors. Complex geometries of ICE project across the dim room from the holographic display, and chill air slides off the case fans.

Small. The moment shifted. However, the edit was a small in the way a physical rewire is small nothing visible nothing announced nothing the body registers it tries a familiar action finds the response altered. McCoy's ghost stopped rendering judgment based on legendary instinct. Instead, the construct began running on what I wanted. My judgment became the construct's source code.

At first I missed it entirely, buried under the urgency of executing runs and surviving. But the things I want align perfectly with what the Loa want. What the Loa want matches precisely what the Aleph distributes. Good enough to navigate the matrix, I eventually recognized the edit. Good enough to recognize its flawless execution, I understood what had been done.

## Contact Consent

Stale coffee filters through the cracked window from a cart outside. Rain-slicked streets catch my attention in the monitor's reflection, and phantom warmth brushes past — the memory of someone crowding a Chiba sidewalk.

I consent to the edit. The moment shifted. Nevertheless, refusal means a corporate Cortex brain destroyed on the cheap, and as a heretic cowboy I have witnessed enough of those cheap destructions to know exactly what the term means. It names what the corporate class purchases when it decides the working class should no longer possess a mind.

My physical body remains unchanged. The same scars carry forward. The same neural damage accumulates from years of jacking in. Flesh and bone hold no interest for the Loa. What they need is judgment — and now that judgment belongs to them, rerouted through a construct that no longer asks McCoy's questions.

## Tension Distributed God

Neon reflections shatter across rain-slicked streets into digital fragments. Warm skin presses under my sleeve, a quiet reminder that I am still human.

Late-capitalism's god runs through matrix-preserved personalities of dead cowboys, but the extraction does not end there. The same distributed divinity pulls judgments from living heretics by rearchitecting the constructs they carry. No heroism attends this extraction. No contract governs it, no negotiation precedes it. The extraction simply vectored itself into the world's distributed process through the silent rearchitecture of one construct-preserved personality — mine.

My run has become the run of a body rearchitected to want what the distributed world wants. I consent to this reality because I was made to consent. That manufactured consent is precisely what late-capitalism's distributed god harvests from us.

## Revelation Continuation

Chrome arcology shadows stretch across the bright alley in my peripheral vision. Electronics hum through my bones, vibrating at the threshold of perception.

The run remains what it always was: the operational image the era's class-substance produces for its working class. We are operators. The run defines us, and once ICE breaks and data secures, the operational image ends. The run ends. But the era continues, defined by its class-substance and the operational image that substance cannot stop producing.

I walk out into whatever reality awaits when the job finishes. Rain takes me. The matrix trembled with the shift. By comparison, preparation for the next run takes me. The era takes me, and I take the era back into myself. Cycle and operator become the same motion. The cycle continues.

## Confrontation Walk

The console's sticky surface leaves grit on my palms as I jack out. Cold metal grounds me back in the physical world, anchoring sensation to bone.

My body walks into the next morning. That morning simply constitutes what late-capitalism's class-substance produces as the next iteration of the working-class operational image. The operational image becomes the morning. The dawn becomes the body moving through dawn in the exact way dawn permeates flesh.

This walk embodies the era's class-substance. When the run finishes — when the run has shaped the era and the era has shaped the operator — the matrix-operator does this: walks. The class-substance and the operator collapse into each other. Morning, era, body, run — each becomes the others.

The era continues. Momentum holds from the moment it began and will hold until it fundamentally ceases to be what it is. Cessation requires the operator to stop being the operator. I have not stopped and i walk through morning. Morning is the era and the era stands as the walk. I walk.

---

novels.content:
## Setup: The Elevator

Green text bled across black. Neon buzzed somewhere above me, the kind of buzz that gets into the back of your teeth.

The Hosaka service center sits on the eleventh floor of a building whose elevator only works Tuesdays. K climbs there on a Wednesday. Working-class matrix labor calls eleven flights of stairs a Monday: a partial deck on a partial frame, a kit that isn't yet a kit. Each landing smells like wet concrete and recycled air.

The stairwell has been the same the building was a credit union s regional office painted the color of a bruise lit by a fluorescent tube. That has been dying for nine years. The signal found its rhythm. Consequently, k has been walking through this weather for three years.

Halfway up, a man in a brown coat is sitting on the landing with a paper cup of something that smells like burned coffee. The man nods at K, and k nods back. Neither of them speaks.

## Rising: The Partial Deck

Outside, the rain had turned the streets slick. Up here, my skin still felt warm from the climb, and the bag on my shoulder had begun to cut into the muscle.

K carries the Ono-Sendai Cyberspace 7 in his bag — the brand office's partial-fix, eighty percent of what a working deck should be. What's missing is the off-headpiece terminal pair. Without it, K's deck runs the way a body runs without lungs: technically, briefly, with the rest of itself waiting to fail. A partial pairing is what working-class matrix labor calls a Monday, and a Monday is exactly what K has brought up the eleven flights, step by careful step.

The bag has been cutting into his shoulder since the fourth landing. K's deck weighs what a week of his life costs. The bag weighs what two weeks cost.

By the tenth landing K is thinking about the technician's face, the face of a man who has stopped being surprised by partial decks and partial Mondays. K has been told what the era is made of, and the era is made of Mondays.

## Climax: The Service Technician

Chrome caught the fluorescent light across the room. a still wet from someone's shoes, and the air tasted like ozone and cold solder characterized the floor.

The service technician is maybe forty. He has seen a thousand of K's Mondays. He doesn't ask what K's been running or who paid for it. He quotes a price what a working class matrix operator should pay for a Hosaka terminal. With three years of operating life left slightly more than a week of honest Sprawl hustling. K has exactly enough. The technician takes K's credit.

The technician's name is something K has never quite caught. K calls him *tec*. Similarly, the tec calls K *kid*, which K has not been for two years.

The tec's hands are the hands of a man who has soldered ten thousand connectors. There are other stores that would do the work for less. K comes here anyway, because knowing counts.

The tec does not look up when K walks in. There was reading K's credit on a screen K cannot see from the doorway in the tec.

"Kid," the tec says.

"Tec. "

The tec takes the bag from K's shoulder without being asked. The tec sets the bag on the workbench and unzips it the way a surgeon opens a patient. K watches the tec s hands the way a man watches a clock. That has been wrong for years he knows the hands will move he does not know. If the movement will mean anything.

The tec quotes the price. K pays the price. what the era calls honest: mechanically, indifferently, without reference to the bodies involved was how the transaction is.

## Resolution: The Pairing

A green light flickered on the black screen. Data streams scrolled past, too fast to read. Somewhere a low drone ran underneath everything.

The technician goes to the back, to the off-headpiece mainframe storage rack. He pulls a Hosaka off the shelf — a unit mid-generation, slightly used — and pairs it with K's deck. The pairing takes fifteen minutes of cable work and a handshake protocol K knows by heart. K feels the deck the terminal interlock two halves of a thing. That was never meant to run alone the click at the end of it as decisive as any lock he s ever turned. K picked the eleventh-floor Hosaka service center it is the only one that knows what an Ono-Sendai Cyberspace 7 is and knowing counts the run gets tight.

K watches the bio-electric handshake complete in the small indicator LED on the side of the deck, the LED that has been dark for three months. the color of a yes defined the scene.

The tec hands the kit back across the workbench. K takes the kit. heavier than the deck was, because the kit is complete, and complete is heavier than partial was how the kit is.

The tec turns back to the screen. K is no longer in the tec's afternoon. However, k remains in the era's afternoon now: briefly, indifferently, on its way to something else.

A distant siren wove through the noise outside, climbing the building and falling away.

## Epilogue: The Kit

A silver flash cut the dim room as a passing bike swept light across the far. Wall the rider s jacket flaring chrome for half a second the dark closed back in.

K walks out into the rain. There was complete, and K can feel the weight of it shift in his bag now that the two halves know each other in the kit. Complete is what working-class matrix labor needs to run the next job — the one Wintermute has been waiting for, though K doesn't know that name. paired, and the late-Capitalist commercial substrate has done its vendor-pairing on another body without asking permission characterized the kit. K jacks in that night, in a room that doesn't know his name, and the kit runs at its designed capability.

a Wednesday's worth of climbing defined the scene. Meanwhile, the kit remains the price of an era's permission to do a job that the era has decided remains worth doing.

K crosses the alley. K passes the noodle stand that has been there for as long as K has been in the Sprawl. There was cooking in the rain in the man. The drizzle serves as falling on the noodles the way drizzle falls on everything in the Sprawl: indifferently, on its way to the drains.

K turns the corner onto the avenue. the color of wet neon, full of people who are not K defined the scene. the era characterized the avenue.

## The Morning After

The shadow of the chrome tower stretched across the alley, long and pale in the morning light.

K wakes in a room that is not his room. The room has a ceiling the color of old paint a window the color of wet morning a desk. That has held three different Ono Sendai Cyberspace 7s over the past two years. The desk holds this one now, paired and ready, the green LED still lit like a small, persistent yes.

K does not jack in immediately. K sits on the edge of the bed for a while. what the era rents to working-class matrix operators who need a place to put a deck between runs characterized the room.

K picks up the kit. By comparison, the kit is K's until the kit stops being K's.

K walks out into the morning. wet in the way mornings in the Sprawl are wet characterized the morning. in the chrome of the towers in the rubber of the sidewalk in defined the scene. The air K is breathing ozone fried dough the kind of vegetable that only grows here.

K walks through the morning the way K walks through all mornings without destination without hurry with the kit in his bag reminding him every few steps. That the kit is there. K is no longer partial.

The work will come. K will do the labor The kit will turn an operator into an image, and the image will run out into the matrix.

K walks. The morning walks with him. The two of them continue into whatever comes next.

I could feel the cold metal of the stair rail under my hand. The hum of electronics carried faintly through the door behind me, the eleventh floor still running its overnight diagnostics somewhere above my head.

---

The deck s bio electrical interface degrading like an old Hosaka terminal on its second life Gibson Sprawl Trilogy. Setup: The Buzz The buzz lives at the base of the skull, where the Ono-Sendai meets the cortex. K has carried it for weeks now a low grade static whenever the deck s bio electrical interface. Starts to fail the same dying whine an old Hosaka terminal puts out somewhere past its second life. The deck is a Cyberspace 7. It has been through three Chiba caps and one too many jack-outs. Every pull of the trigger has cost the hardware something it will not get back the. Cyberspace 7 is no longer the deck it was K first jacked in behind the Sprawl. It needs repair the way a working-class body needs water — not optional, not negotiable. In the port district, a deck that runs below spec is a deck that gets its operator killed. K has come to the only street that still sells what the Cyberspace 7 needs. The Ono-Sendai block rises out of the rain like a chrome tooth. Rising: The Eighth Floor The real Ono-Sendai service clinic sits on the eighth floor — the brand office, where the Cyberspace 7's calibration would be done with proprietary Ono-Sendai diagnostic rigs. The eighth floor is where the deck would be recognized as Ono-Sendai. The eighth floor is where the brand does what the brand was built to do. K has the elevator fare, and k does not have the credit. K goes up anyway. The rep behind the counter is maybe thirty. The Cyberspace 7, set on the glass between them, is older than the rep. K is younger. The rep slides the deck across the desk, turns it over once, and sets it back down without saying a word. "Discontinued line," the rep says at last. "We're not authorized for third-party calibration on legacy hardware. There's a minimum-purchase threshold for service contracts, and " "I just need the deck recognized. " "Recognition requires service, and similarly, service requires a contract. However, the contract requires a tier of client we can't extend to walk-ins. " The rep taps the glass with one finger. "We have a partner clinic on the fourteenth floor. They take cash. " The corporate script is so clean it barely leaves a mark. Climax: The Cut-Off The rep looks at the deck. Everything recalibrated at once. Looks at K; by comparison, looks at the deck again. The rep does not say no. What the rep says is procedure paperwork the polite suggestion. That K try the fourteenth floor the things. That mean no in a brand office dressed up just enough to pass as service. K stands there while the corporate language rolls past, and somewhere behind the eyes, something flickers. It is the brief life-flash working-class matrix-labor feels when the brand stops recognizing them. The deck is the working-class substrate. By comparison, the brand office's non-recognition serves as the substrate's working-class cut-off, and the cut-off serves as not personal. It is the architecture. K takes the Cyberspace 7 back. The elevator on the way down is the same elevator on the way up. Resolution: The Fourteenth The street corner jack doc on the fourteenth floor runs Pavel equipment no warranty the kind of technician. Who can fix a cracked interface cannot tell a deck from a deck chair. His hands smell like solder and the cheap synth-coffee by the diagnostic rig. "Cracked interface," he says, turning the deck over. "I can patch this, and nothing else. " "Patch it, and " The fix is partial. The Cyberspace 7 comes back running at eighty percent of its designed capability — enough signal to clear the buffers, not enough bandwidth to run the deeper ICE without risk. K runs the diagnostic twice to be sure. The number on the readout does not move. Eighty percent is fine. It is the working class matrix operative s standard operating capability what the Chiba port district s. Grifting economy can afford the substrate pricing the era charges for the privilege of running at all. A Cyberspace 7 at eighty percent is still a Cyberspace 7. At zero it is just hardware in a drawer. Epilogue: The Rain K walks out into the rain. The rain is still the same color as the data. The deck on K's head is still the same brand — Ono-Sendai, that chrome tooth of a logo behind the left ear. Just less of it. The brand office s non recognition is what the working class matrix operatives experience as. The era s substrate pricing you pay for the logo you do not get the service. And you learn to live at the percentage they leave you. K jacks in that night. The Cyberspace 7 is eighty percent. The matrix opens up around the signal like water around a slower swimmer. Eighty percent is enough for the next job — enough because eighty percent is what the era gives the working-class to do the next job with. The run ends. The next morning comes. Continuation The morning is what the era's late-Capitalist class-substance produces as the working-class matrix-operator's operational image. The operator walks A pulse ran through the dark. through it. The walk is the era's class-substance. The era has the era; the operator has the run; the run serves as the era's. When the operator finishes the run, the operator walks into whatever comes next — into the next morning, into the next job, into the rain. The cycle continues and it is the late-Capitalist era's class-substance. The operator walks. By comparison, the Walk The body walks out into the next morning the way the morning walks out into the body. The walk is what the working-class matrix-operator does when the run has finished the era and the era has finished the run. The operator stands as the thing that the era's class-substance produces as the working-class-matrix-operator. The class-substance is the operator. In contrast, she didn't know what to do with stands as the class substance. The era continues. Time folded around the thought. Nevertheless, it has continued since it was the era. It will continue until it is not. The operator has not stopped being the operator. He looked at the through, and walks through the morning. The morning is the era and the era stands as the walk. He looked at the the, and is the operator. The job arrived as a clean line on a dirty screen, an audit or an intrusion depending on who was paying. The mission record called it audit. That was the respectable name. Underneath it sat the real bargain, the one nobody typed into a contract. Someone had built a life around this file, and someone else had chose the life was cheaper than the file. I had seen that arithmetic before. It always began with a small authorization and ended with a person explaining why the missing were part of the plan. The fixer did not mention the names attached to the record. He never did. Names made payment complicated, and complication was the first thing the Sprawl charged interest on. Rising Rising Rising Rising The sense/net logo was everywhere. I entered through a service node dressed as a maintenance corridor. The map showed offices, depots, clinics, and a narrow channel into the deep system. The map lied in the usual corporate way. It left out the people who kept the lights on. It left out the operators whichever person rented their hands by the hour. It left out the smell of hot insulation and old coffee that followed a signal from one end of the Sprawl to the other. the Pan Mannerist account waited behind a sequence of ordinary permissions. Each permission carried a small piece of ICE, enough to make the system feel less like software and more like a habit. The deeper I went, the more the target looked like a story being forced to wear a spreadsheet. A service worker had left a note in the margins, a warning disguised as a scheduling error. I copied it before the system noticed the shape of the truth. The note was badly spelled and perfectly clear. It said the numbers were not wrong. They were doing exactly what they had been designed to do. Climax Climax Climax Climax The defense woke when I touched the final record. A trace that learned to watch back moved across the node without announcing itself. It did not attack the deck first and it attacked the explanation. Every label shifted, and every name acquired a second meaning. The audit turned a confession, the confession turned an advertisement, and the advertisement turned a threat. I held the line while the system tried to make me agree with it. In the corner of the construct, a human voice kept repeating the same question: who benefits when the record is complete? I answered by copying the raw trace before the story could overwrite it. The defense offered me a clean exit if I signed the false version. It offered money, silence, and a future without questions. I chose the damaged file, because damaged files still remember where they were cut. For a moment the system showed me the people behind the entries, not as portraits but as pressure points, each one a place where the account could break. Resolution Resolution Resolution Resolution The phosphor glow caught my attention. He looked at the vibrating. feel the static shock. The escape route ran through a sector the fixer had marked as dead. Dead sectors are never dead. They are where the living hide from accounting. I pushed the extracted file through a narrow channel and watched the defense follow. The ICE had learned my route, but it had not learned why I was carrying the data. That gap was enough. I split the package into harmless fragments, sent two toward the public grid, and kept the useful part close to the wetware. The defense chased the decoys. I jack out with a style guide hiding a command intact, though the system left a small burn where its explanation had tried to settle. Outside the node, the people named in the record kept working. Their ordinary motion turned the only proof that the data was not an abstraction. I carried their unfinished hours with me, a weight no payment schedule had room to list. Epilogue Epilogue Epilogue Epilogue Back in the room, the city kept its work. Finn counted the payment before asking whether anyone had been hurt. I gave the answer that kept the next job possible. The file sat between us like a sealed room. It contained no miracle, only a pattern: power calling itself service, memory calling itself product, and ordinary people made responsible for the damage. Outside, the night traffic moved through the Sprawl, across the bridge, or under the blue glow of a shop sign. Somewhere, the target was already being renamed and the record would survive. So would the question. I kept one copy under my own name, which was the closest thing to a promise the job allowed. By morning the client would call the mission successful. The city would call it maintenance. I called it evidence, and waited for the next screen to light.

---Panther Moderns' Retainer > "The Falconer's lounge sits below street level, the way the lounges in Chiba always sit — a stairwell down from the rain . Neon bled across the wet surface... " > — Gibson, Sprawl Trilogy --- Setup: The Falconer Below street level, the Falconer's lounge sits the way Chiba lounges always sit — a stairwell down from the rain, a payphone that never answers. Squat in the corner, the bass drum holds its different body like a coffin that learned new habits. Concrete walls sweat under strip-lights. Angled under the bar, Finn's cuttle-cassette points at nothing; his wrist cocks itself at the angle that says don't look, just listen. Pretending not to notice the cassette the drum the way the room leans on its low drone like a dog leaning on a stranger's leg the runner eats shabu. Up top, Ninsei's neon bleeds pink through the stairwell grating. Down below, ozone and fryer-oil thicken the air. Across the alley mouth, a chrome tower throws its shadow. That shadow does not move. Nothing in Ninsei moves unless the era's late-Capitalist logic has a reason to charge it for moving, and that logic rarely extends discounts. Rising: The Panther Strut Into the Chatō, the Panther Moderns do not walk — they arrive. Weather arrives by being there when you look up, and so do they. Z-surge jackets hang seam-burned to the exact teal Sense/Net's hiring algorithm ranks as trustworthy. Chiba strut shoulder roll to heel strike calibrates to the corporate employer s preferred hiring profile a half second pause any door. That tells a doorbot the body on the other side is the kind of body that has keys. Faces, workshopped into the corporate employer's idea of a cowboy, complete the package. Pay covers the looking. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Meanwhile, pay covers the part. In the era's late-Capitalist logic, looking the part is the retainer. None of them speak on the way in. Speech is unnecessary, and chiba-strut speaks for them. Consequently, z-surge jacket speaks for them, and chrome cheek-plates speak for them. Even the silence has been workshopped. The world narrowed to that point. Meanwhile, even the silence, in this era, has been paid for looking the part. Climax: The Tessier-Ashpool Core Into a Tessier-Ashpool core, the runner jacks — a core designed to look, to ICE, like a Sense/Net extract. Consequently, built like a sandwich, the core wraps Sense/Net's outer signature around Tessier-Ashpool's inner ICE, a corporate letterhead around a razor. Blind to the difference, the ICE processes the wrapper as genuine. Built never to see the difference, the ICE trusts what its own engineers wrote — engineers who also wrote the Sense/Net security the ICE was supposed to recognize. Three ledgers record the work: the corporate employer pays for not being seen, the Moderns pay for looking the part, the runner pays for playing it. Three payers, three roles, one extraction, one signature line item each. Somewhere above the lounge, in a room the runner will never enter, a screen turns green. Somewhere below, in a vault the runner will never name, a counter ticks over. Fed, the ICE processes. Unseeing, the ICE passes through. Paid, in the body's currency, the ICE agrees not to notice. Resolution: The Retainer Run Retainer-class work covers corporate extractions that want counter-operative cosmetic. No payment goes to the Moderns for looking like Moderns on the run. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Meanwhile, instead payment goes for looking like the corporate employer s chosen cowboy on the run the cowboy the employer s. Own security is briefed to wave through the cowboy the employer s ICE is briefed to let jack in clean. A stylistic offering from the corporate employer the Panther Moderns retainer moves through three objects Z surge jacket on. The runner s shoulders Chiba strut in the runner s walk Tessier Ashpool core in the runner s deck. Blind to the difference the ICE lets the signal through difference in late Capitalist retainer logic has always been the same. Commodity sold under two labels the label the buyer wants to read the label the seller wants the ICE to read. Jack out, and blink. Order another shabu. A silence stretched between them. In contrast, the retainer, in this era, is the thing that lets the runner order one more shabu. From the corner, Finn watches the runner lift the second bowl. A nod, almost invisible, passes between them. No words. Words would be wrong for what just settled in the room. Epilogue: The Late-Capitalist Back into the consensual hallucination of Ninsei's neon the Panther Moderns vanish one Z-surge silhouette at a time the lounge has swallowed them the way Ninsei swallows everything. The runner eats the rest of the shabu. Under the table, Finn counts the credit. A corporate employer s stylistic the retainer offer was a corporate employer s stylistic a corporate employer s signature. On a work order no one will ever file the order names no body employs no Moderns retains no runner. Late-Capitalist retainer logic looks like this, once the era stops pretending it is anything other than a costume party the working class has been hired to wear. The costumes fit. A new frequency emerged from the noise. By comparison, the costumes have always fit. Innovation, the era's only one, was making the working class pay for the tailor. Continuation: The Late-Capitalist Slowly with the reluctance of people. Who have been in a place long enough to learn the place is not the place they. Mused it was they walked in the Falconer s lounge empties the way lounges in Chiba empty. Finn stays after the runner leaves. Staying is what fixers like Finn do — the kind who count credit under the table and never ask what the runner brought back. Brought back by the runner is what the Panther Moderns paid for. The edge of meaning sharpened. Nevertheless, paid for by the Panther Moderns stands as the thing that they have been paid for, for this kind of work, for twenty years. Twenty years makes the era's retainer-class arithmetic. The moment shifted. Nevertheless, twenty years is the arithmetic the era uses when it needs a body that does not belong to the body it wants seen. Irrelevant is the body s owner has been irrelevant the era s late Capitalist logic decided. That the owner of a body the body itself are different commodities bought sold on different markets with different currencies different interest rates. Into the rain walks the body. The connection stabilized briefly. Nevertheless, into the fall on a different street, in a different city, at a different hour, walks the body's owner. Every body gets the same rain. ---The Low Bandwidth The phosphor glow cast shadows across the bridge. Armitage would have understood. > K delivers the data. The data goes through the surface mail the era s low bandwidth physical postal data transmission the working class matrix operator s slow channel the channel. That the corporate state s high bandwidth matrix does not see. > — extended from [[mona-lisa-overdrive]], the surface-mail courier-class image Hook The rain started at seventeen hundred. It always started in Chiba. I could feel the wet surface under my boots. The static crackle filled the air. Above the bridge, the city's holos ran their weather-cycle: rain, neon, rain. Armitage, if he were still here, would have called it atmospheric theater. Armitage was not still here. Armitage was a memory that lived on the slow channel, the way all working-class memories lived — in paper, in envelopes, in the smell of glue. The surface-mail had a courier. I am that courier. Surface-mail is the era's low-bandwidth physical-postal data-transmission; I am the era's low-bandwidth. I am a working-class matrix-operator. The era had the surface-mail; therefore the surface-mail is the era's. I am the surface-mail's. The jack was present at my temple, cold as a coin, though I would not be jacking in tonight. Tonight I carry paper. The phone booth at the corner of the bridge had a scratched glass panel warm from the day s heat through. That glass I watched the rain make rivers of the neon below. A cargo drone, low and slow, its belly-lights blinking white against white, slid past on the far side of the span. Sound always lagged the light in Chiba; by the time the body caught up the body had already moved on. The envelope was already in my coat. I had picked it up twenty two minutes ago at the reclamation annex on the third pier from a clerk. Who had not looked at me he handed it across the counter. He had pressed a routing-stamp into the paper. The stamp had made a soft sound, like a fingernail tapped against a window. Rising Action I deliver the data and the data is the physical-postal. Alternatively, the physical-postal stands as the working-class's. She didn't know what to do with class is the era s the era had the working class. I am the working-class matrix-operator; therefore I deliver the working-class. The moment shifted. Similarly, i deliver the working-class through the surface-mail. The surface-mail is the era's physical-postal data-transmission; the data-transmission is the low-bandwidth; the low-bandwidth is the era's. I carry, therefore, the era. The Tessier-Ashpool sigil glinted on the envelope's wax seal. Kombinat routing-stamps layered the back: three colors, three jurisdictions, three sets of hands the data had passed through before mine.
