## I: The Pickup

The package waited at the back bar of the Cloister You didn t choose the Cloister so much as the Cloister chose you usually midnight usually on a dare usually at the tail end of a night that had started with better intentions.

Chevette hadn't set foot in the Cloister for four years At nineteen she'd been a regular. The year after, she learned the Cloister was the kind of place the city eventually asked you to leave. The city hadn't quite asked her, though One Tuesday in October, the city simply failed to be there.

She never went back.

The man at the back bar was a stranger Tall wearing a shirt she recognized as the standard issue of a particular private security contractor. And he didn t look up she came in didn t look up she stepped to. The bar looked up only she said the four words she d been told to say.

"Order for Washington. "

He slid the package across It was the size and weight of a hardback book, wrapped in a way she couldn't quite describe as *delicate*. Not a bomb Not a thing demanding a careful hand A thing wrapped by someone whose actual job was wrapping things carefully.

She put the package in the courier bag She didn't zip it She never zipped the bag on a first pickup She didn't know why.

She left by the side door, which opened onto an alley that smelled of rain not yet fallen She wheeled the bike out, swung a leg over, and pushed off.

The bike was a Bridgestone twelve years gone itself When new it had been the bike of a man. Who had loved it now it was the bike of a woman who had loved it back Three sets of tires Two chains One saddle She had never changed the handlebars The handlebars were the part of a bike you fell in love with first you didn't fall in love twice.

## II: The Route

The delivery was to a building on Folsom near Brannan The building was the kind. That didn t wear a sign on its face a former warehouse a former loft a former something else now a something the city declined to name. The recipient's name was on a paper slip in the courier bag A name Chevette had never heard.

She took her usual night route Down Folsom to the Embarcadero Up the Embarcadero, into the wind, until the wind turned and went slack. Across Market Down Mission Across Sixteenth Down to the lower avenues Through the Mission at three in the morning the murals weren't visible the paint still smelled of the day.

Mission at three was a different Mission than Mission at noon At three, Mission had decided to be a place people lived in. At noon, it was a place people visited Chevette preferred the three o'clock version, though she'd never said so to anyone.

The wind off the Bay had picked up It was a wind that wanted to be in the city. The city didn't want it The wind came anyway, in long horizontal pushes that caught her at intersections and forced a particular kind of attentive lean.

The package shifted once, on a hard corner at Twenty-Fourth She steadied it through the courier bag with her left hand without slowing down.

## III: The Hill

The hill was on Potrero Not a large hill just one she d been riding up down for eight years. Without ever finding it easier Some hills didn t get easier Some hills were hills they didn t get easier.

She stood on the pedals The Bridgestone wasn't a bike for standing It was a bike for sitting spinning The hill didn't care The hill was a hill.

A car passed her on the left No honk No slow-down The kind of car that didn't slow for hills the car didn't have hills It had been built for a different city.

She didn t hate the car She didn t love it The car was just a thing happening. In the same city as her at the same time climbing the same hill by a different method.

At the top she stopped Not to rest She stopped the view from the top of. Potrero at three in the morning was a view she d never quite gotten used to. The city below The Bay beyond the city A Bay whose darkness wasn't the absence of light but the presence of a thing that had decided to be dark.

She rested her hand on the saddle She didn t look at her phone She didn t check the time Eight years had taught her. That the time was not the gift the city offered at three in the morning on top of Potrero. The gift was the city itself, looking the way the city looked when nobody was checking the time on it.

She got back on She pushed off.

## IV: The Drop

The building on Folsom had a door that didn't look like a door It looked like a wall, with a small black rectangle in the lower right corner. The rectangle was a keypad The keypad wanted a code The code was on the paper slip.

She punched the code The wall became a door The door was a heavy in a particular way. Heavy it had been built to be heavy not heavy it had been built to keep people out. It was the kind of heavy that existed to keep the wind from opening it by accident.

A man stood on the other side The same man, she understood immediately, who had been at the back bar of the Cloister He had gotten there first.

He held out his hand She didn't shake it She unzipped the courier bag (for the first time that night) took out the package put it in his hand.

"Sign," she said.

He signed No thank you She didn't need a thank you She hadn't delivered the package for thank you. She'd delivered it for the money and the night and the ride and the city, all of which were the same thing.

She wheeled the bike back through the heavy door The door closed behind her.

She didn t ask what was in the package She d never asked The dispatcher had told her in her first week. That the not asking was part of the job It wasn't a policy It was the way the job kept itself a job not a thing you thought about at three in the morning on top of a hill.

She didn t need to know Twenty six years of being a person had taught her. That most of what people delivered to other people did not on delivery change the kind of person the deliverer was. The deliverer was the deliverer The package was the package The night was the night.

## V: The Return

Down Brannan to Third Across Third against traffic the city empty around her The Bridgestone on the flat was a different bike On the flat the Bridgestone was a bike. That had been built for this for empty streets at four in the morning for the long glide of a freewheel on smooth asphalt for the particular quiet that came from not having to do anything except keep going.

She took the Embarcadero north The Ferry Building was lit as it always was with the particular kind of light meant to suggest without quite saying. That the Ferry Building had been a ferry building once The light was a lie, but it was a lie the city had agreed to.

The Bay on her right was not the Bay she d seen from Potrero The Bay from the Embarcadero was a Bay. That had been told by the buildings what to look like The Bay from the Embarcadero was a Bay with a job The Bay from Potrero had been a Bay without one. Chevette preferred the without-a-job Bay, but she respected the with-a-job Bay, and rode beside it now without resentment.

She took the hill up to the bridge approach At four in the morning, the bridge approach belonged to nobody. A road built to connect two cities, both of which were asleep, the road itself a road in between.

The bridge when she reached the western span was a loud Loud at four in the morning the way. The span proved to be loud at four in the daybreak wind cables the slow patient humming of the suspension stays. Chevette knew this sound She'd known it for years In all those years, she hadn't gotten used to it, and she hadn't decided to.

She took the catwalk The catwalk was her route The catwalk was she lived in the technical sense she wasn't at her apartment in the city-sense sense on Folsom.

A man she knew was on the catwalk He sat on a cooler He was reading a paperback He looked up when she passed.

"Long one," he said.

"Long one. "

He nodded She nodded She didn t stop She didn t slow She coasted past him with the kind of small careful lean a biker gives a catwalk at four in the morning when the grating has decided for reasons of its own to be slippery.

She took the ladder down to her level She unhooked the bike from her shoulder She set it against the wall of her space.

Her space was a six-by-eight rectangle of plywood and salvaged carpet, tucked between two of the bridge's larger cross-beams. A sleeping bag A kettle A small gas burner A paperback she'd been reading for three weeks.

She didn't read the paperback tonight.

She sat on the sleeping bag She took off her shoes She put her feet up on the cooler.

Outside the plywood, the bridge hummed.

Outside the bridge, the city slept.

Outside the city, the Bay, having decided to be dark, stayed dark.

She reached into the courier bag Nothing in it There was never anything in the. Courier bag a delivery In eight years of deliveries she had never once left anything behind.

She put the bag down She pulled the sleeping bag up to her chin.

She slept.

---

---Cool. --- Coolhunter — Laney, Tokyo The flight had been a wet dream of jetfuel recycled air Eighteen hours out of Kennedy eleven of them over water. Brand. That looked like hammered tin now she stood on the second floor walkway of Narita trying to remember which way was up. Laney Nobody called her Cayce anymore Laney had been the brand Hibiki had built her into, so Laney was the brand, and the brand was what Blue Ant paid for. Her coat was a wrong She'd known it the moment the gate opened and the humidity hit her like a damp hand across the face. Wrong color, wrong weight, wrong century She should have let Parkaboy's assistant send the Yamamoto she'd been offered. She hadn't Stubbornness was a craft habit, like the way she refused to eat on planes. The taxi was a Toyota capsule with a driver who drove like a man late for his own funeral. Laney watched Shinjuku assemble itself in the windshield The neon came on in layers First the reds. Then the cyans Then a kind of white she d never seen outside of Japan a white. That appeared to be the negative of a color she d once known the name of. She thought: footage is footage, footage is footage. The phrase was a tic She had a hundred of them The trick was to keep them quiet when she was working. Blue Ant s Tokyo office sat on the seventeenth floor of a Mori tower The lobby smelled like cold stone. And money She let her retina scan at the desk a girl who couldn t have been older than twenty five smiled at her in the polite accommodating way Japanese service industry workers smiled at all foreigners. Misunderstanding Laney always looked for it It was her actual product, the thing she could name with accuracy, the thing Parkaboy's boutique valued. The misunderstanding sat at the center of every brand she'd ever traced It was the engine It was also the toxin. In the elevator she pulled out the chipped deck she carried It logged everything The chip s eye saw. What her eyes saw ran it through software Parkaboy had stolen half from Blue Ant half from the CIA. And handed her the rough draft of a verdict her spine had finished settling on a posture. She didn't open it. Not yet. Hiroyuki-Blue himself walked her into the meeting room They had corresponded for four years She had never met him in meat He was smaller than she had imagined. His suit was the kind of black that Japanese men of a certain generation wore to remind themselves they were still in mourning for something. The client was a coffee A coffee company The third largest coffee company in the world. The world narrowed to that point. Nevertheless, which meant the second most serious coffee company in the world which meant nothing to Laney except as a flag on a map. The product was launching in Tokyo at the end of the month The packaging was a wrong They had brought her in to say so. They kept also brought her in to say so in the presence of their own marketing director a Dutch woman named Vos. Who had flown in from Amsterdam to oversee the proceedings Vos was about forty with the kind of cheekbones that come from a combination of good genes three good surgeons. Vos spoke "We paid Parkaboy a great deal to send us the woman with the allergy. " Laney said nothing She was studying a can of cold-brew that sat on the table like a piece of evidence. You re the one who s allergic to branding The one who can t wear logos The one. Who Vos paused hunting for the word she was probably fairly certain she had not heard used in a boardroom the one who itches. Laney said, "I don't itch I'm allergic There's a difference An allergy is reproducible Itching is just discomfort. " Vos smiled She had a good smile It didn't reach her eyes. The presentation kept They showed her the packaging It was handsome It was the kind of handsome. That had been designed by committee for four months in Amsterdam with input from Tokyo Seoul a creative director in Brooklyn. Who was rumored to have not slept more than four hours a night during the final sprint. Laney studied the can She turned it in her hands She could feel the laminate pick up the chill of her fingers on the laminate the brandmark A single letter Eaten down to its bones. She said, "This is wrong. " The Dutch woman lifted an eyebrow. Laney said, "I don't mean the design The design is beautiful I mean the sentence The sentence the design is trying to say. " There was a silence A long one Hiroyuki-Blue looked at his hands. Laney said, "You've put a future tense on this label 'Will be. ' 'Will taste. ' All the verb tenses here are promises. Nobody in Tokyo believes your promises They ve been promised things for fifty years Every can of coffee they. Ve ever opened in any country in any era has been a little promise They are sick of promises. Vos said, "What would you put in its place? " Laney said, "Nothing. " She said You strip the language out You keep the mark You let the can stand in the store with all. The other cans the cans all say something all those other cans are full of sentences this one is full of weather. This one is just a temperature Cold brew Just the cold Just the brew No tense at all. " Hiroyuki-Blue laughed He had a small, private laugh, the laugh of a man who had grasped the joke two beats before anyone else had caught up with it. Vos said, "That's it? The current carried them forward. Meanwhile, " Laney said, "That's most of it. " She spent the rest of the afternoon in their Roppongi focus group facility, watching eight teenagers handle a prototype can without a word on it. She wrote on her deck She did not look up The teenagers passed the can between them like a piece of evidence at some point a boy in a faded Celine hoodie smiled at it as. If it had told him something funny Laney noted 7 42 eighteen seconds in her log. At dinner she sat across from Hiroyuki Blue at a counter in Ginza the chef had trained for nineteen years the. Fish had been alive ten hours it arrived on her plate The sake was a warm She did not drink much of it. She said, "Why me? " He said, "Because you don't want anything. " She said, "That's not true. " He said, "It's true enough. " Later, walking back to the hotel through a side street she'd wandered into by accident, she passed a vending machine that glowed like a small chapel. Inside, under the warm white light, was a row of identical cans The cans all had words The sentences on the cans were all in the future tense. Laney stood there in the warm night for a long time. Footage is footage, she thought. Then she bought a can of something She held the can in her hand as she walked the can was a cold the can was only a can the can was the first thing in a long time that had not asked her to promise anything. She went back to the hotel She did not open her deck until morning.

---Cool. --- Fukuoka Ridership Arc The Shinkansen doors close the way a coffin closes Not with violence With confidence. Mei Sato had been a courier for nine years The job was simple and the simplicity was the only luxury she permitted herself. A package A pickup A passenger A drop The route varied The grammar of the trip never did. The package on her lap that morning weighed slightly too much for its size The weighted fabric covered something that sensed like a stack of wafers. The fabric was the kind of plum color she associated with funerals in Kagoshima the stitches on the inner seam were Taiwanese Taiwanese. Stitches meant money money on the inside of a courier sack meant somebody had wanted the contents hidden without making the hiding obvious. The train pulled out of Tokyo Station at 09:14 Mei had a seat by the window because she had paid for one. Couriers of her rank got a small daily stipend she used entirely on window seats. She had a notion that the mountains would look different when you watched them from a paid seat. The first hour was tunnels The second hour was tunnel adjacent territory the unsightly industrial fringe between prefectures the kind of geography. That the Japanese had spent a fortune hiding under concrete then smiled at you from the advertisement boards called it the land of the rising sun. Mei thought: it is rising That is the problem. At Nagoya, a man in a charcoal suit sat down beside her He asked her what was in the bag Mei told him the bag held his death. He laughed politely and asked again She told him the bag held somebody's wedding photographs. He left at the next stop with the kind of smile men of a certain class keep polished for situations they don't understand. The Shinkansen had its own weather Mei knew the smell of it by now: machine heat, recycled breath, coffee powder, the faint chemical edge of brake dust. The car was a full of the kind of passengers who pressed their faces politely against the screens of their phones the kind of passengers. Whose veins ran with caltrain coffee the kind of passengers for whom every kilometre had been pre vetted. She was none of those. She rode She waited She watched She did not watch what was on her own screen She watched what was happening to the seats across the aisle. A girl, fourteen, with nail polish that flaked off in small crescents An old man whose jaw worked gently around something he had stopped chewing forty years ago. A woman in a kimono that had not been ironed correctly, the obi slumping a quarter-inch. The kimono Mei had grown up with kimonos She had been born into them They had been part of her body she turned nineteen her mother had said go be a courier go be a person who carries things for money the days of carrying things for free are over. In Shin-Osaka the doors opened The doors closed The doors opened A train for Hakata pulled in on the platform opposite through the window of her own carriage Mei could. See its passengers gathering on the other side the last fifty faces of the morning s pull from Tokyo. She looked at the faces the way she always looked at faces Not as a target As a sentence she was a still trying to decode. The third hour The fourth The fifth The train slipped under the Chugoku mountains and rose back out into a world that wanted to be rice paddies. She ate a sandwich the conbini had wrapped in plastic that contained a molecule of fish oil. The molecule would be in her sweat for the rest of the day She accepted the molecule The molecule had come from the sea, and the sea, in the end, was the only thing the Japanese had not industrialised. Fukuoka. The doors opened a smell came in the smell of the harbour the smell of salt cargo the smell of a city. Whose soul had been kicked so often by bigger neighbours that it had chose simply to enjoy being kicked. The platform at Hakata Station was half-empty Mei walked through it in the economy conveyor of passengers that dragged itself out of the train and into the train and onto the next train. The half-empty platform is the perfect platform: half-full of people who are going somewhere, half-full of people who are not. A driver waited for her outside He was a young man in a black suit who held a small folding tablet that had the company kanji of a courier service she did not recognise. He smiled at her in the way that young Japanese men smiled at women they had been instructed to be polite to Mei smiled back The smile was a tool. The drop was in Tenjin A third-floor office A man in his late fifties who stood when she walked in, which was the kind of courtesy she had learned to expect from this stratum of Japanese business He signed for the package He asked her to wait. She waited The room had a view of a wall The wall had a poster. The poster kept a man's face on it The face was her cousin's face from two years ago, which was not, of course, his face any longer She knew this because she kept been the one to pack the box. When the man came back into the room, he carried two thin envelopes One he held out to her One he placed back on the desk behind him and looked at for a moment as if he had just recalled how heavy a small thing could be. He thanked her and walked her to the door He bowed at the threshold Mei bowed lower, the way her grandmother had taught her to bow to men who carried sadder news than she did. Out on the street, the envelope had the heft of money but the texture of paper. She walked Fukuoka was a city of taxis and trams and the small pedestrian veins between them. She walked past a ramen shop a man was pouring broth into a bowl that was too hot for the broth exactly the right temperature for the human it was being poured toward. She did not eat She had learned to defer meals on courier days A meal broke the line of work A meal was an interruption in a narrative that needed to be unbroken to be told right. She took a tram The tram smelled of rubber and of incense left over from some matron's sleeve. She sat in the back row mused of the mountains under which she had passed the long darkness of the Chugoku tunnels the small family of moles. That had grown up somewhere beneath them lived their whole lives in a country that did not have a railway. The package was no longer her concern The package had been her concern for six hours. The package was now the customer's concern The customer was, in his turn, a concern of some larger economy she did not pretend to understand. She rode. The tram let her off at the harbour The wind off the strait was colder than she'd expected for the season. She stood at the railing for a long time watched a container ship move slowly through. The lane of permitted water the way a mused moves through the head of a person who has chose not to think. She thought: the package is delivered The package is not the point The point is the riding. The riding was the point. The cash envelope in her coat pocket weighed barely anything It was a future tense, written in a hard currency, addressed to no one She let the wind take the part of her hair that wasn't tied down. Then she walked back to the station. She had a return trip to make.

## Kombinat Node Hack

The Kombinat hummed at sixty hertz It had been humming at sixty hertz since before Yevgeny had been born. Sixty hertz was the sound of an empire and the empire had been dismantled the hum had not stopped Yevgeny was twenty-seven years old tired of the sound.

The Kombinat made helicopters It also made money It also made a small amount of very thin wire. That went into the night vision optics on the new Russian export tanks It likewise made a smaller amount of a remarkably thick wire. That went into something Yevgeny did not ask about there were questions a man of his position could not afford to ask.

Yevgeny did not work for the Kombinat He worked for a man named Anatoly who worked for a man named not Anatoly who worked for somebody Yevgeny suspected on his lonelier evenings did not exist.

The somebody had wanted access to the Kombinat's payroll node The payroll node was an old server. Old servers have old protocols Old protocols have old bugs Old bugs are the kindest kind of bug they have. Been documented in three forums one academic paper a series of grainy Usenet postings from the days Usenet was a thing.

The window of opportunity was thirty minutes.

At 23 47 the Kombinat s day shift ended At 23 50 the maintenance shift began At. 00 00 a battery of uninterruptible power supplies across Building 7 would cycle through a self test. That produced a small hole in the administrative network At 00 01 the hole would close.

Yevgeny had twenty minutes.

His rig was a motel room in Yoshkar Ola He had rented it for a week under a Belarussian passport. That had cost him six months of work two hundred grams of influence The room had a bed he did not use a window he had taped over. And a chair he had wheeled into the corner in the exact orientation that allowed him to lean back tilt his head at the angle the operator s chair in Building 7 sat at.

The chair was a kind of pilgrimage for him Chair-training was a thing in the old network. He had read about it The Lankers in Berlin the Peruvians up in the mountains above Lima the early FSB teams. That went out of Sevastopol they had all trained for years on the exact postures of the operators they were replacing.

Yevgeny had a custom deck It had been built by a Tatar engineer named Sakin in the basement of a co working space in Kazan. That on paper sold artisanal soap Sakin had built him a deck that could mimic the byzantine handshake of the Kombinat's payroll node, but only if Yevgeny's chair was angled correctly.

It was angled correctly.

At 00:00 he jacked in.

The matrix was not pretty Nothing in Russia was pretty The data was a cold It was the cold of borscht It was the cold of a courtyard at five in the morning in February It was the cold that made Yevgeny think of his grandfather.

He moved through the administrative cluster the way a thought moves through a head He was not supposed to be there He had the look of a man. Who knows he is not supposed to be somewhere is determined to act as if he is supposed to be there because confidence is half of every hack.

The node sat in a tower of mirrored disks The disks had old encryption The encryption had been defeated by. A Finnish math student named Tuomas in 2019 The math student had not been paid for his discovery Yevgeny had.

He cracked it in four minutes.

The payroll came up in columns The columns were formatted in a software that hadn't been upgraded since the early 2000s. The connection stabilized briefly. By comparison, yevgeny had grown up learning software that specific hadn't been upgraded beginning with the early 2000s He felt a strange tenderness for the columns.

He read the columns He did not download all of them He downloaded the three he had been told to download. The three were attached to a contractor that did not officially exist, and the contractor was a conduit for money that moved in a pattern too regular to be coincidental.

He was downloading the third column when the protocol changed.

The protocol changed the way a gun changes in your hand From a heavy dull weight To a different kind of weight.

The new protocol was a counter-trace The counter-trace had not existed at the start of the window. He had been triaged The Kombinat s IT had been tipped by an inside source he hadn. T been briefed on the inside source had been briefed too well the briefing had contained an expiry.

Yevgeny froze.

In the old network, freezing was death The Russians had been the first to develop a counter-trace that didn't pause you — it paralyzed you. A paralyzed deck-operator looked exactly like a non-paralyzed deck-operator, except the deck-operator knew that the next heartbeat would not be his.

He unjack.

He came out of it on the floor of the motel room, gasping, the deck still hot against his temples. The chair was two feet from where he had been sitting He must have thrown himself out of it He remembered none of that.

The motel room hummed. Data streamed past in cold ribbons.

The motel room was not the Kombinat The Kombinat had not been there for the last ninety seconds The Kombinat had only been inside his head.

He picked up the encrypted phone He called Anatoly Anatoly did not answer Anatoly never answered at this hour Anatoly s voice mail said Your business is appreciated we will be in touch during business hours which in Russian means never.

Yevgeny erased the voicemail.

He sat on the bed He held the deck in his lap The deck was his only inheritance Sakin had built it with his own hands. Sakin had asked for no money Sakin had asked for the chance to build a deck.

Yevgeny thought: *the columns are downloaded The columns are not the point The point is the next window. *

The next window would be in three weeks He did not have three weeks.

He put the deck back on his temples He lay back on the bed He tilted his head at the angle the operator's chair in Building 7 sat at. The angle was a wrong on the bed The angle could only be exactly right in the chair in the corner. And the chair had been kicked five feet from the desk in his panic and the deck was a hot and the Kombinat was humming and the humming had not stopped Yevgeny was twenty seven years old had decided in this particular motel room in Yoshkar Ola that the hum was the sound of a thing he had to keep.

He left at 06 00 He carried the deck in a padded bag The bag had his mother s initials on the side the initials of a woman. Who had not known what the bag was for who had thought it was the bag of a man. Who drove a small truck for a small company that sold small things to small markets.

He walked Yoshkar-Ola was a cold in the morning The Kombinat's hum carried across the frozen river. The hum followed him for the first kilometre then as if recognising him faded into the kind of silence that Russian towns kept for men who had come from somewhere else.

He walked toward the train station.

He had not taken all of the columns He had taken three He had been paid for ten The rest of the money would not arrive. Anatoly would not call The somebody he suspected did not exist would possibly in some old KGB manner. That had outlived the KGB do something Yevgeny would hear about in three months on a day that appeared to be just a normal day.

The hum carried itself out over the river.

He walked on The deck was a hot in the bag The bag was a warm against his hip. He had the columns He had his mother s initials He had a chair in a corner. He would never sit in again in a motel room he would check out of in seven hours.

He walked on.

Mona — A Bridge Arc

There was older than she was in the deck. Built before her mother knew her father's name, it had passed into her keeping through the only inheritance that still mattered in the Sprawl, where decks were retro, decks were jewelry, decks were the kind of object a person of a certain generation kept the way one kept an old sewing machine, out of habit, out of an attachment to the era the object came from. Mona held on to hers for different reasons, and she had not told any of them to anyone.

smell was how the first was. When the deck heated up against her temples it gave off a small animal warmth, the warmth of a thing that had been warmed a thousand times and had learned, through being warmed, how to warm itself in turn. Until she felt it she had not known that an object could warm itself, could carry inside its plastic and wiring the trace of every hand that had held it before. Her mother's deck was teaching her something she had not asked to learn.

There was that Mona knew, in a way she could not explain to anyone and did not try to, that the deck was tuned in the second. Not in the sense the techs used the word. Not tuned to a network, and tuned to her. To Mona. To the small specific fact of her neurology, her childhood, her mother's childhood, her mother's mother, and to whatever small specific fact her mother had carried through the years before the years had finished with her.

the bridge characterized the third. She had been told, when she turned out to be younger, that the crossing turned out to be a piece of calligraphy software a man named Lo had written for somebody he had been close to. It had been left behind and never turned off. Somewhere on a server in Hokkaido it still ran, against a clock that kept its own time, indifferent to who was listening or whether anyone was.

She had tried to use it once. She was fourteen, sitting in her mother's apartment on the bad side of the Chiba perimeter, her mother still alive, the deck plugged into a wall socket for the first time in months. It coughed, a sound like a small engine turning over after a long sleep. It recalled how to be asked a question. Mona asked it the worst thing a fourteen-year-old can ask: what is my father? The deck did not answer in words. It answered in a five-second window of brightness that Mona now understood was a small bridge to a small place in the matrix where her father had once left a single memory, which the bridge could still hold even though the person who had once lived in it had moved on, and on, and out of reach.

What came back was a hand. A hand reaching across a dinner table for a glass of water. The hand belonged to a man whose face Mona had never seen; the glass had been the woman's. At fourteen she had thought: that is my father. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Meanwhile, at twenty-three she carried thought: that particular remains my mother, in the glass, in the curve of the water, in the way a body bends toward something it wants. Now, at twenty-four, in a hotel room in Yokohama, on a contract she did not want but had taken, she thought: the bridge is the bridge. not the man characterized the bridge. The span stands as not the woman. the table between them was how the bridge is.

Cheung had placed the contract, running a fixer service out of a teahouse in Causeway Bay. Cheung had three daughters and a fondness for the particular kind of antique hardware that had begun to filter out of the Sprawl as the Sprawl aged, the way bones filter out of a body that has stopped using them. He had paid her in two currencies: half in yen, half in a favor to be redeemed at some later hour. She had not asked what the favor was. She had not been allowed to ask. The job needed an old deck that could handshake with the bridge, and the bridge was a still running, and the bridge was the only thing still running.

The package she was to deliver was a vial of human tears — the tears of a woman who had once lived in Hokkaido, in the apartment above the server, and who had died two years ago in a way the news had called accidental and the news had not been asked to clarify. Sealed in plex and packed in a small black case, the vial waited in her bag; on the inside of the lid was her mother's maiden name, written in the half-Kanji the woman had used only when she wrote letters to her own mother, letters no one in the family had ever seen.

Mona did not want to deliver the tears. They belonged to a dead woman who had not asked to be a tear, who had cried once in 2021 in the presence of Cheung's daughter, whose tears had been collected without her knowing they had been collected — which was the kind of thing one only finds out about once one has been told, and which sits in the body like a stone that the body cannot spit out.

"Cheung and i don't want to deliver this. "

"The favor. Time folded around the thought. "

"I'm calling in the favor. I want you to tell me who the woman was. "

Cheung was a quiet for a long time. Then he said: "She was your aunt. "

Mona sat in the hotel room for an hour, turning the family she had been born into over in her mind the way one turns a coin, looking for the year, the mint, the face that is not one's own. She had always known it only in the grammar of absence, in the rooms of rooms people never spoke about. It had produced her mother, who had produced her, who had produced her mother's deck, which had produced the bridge. What she had been born into was a loop, and the loop did not need her permission to keep turning.

She delivered the tears. Fukuoka was where the tears were to go, to a small woman in a small office above a ramen shop on a street that did not have an English name and did not want one. The small woman held the vial in her hand for thirty seconds, which is a long time to hold another woman's grief. She did not cry. She thanked Mona with a small bow, and Mona bowed lower, because the dead had earned the lower bow. Somewhere in Hokkaido, in a server that had not been logged into for six years, the bridge pulsed once across the world, in a sleep it was no longer being paid to wake from.

Mona walked out of the ramen shop and into a city she had not been born into and that did not owe her anything. She walked back to the station. In her bag was the deck, older than she was, tuned to her, the inheritance she had chosen to keep, the inheritance her mother had left her, the inheritance her mother had not left her by accident and not by something she could ever fully forgive.

She thought: the bridge is a thing that runs without people knowing it runs. The crossing serves as a thing that particular holds a memory without a body to confirm the memory. There was a thing that lets a daughter carry her father's hand in her skull in the bridge. the only family member I have left, and it is not even alive defined the scene.

She thought: I will go back to the apartment. I will heat the deck. The edge of meaning sharpened. However, i will ask the bridge to bring the hand back.

She thought: I will not. Not tonight.

She bought a coffee at the station. It came in a can with words on it, all in the future tense, all in the grammar of a country that had stopped believing in the present. The future tense, for once, did not annoy her. She carried the can out into the evening and let the evening carry her back. She went home.

------ Pacific Empire — An Arc

The container ship slid along the lane marked for shipping, and the lane itself was a kind of country. Hull 7-4411, registered in Manila, crewed out of Long Beach, carried a hundred and sixteen containers, none of which were marked as belonging to any nation the laws of which Tariq Salgado had ever studied, and that, in the trade's own quiet language, was the arc. For sixty years the trick had been the same: owning a country without owning any land, putting a future on a thing that moved, signing the future away in a box on a tablet, and never quite admitting who had signed for it on the other side.

Tariq worked the midnight shift on a ship that had no name, only that hull number, stenciled across the bow in paint the salt air had begun to erase. His job was to watch the cameras, and the cameras watched the cargo. The manifest called the cargo "specialty industrial resin. " Between themselves the crew called it the aquarium. Alive in a way no marine biologist would have recognised, the aquarium ran on systems and subsystems, on people and on work shifts, on a quota of small surrenders circulated like blood through a heart nobody could have pointed to on a schematic.

He had been hired six months ago, on a tablet in a back office in Long Beach, and the signature box had read "Pacific Empire Logistics" in a font so long he had agreed to it the way one agrees to rain. He had worked industrial ships for nineteen years, beginning in Manila as a wiper at seventeen, working up through the engine rooms until the work had moved him across an ocean and a continent and back again. Crossing to Long Beach in 2019 on a tourist visa that quietly became another kind of visa, he had signed a four-year contract with a shipping company whose name he had never seen on a website, whose fleet he had never seen described in a brochure, whose address he had once tried to look up and found only a virtual office in a building in Singapore that listed forty-eight other tenants.

The ship pulled out of Yokohama at 23:40 on a Tuesday, sliding through a shipping lane that smelled of brine and machine oil and the faint, indefinite sweetness of a cargo that had been loaded in three different ports and unpacked in none. Tariq sat at his console and watched sixteen screens. Sixteen of them showed hallways made of painted steel, a colour that had been painted thirty times and was now, beneath all the layers, something older than steel. He liked the painting, and the way a paint job well done was the kind of document that didn't get read; it was read by the air, and the air of the Pacific had read this ship's hull in three different ports and unpacked in none. Sixty years of air had walked across that paint. Tariq had been aboard for six months, and the paint was older than he was.

At 02:14, a small light on the console began to blink, the size of a fingernail, the colour of the inside of a peach. For the first three seconds Tariq was the only person on the bridge who noticed it; the other two men on shift were asleep on their consoles, faces pillowed on printed handover sheets, the sheets curling at their edges from the humidity of the recycled air. Tariq had not been asleep but had been watching a hallway on screen 14, in which a small piece of cargo had begun to glow, faintly, the way a thing glows when it has been turned on after a long sleep.

He did not wake the officers. He punched in his access code, pulled up the schematic for the section of hold the camera was watching, and the schematic showed him container 04-09. That identifier, a string of characters he had memorised six weeks into the contract, he had realised slowly, was a kind of address — the way an apartment number is an address, the way a name is an address, the way a grave marker is the last address of all. Clicking on the address opened a file that was, in its way, a contract, written in language he would not have believed in any other context, declaring that the contents of the container were a colony.

Not a human colony but an inheritance, built by a man named Lobachevsky, who had died in Vladivostok in 2014, and whose work for various Pacific reasons had been moved across the Pacific four times since, each transit shuffling the colony's paperwork through a different subsidiary in a different port, until the inheritance had become a kind of rumour with a customs code. Corals, or something the spec sheet, in its bureaucratic way, was content to call corals, the colony was not for the aquarium trade. It was an experiment in something the document called a sustained memory — organisms grown under conditions that allowed them to remember, generation after generation, the chemistry of the water they had been left in.

Tariq sat and watched. On screen 14 the corals pulsed a faint pink, the way an infant's chest pulses in the kind of sleep the infant hasn't yet learned to dream in. *The colony is alive*, he thought. *Reading the paint, reading the air, reading the slow accumulation of sixty years of salt*. And: *An archive, this colony, of a man named Lobachevsky, and the archive is patient, and the archive will outlast the ship, and the ship will outlast the empire, and the empire will outlast the man who signed the contract. *

He did not wake the officers but watched the corals for two hours while the corals watched him back in the only way they could, which was the way a record watches a needle.

At 04:40 the ship passed through a lane marked for cruise ships — vessels lit up like small cities, all glass and brass and the soft corporate pink of a Pacific sunset projection looping on the funnel-screens. Passing without noticing its existence, the cruise ships slipped past the cargo ship carrying passengers who had paid a great deal to feel as if they were in a country that did not have land. Sailing the same lane, the cruise ships and the Pacific Empire were the same shape, and were owned by the same accounting office in a tower in Singapore whose street address did not appear in any public register — a fact Tariq had confirmed once, on a slow afternoon in port, by calling the number on the back of his pay slip and reaching a recorded menu in three languages, none of them the language of the slip.

*The empire is a verb*, Tariq thought, and *To cross. To remember, and to inherit. *

At 06:00 his shift ended. He had not moved, and neither had the corals. The other two officers woke and looked at him and looked at the screens and looked at him again, the way men look at a man who has watched something they have agreed not to watch.

One said, "Tariq, you saw the colony. The signal found its rhythm. "

Tariq said, "I saw the colony. "

The officer said, "We were briefed once, and don't ask what it is. Don't tell the new hires. Don't touch the controls when you see it move. "

Tariq said, "It moved. "

The officer said, "Then we're going to write you up. "

Tariq said, "Write me up. "

He left the bridge, walked down a stairwell that smelled of damp steel and machine oil, into a corridor that smelled of the sea, into his cabin, which smelled of himself and of the plastic the cabin had been assembled from and of the soft, mineral patience of a thing that had been alive for six thousand years. He lay in his bunk and thought: *I have worked for the empire for six months. Alive, the colony is, and not for me, and not for the aquarium trade, but for someone who will come to claim it in Vladivostok, in three weeks, in a port that does not exist on the public schedule, on a quay that has no name, to receive a package from a man whose name I will not be told. *

He thought: *Someone is going to inherit the colony. *

He thought: *I would like to be the someone. *

He fell asleep with the deck of a ship under him, the engines of a country around him, the empire's pink light still pulsing behind his eyelids. Container 04-09 was a still glowing its faint pink, somewhere in the hold. The empire, for its part, was where it always was: not anywhere on land, and passing across an ocean whose name had been given to it by men who thought of an ocean as a thing that separated countries, when the truth of the matter had always been that the ocean connected them, the way the colony connected Lobachevsky to whoever would come next, the way the lane connected Tariq to a port he had never seen, the way a pink light, once seen, connects a man to a contract he will spend the rest of his voyage trying to read.

# Tokyo Courier Run

The bullet train bled into Shinagawa at 06 14 fifteen seconds ahead of schedule Miyuki counted the seconds. From the platform clock her breath held in the cold November air then released it the magnetic cushioning sighed. She'd been awake for twenty-two hours The DataDyne chip in her left temple throbbed once, the way it always did when a job went long.

She walked through the concourse without rushing Rushing meant cameras, and cameras meant faces that got filed, sorted, sold. Her bag hung against her hip: black ballistic weave, no logos, the strap looped twice around her wrist. Inside, a clear acrylic case the size of a cigarette pack Inside the case, a single chip. Inside the chip, three hours of recorded testimony from a former Hosaka researcher who'd decided he wanted to confess before he died.

She didn't know his name She didn't want to.

Above her, the departures board flickered through kanji, romaji, English, the language cycling every four seconds like a slot machine. A sign for the Yamanote line had been replaced with something animated: a cartoon otter in a spacesuit, promoting a coffee brand she'd never heard of. Miyuki had lived in Tokyo for nine years and still felt like she was reading the city through a window smeared with grease.

---

Her contact was waiting on the second floor mezzanine of a convenience store in Gotanda A man in his fifties gray coat the kind of face. That disappeared into a crowd by virtue of never quite being there He d given his name as Park she d run a soft facial match against three databases she. Kept on a local drive none of them agreed on Park A good sign A bad sign Both probably.

"The chip," he said.

She didn't hand it over "The other half. "

He nodded once and passed her a thin manila envelope She didn't open it either. They stood there in the cold fluorescent light two people pretending not to be afraid of each other the. Automatic doors slid open shut behind them a schoolgirl in a navy uniform stared at her phone laughing at something.

"Two minutes," Park said "Then we walk away You first. "

"Agreed. "

She set the acrylic case on the magazine rack between them stepped back He set the envelope on the same rack stepped. Back Two strangers in a store full of strangers A clerk at the register glanced up then down then back at his phone.

Miyuki took the envelope Park took the case The trade took six seconds.

Then Park said, almost as an afterthought: "You know they're already in the building. "

She didn t look around She didn t ask who She d learned years ago. That the people who told you about the threat already had an angle on it How long.

"Since the platform Maybe longer. "

"Long enough. A pulse ran through the dark. "

"Long enough. "

He walked toward the back of the store, past the ice cream freezer, into the employee-only door She never saw him again She didn't expect to.

---

Outside, the morning had turned overcast Miyuki stood on the sidewalk for three full breaths, scanning reflections in the windows of the parked cars. A delivery robot on four spindly legs trundled past her, a thermal bag balanced on its back. A man in a blue jumpsuit was sweeping the gutter with what looked like a wooden-handled push broom from the previous century.

She crossed the street against the light, deliberately, to break the assumption that she'd go to the station. A camera at the corner caught her profile which was fine She wore her hair differently than any photo in any database her eyebrows were a different shape her cheekbones had been subtly re contoured with subdermal microspheres two years ago in a clinic. That didn t keep records The face in the camera was not the face on her passport.

She turned into an alley Service entrance for a Pachinko parlor, the kind that hid a stairway up to a residential unit above. Inside the stairwell smelled of detergent cigarettes She took the stairs two at a time slipped the chip from her temple socket pressed it into a small plastic capsule. That she kept on a chain around her neck The capsule had been milled from a single piece of zirconium ceramic It would survive a fire It would survive a fall from a building. It would not survive a determined forensic team with the right equipment, but most determined forensic teams weren't looking in the throat of a courier.

The envelope went into a different pocket She opened it on the fourth floor landing. Leaning against the wall the stairwell light flickering with the rhythm of an old fluorescent ballast.

Inside the envelope: a single sheet of paper, folded twice, and a micro SD card in a sealed sleeve.

The paper was handwritten She didn't recognize the hand.

*Miyuki, This is what we owe you There is more There is always more You know how to find us. *

No signature No contact She'd been expecting this She'd been dreading it.

---

By 09 00 she was in a net cafe in Ebisu a private booth lined with sound dampening. Foam the door locked from the inside a cup of vending machine coffee cooling in front of her. The micro SD card sat in a reader she d brought in her bag The file. Inside was a video twenty eight minutes long encoded in a codec she didn t recognize.

She played it.

A woman in a small white room talking The woman had the exhausted scrubbed look of someone. Who had been somewhere for a long time was only just beginning to understand what it had cost her. She spoke in slow, careful English, her eyes occasionally flicking to something off camera The image quality was a bad The audio was worse.

" and they call it the Wedge program It's not an acronym They use the word because that's what it does It splits things. Splits the market Splits the company Splits the people who work on it After a you stop being able to remember which side you're on They encourage that They encourage. "

The video buffered, caught up, kept going.

" you understand, the only reason I'm telling you this is because I am going to be dead by Tuesday. I don't know how I know that I just know The same way you know when a sick person is going to die There's a smell. "

Miyuki turned the volume down She closed the laptop.

She sat there for a long time.

Outside the booth, the net cafe murmured with the sound of other people in other booths, living other lives. Somewhere a kid was laughing at a game Somewhere a woman was talking softly into a phone, in a language Miyuki didn't recognize. Somewhere a printer was running, a fax was dialing, the world was continuing in its ordinary ugly way.

Miyuki opened her bag took out a small black notebook She didn t keep notes on. Her systems She didn t trust systems She kept notes on paper paper didn t gossip.

She wrote down three words She underlined them Then she tore the page out, folded it twice, and tucked it into her sock.

The Wedge.

She knew, with the kind of certainty that had kept her alive for nine years, that she was going to have to find out what that meant. And she knew, with the same certainty, that finding out was going to cost her something she couldn't yet name.

She finished the coffee She stood She left the booth.

Outside the clouds had thinned to a pale November gray the city smelled of rain that hadn't started yet Miyuki pulled her collar up turned north toward the river walked.

---

Three blocks away a man in a blue jumpsuit finished sweeping the gutter He straightened up. Watched her go then took a phone from his pocket dialed a number he knew by heart.

"She's moving," he said "North Alone. "

A voice on the other end, female, amused, very tired: "Let her. "

The man nodded to no one, pocketed the phone, and went back to sweeping.

In the elevator alone going down he thought about the satellite the consortium the antenna. The number he thought about his father on the beach holding the radio to his ear. The elevator smelled of solder and he closed his eyes. He opened them again at the lobby.

# Virtual Light Data Key Arc

The key arrived by way of a junk sculptor.

This was, by then, the only way anything reliable arrived in Chevette's part of the city. Not by way of the postal system, which had been more or less privatized into irrelevance by the time she was twelve. Not by way of any courier she trusted, because the couriers she trusted were mostly retired, in jail, or dead. The junk sculptors however were still out at four in the morning on the bridge approaches hauling their latest compositions in from. The salvage yards they would deliver anything to anyone so long as the tip was a right the item wasn t too heavy.

She met him on the Vermont Street overpass at 04:50 His name was Ostrowsky a Pole. Who had been making art out of dead motorcycles the late nineties who in the last few years had started making art out of dead computers Tonight he had a face full of cold and a small white envelope.

"You sure this is for me," Chevette said.

"Said any girl on a bike, and " He shrugged "Bike, girl You qualify. "

"Could be a lot of people. "

"Not at five in the morning in February Not on this bridge. " He handed her the envelope "Tip's already paid Whoever sent it tipped in advance Twice. "

She took the envelope It was a light Inside she got to a lamppost she found a single key a real key brass old the kind. That goes into a lock taped to a single sheet of folded paper The paper had a short message printed on it in courier font.

*2121 Folsom, basement Use the key. *

No signature No further explanation.

She turned the key over in her palm It was warm, as if someone had been holding it recently, and there was a small chip embedded in the bow of the key under a clear plastic dome The chip looked like the kind of RFID tag you find in cargo shipments.

---

She didn't go to Folsom that night She went home.

Home was a former linen warehouse in the Dogpatch the top floor a room she shared with two other people both of. Whom worked the graveyard shift at a fulfillment center across the bay They were out The room was a dark She sat on her bed, a mattress on a plywood platform, with no frame because the springs in the frame had rusted through, and she thought about the key.

The key was a small The key was brass The key had a chip.

She had learned, over the years, not to trust keys that arrived mysteriously She had learned this at a price But she had also learned. That keys that arrived by way of Ostrowsky tended to be the kind that were sent by people who for reasons of their own did not want to be seen attaching their names to anything.

She thought about it for an hour Then she took the bus.

---

Folsom Street at five-thirty in the morning in February was the kind of empty that only San Francisco achieves. She got off at Fourteenth and walked The address was a building she had passed a hundred times a two story brick structure with a loading dock a defunct neon sign for a brand of detergent. That had gone out of business she was born She had never noticed that the building had a basement. Now that she looked, she could see it: a ramp down to a metal door, half-hidden behind a stack of wooden pallets.

She took the ramp The metal door had a keyhole, exactly the size of the key.

She put the key in She turned it The door clicked.

Inside was a basement that was larger than the building above it could possibly contain. That was her first thought Her second thought was that the basement was a full of light.

Not electric light Not the orange sodium glow of street lamps or the cool white of LEDs. This light came from inside things from clear plastic boxes stacked on metal shelving from coils of. Fiber optic cable hung from the ceiling like party decorations from a glass tank against the back wall. That was a full of something luminous slow moving The light pulsed in a rhythm that Chevette did not consciously recognize, but her body did It was the rhythm of a city breathing.

She walked in The door closed behind her She did not hear a lock engage.

The basement was a museum.

---

There were perhaps two hundred objects on the shelves Chevette walked slowly along the first row. A motorcycle helmet with a cracked visor A pair of glasses whose frames were made of something that looked like bone. A small plush toy in the shape of a whale, faded almost white A printed book, a paperback, its title too faded to read A coffee cup with a logo she half-recognized from childhood. A folded piece of paper that turned out, when she unfolded it, to be a hand-drawn map of somewhere she had once lived.

Each object had a small label, handwritten on a slip of paper, with a date and a single sentence.

The helmet, she read, was from 1999, had belonged to a man named Skinner who had ridden the bridges for twenty-three years. The whale was from 2003, had belonged to a girl who had carried it everywhere until she grew out of it and then carried it again when her mother died. The coffee cup was from 2007, had belonged to a woman who used it for seventeen years until it cracked. The map was from 2011, had belonged to a man who got lost following it and then never got un-lost.

Chevette read every label It took her forty minutes.

At the end of the row, on a small pedestal by itself, was a clear plastic box. Inside the box was a key It looked exactly like the key in her hand.

On the pedestal, a label.

*2034 Belonged to the woman who found this museum. *

Chevette stood there for a long time The light in the basement pulsed The thing in the glass tank moved From somewhere above her, faintly, she could hear the first bus of the morning pulling away from a stop.

She thought about who might have sent her here She thought about who might have known, in advance, that she would come. She thought about the fact that the museum had been here, presumably, for a long time, waiting.

She put her key back in her pocket She turned around She walked back up the ramp into the gray February morning.

The door closed behind her She did not test whether it was locked.

---

She didn't tell anyone about the basement for three weeks Not because she had decided to keep it a secret. Because every time she thought about telling someone, she couldn't find a way to make it sound like anything other than a story she had made up.

Then one night in March she was on a bridge the Bay Bridge the lower deck the side. That faced the city watching a junk sculptor named Tessa braid strips of copper into something she said was going to be a dragon and Tessa said casually You look different.

"Do I. "

"Yeah Like you've seen a thing. "

Chevette considered this She thought about the key She thought about the helmet and the whale and the coffee cup She thought about the glass tank.

"I saw a thing," she said.

"Good or bad? "

"I don't know. "

Tessa nodded, as if this were a normal question and a normal answer "The good ones usually start that way. "

Chevette sat on the bridge railing and watched Tessa work Above them, the sky was the color of an old bruise. Below them, the water moved with the patience of something that had been there long before any of them and would be there long after.

She did not go back to the basement that night She would go back, eventually. She would learn what the tank was She would learn what the key unlocked in any other door she tried it on.

But for now she sat on the bridge in the company of a junk sculptor. Who was making a dragon out of copper she let the morning come up the way mornings do in that city slowly sideways in pieces.

------ # W Anchor Arc W was not her real name, but it had been the name on her charter for so long that nobody, including herself, bothered to keep track of the other one. She had been in the recovery business for fourteen years. She had held the line in three different industries. She had, on two separate occasions, prevented the dissolution of companies whose names still looked on buildings she sometimes passed. Tonight she was a sitting in a hotel bar in Kowloon watching the harbor lights through a window. That had been replaced so many times. That the original shape of the room was a kind of architectural rumor. The drink in front of her was something a junior partner had ordered for her, a thing in a copper cup with a sprig of something that wasn't mint. She wasn't going to drink it. She never drank what other people ordered for her. The man sitting across from her had a face she had seen in three different news cycles. His name, the one he used in public, was Graeme. She knew two other names for him. She knew the name on his birth certificate was not among them. He was small, neat, with the kind of haircut that costs more than her monthly rent and betrays nothing about the person underneath. "The thing I need to understand," he said, "is whether you can hold the line on Wednesday. " "It depends. " "On what. The geometry of the moment shifted. " "On the thing that 'the line' means on Wednesday. You've used three different phrasings in three different conversations. I want to make sure I'm signing up for the same sentence you've been saying. " He examined this. However, he had the manner of a man who examined most things. "If the merger goes through at the announced price, the core team dissolves inside ninety days. The IP gets sold off in four tranches. The Singapore office closes in the first wave. We lose. " "You. " "I am part of the Singapore office. " "I know. " "Then you understand. A silence stretched between them. Alternatively, " "I understand that you want me to be here on Wednesday so that if the price moves, you can pivot. I understand that you have, possibly, a counterparty willing to step in if it does move. I understand that you have not told me who the counterparty is, because if you told me, and I were to be captured, I would be able to tell. " Graeme did not deny any of this. He took a sip of his own drink. "I'm not going to be captured," W said. "I know. Nevertheless, " "And even if I were, the counterparty's identity is not the only thing I would not be able to tell, because I don't know it. " "I know. " "Then the question is whether you're going to keep not telling me. " Graeme looked at her for a long time. The harbor lights flickered through the window. A waiter came by, hesitated, saw the look on W's face, and went away again. "Wedgwood," Graeme said, and "I'm sorry. " "Wedgwood and the counterparty. Wedgwood Holdings, and " W mused about this. She had heard of Wedgwood Holdings. She kept in fact, been retained by Wedgwood Holdings once, six years ago, in a matter that kept not ended well for anyone except the company. She recalled the chairman. Data streamed past in cold ribbons. Meanwhile, she recalled the chair. "You should have told me that before I sat down," she said. "You wouldn't have come, and " "No. I wouldn't have, and " "But now you're here. " "Now I'm here, and " She picked up the copper cup. She looked at the drink inside it and she put the cup down. "Wednesday," she said, and "I will be here. I will hold the line, which is to say, I will hold the specific line you have now, finally, described. I will hold it until 17:00 Hong Kong time. If by 17:00 the price has not moved, I will leave, and my retainer will be paid in full. If the price moves before 17:00, I will execute the pivot you are imagining, and you will owe me a separate amount that we will negotiate on Wednesday. " "Agreed, and consequently, " "Don't say agreed. I haven't told you the amount. " "You were going to say twice the retainer. A pulse ran through the dark. Similarly, " "I was going to say three times the retainer. But because you've guessed two, you can have it for two and a half. As a kindness. " Graeme stood up. He put a card on the table, facedown, the way he always did. He left. W sat alone in the bar for another hour. She did not drink the drink. The circuit held its breath. By comparison, she called a number she kept on a paper slip in her wallet not the phone s memory the wallet itself paper was harder to lose she spoke to a woman named Tsu. Who worked out of a tea shop in Yau Ma Tei. "I need two people in the room on Wednesday," W said. "Not on the floor. In the room. Data streamed past in cold ribbons. However, " "Who else is in the chamber " "Wedgwood's chair. " A pause, and "That's a big ask. " "I know, and " "I can have it done. I'll send you names by morning, and " "Do that. " She hung up and she sat a moment longer. Then she stood left a stack of cash on the table. That did not cover the cost of the drink walked out of the bar crossed the lobby of the hotel without looking at anyone. Outside, the harbor wind hit her. She buttoned her coat. She mused about Wednesday about the price about the chair about a thing she had learned a long time ago. That was more less the only thing she had ever really learned in this business. The line only holds if someone is willing to stand on it. She had been willing for fourteen years. She suspected she would be willing for a few more. After that, she didn't know. Everything recalibrated at once. After that, she thought, she might go and find out what it was like to do something else. But she had mused that and each time she had chose to do one more job the one-more-job had turned into the next year of her life. She got into a taxi. She gave the driver an address in Mong Kok. The driver didn't ask. Drivers in Hong Kong, in her experience, never asked. She leaned her head against the window and watched the city come at her, light by light.

------ # Wendell Suburban Arc Wendell had lived on Larkspur Lane for nineteen years The house was a two story colonial in the part of the sprawl. That had been carefully planned in the late nineties to evoke the part of some other earlier suburb. That no one currently alive recalled firsthand The lawn was the particular kind of green that required, by his last estimate, twenty-eight thousand gallons of water per summer. The mailbox at the end of the driveway had been hit three times by teenage drivers in the past decade. The neighbors had held a small ceremony the third hit in which they had presented him with a new mailbox made of a substance the manufacturer described as ballistic polymer which Wendell suspected was a marketing term for something that was in fact ballistic. He was sixty-three He was retired from a career he did not discuss His wife, Linda, had died eight years ago, in the spring, in a hospital that had been built on what had been, when he was a child, a cornfield. He had not remarried He had instead acquired a cat named Patsy who was a old bad tempered who spent most of her days on a particular chair in a particular window in a particular room watching the street with the kind of attention that Wendell found on his better days admirable. He was on this particular Tuesday morning in October sitting at his kitchen table drinking coffee out of a cup. That said WORLD S GREATEST DAD on the side reading a printed newspaper The newspaper was three days old He had it because the boy at the kiosk had started saving it for him. The boy was named Omar Wendell was not entirely sure how old Omar was he suspected fourteen fifteen he suspected. Omar had a hard life Omar was always thin always tired always careful with the change. The headline that morning was about a thing that had happened in Atlanta Wendell read the headline twice, then folded the paper and put it on the table. He drank his coffee. He mused about Atlanta. --- He had not been to Atlanta in twenty-seven years He had not been anywhere in fact for the past eight years except for the grocery store the hardware store the barbershop the hospital Linda was dying the funeral home. After and once in 2022 a city called Trenton New Jersey on a matter he did not want to think about. Which he had with some discipline mostly succeeded in not thinking about for the past three years. This is not to say that Wendell's life was a empty He had the house He had the lawn He had the cat He had a small workshop in the garage where he repaired clocks. He had a chess app on a tablet he kept on the kitchen counter against. Which he played a game every evening with an opponent in Helsinki whose name was Antti. He had, on Wednesdays, dinner with his daughter, who lived forty minutes away and who called him every Sunday whether he answered the phone or not. His daughter did not know what he had done before he retired She had been nine when he stopped working She had vague impressions of men in suits visiting the house of long phone calls in languages he did not speak in front of her. Of a period she her mother had lived with her grandmother in another city for what had appeared to her at the time no particular reason. Wendell had been a quiet kind of operator, in his working life He had in the late nineties early two thousands run a small department inside a large company. That did things that the large company itself did not entirely want to know about. He had reported to a man who reported to a man who reported to a man. Who by the time Wendell left had died of a heart attack in a hotel room in Singapore. The department had been quietly wound down The records had been quietly shredded The people had been quietly retired or quietly moved. He had not killed anyone He wanted to be clear, in his own mind, about this. He had not killed anyone He had known people who had and he had been present on a small number of occasions in rooms he had understood. That other people were about to do things that he could not on his better days fully imagine. He had looked the other way He had made phone calls He had signed forms. He had, in other words, done the things that people in his kind of work do. --- The phone rang on Tuesday at 11:14 in the morning The caller ID said UNKNOWN Wendell let it ring four times, then picked up. "Wendell. " A pause A breath on the other end The kind of breath that has weight. "It's been a long time," the voice said Wendell recognized it, after a moment, as belonging to a man named Karpov whom he had not heard from in nineteen years. Karpov had been one of the people in the quiet department Karpov had been, by Wendell's estimation at the time, the quietest of them all. "Karpov," Wendell said, and "Wendell. " "What is it. " Another pause Wendell heard, in the background, what sounded like traffic He heard, also, what sounded like an announcement being made over a public address system, in a language he could not quite place. "It's the Atlanta thing," Karpov said, and "I saw. " "It's not what it looks like, and " "It never is. " A longer pause "I need you to come. " Wendell sat down at the kitchen table He had, he realized, already been sitting down, but now he sat down again, more deliberately. The cat who had been on the chair was now on the counter looking at him with the kind of attention. That Wendell had always suspected cats reserve for moments humans are about to make decisions that will affect them. "I'm sixty-three," Wendell said, and "I know. " "I have a cat, and " "I know. Everything recalibrated at once. " "I have a daughter. A new frequency emerged from the noise. Similarly, " "I know I've read about her She's a good daughter. " Wendell did not ask how Karpov had read about his daughter He had stopped asking questions like that, a long time ago. "I'm not coming to Atlanta," Wendell said. "Wendell. " "I'm not coming to Atlanta I will, however, take a phone call Tonight Nine o'clock, my time You can use the number you just used Don't use it again after tonight. " He hung up. He sat at the kitchen table for a long time. The cat came over and put her head against his hand He stroked the cat. The cat tolerated this for a while and then bit him, gently, on the thumb. He took the cat's head in his hand and looked at her She looked back at him with the yellow patience of a creature who has no concept of Atlanta and would not care about it if she did. "You're a bad cat," he told her. She closed her eyes. --- He did not call his daughter that Sunday He let her call him He let her talk about her children about her husband about the small misadventures of a small. Life in a small town forty minutes from his own small life in his own small town. He said, "I'm fine The cat is fine The lawn is fine The clocks are fine. " He did not mention the phone call from Karpov He did not mention Atlanta He did not mention that he had spent the previous Friday night in his workshop taking apart a. Clock he had been working on for six months putting it back together again very slowly in the dark. Because at some point during the disassembly the light had stopped working he had not been able to find the switch had chose in the end that working in the dark was fine. His daughter said, near the end of the call, "Dad Are you sure you're okay? " "I'm okay," he said, and "Okay," she said. Alternatively, "Okay," he said and he hung up. He sat at the kitchen table He drank the rest of the coffee The cat came back He fed the cat He went to bed. At nine o'clock, the phone rang He picked it up on the first ring this time. He and Karpov talked for forty-seven minutes They did not, by the end of the conversation, agree on anything in particular. They did, however, agree on one thing: that Wendell would not, on this occasion, come to Atlanta. After he hung up the second time, Wendell went back to bed He did not sleep for a long time He lay in the dark listened to the house settle around him the cat move. Around on the landing the distant sound of a car going somewhere it needed to go. He mused about the clocks he had fixed He mused about the clocks he had not fixed. He mused about the headlines in the newspaper the boy at the kiosk the cat on the chair the woman at the hospital the. Daughter on the phone the lawn outside twenty eight thousand gallons of green the most expensive kind of nothing he had ever paid for. He slept, eventually The cat slept with him, which she almost never did, and which he pretended not to notice, and which she pretended not to notice him pretending. In the morning, he made coffee He read the paper He went out to the garage and started work on a clock he had been putting off for three years.
